topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 2-D shapes
topic.description: Recognise and name common 2-D shapes (circles, triangles, rectangles including squares)
evidence: Name a triangle, circle, rectangle, and square when shown them
Identify a shape correctly regardless of its size or orientation
Pick out all the triangles from a mixed set of shapes
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} point to shapes around the house — like a clock, a window, or a pizza — and correctly name whether each is a circle, triangle, rectangle, or square?

pedagogy.summary: Recognising and naming 2-D shapes is the entry point to geometry, but the real target is recognition by DEFINING FEATURES (a triangle is a closed figure with three straight sides) rather than by matching a single remembered picture. Young children form each shape category around a visual PROTOTYPE — an equilateral, horizontal-based triangle; a long, brick-like rectangle — and judge new figures by how much they resemble it. So they reliably name prototypes but reject perfectly valid non-prototypical shapes (long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down triangles; a tilted square they call a 'diamond'). It is taught well by presenting many VARIED examples (different sizes, orientations, proportions, colours) alongside carefully chosen NON-examples, naming them precisely, and asking the child to say WHY.
bestPractices: Present many varied examples of each shape — different sizes, orientations, colours and proportions (fat, thin, tilted) — shown together, so identity is built from features rather than one prototype.
Pair examples with NON-examples ('is it or not? — and how do you know?'), e.g. an unclosed figure or one with a curved side, so the child has to name the defining feature.
Include non-prototypical and rotated cases from the start (a tilted square, a long-thin scalene triangle, a triangle pointing down), because these are exactly the ones children wrongly reject.
Name shapes precisely and model the reasoning ('this is a triangle — three straight sides, all joined up'), while accepting informal language ('pointy', 'fat triangle') as a bridge to correct terms.
Have children sort and pick out ALL of one shape from a mixed set and justify the borderline cases — the sorting surfaces the prototype and orientation errors for the teacher.
keyRepresentations: A set of varied exemplars of one shape (many sizes/orientations/proportions) displayed together
Example / non-example pairs ('is it or not?')
Feature cues: 'closed', 'straight sides', counting the sides and corners
Shape sort / shape hunt (find all the triangles in the room)
commonMisconceptions: Judges a shape only against a visual prototype: accepts the equilateral, horizontal-based triangle but rejects long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down triangles (non-prototypical TYPES are hardest — about half of children miss isosceles and right triangles).
Treats ORIENTATION as if it defines the shape: a square rotated 45° is called a 'diamond' not a square; a triangle without a horizontal base is rejected.
Names by overall resemblance to an object (a 'roof', a 'mountain') rather than by counting straight sides and corners.
Uses 'diamond' for a rotated square, rhombus or kite — there is no 2-D shape called a diamond.

learn.summary: Help 4–6-year-olds recognise and name common 2-D shapes (circle, triangle, rectangle, square) by their DEFINING FEATURES — a triangle is a closed figure with three straight sides — rather than by matching a single remembered 'prototype' picture. Young children build each category around a prototype (an equilateral, horizontal-based triangle; a long, brick-like rectangle) and wrongly reject valid non-prototypical cases (long-thin, right, obtuse or point-down triangles) and mis-name a tilted square as a 'diamond'. Teach with many VARIED examples (sizes, orientations, proportions, colours) shown together, carefully chosen NON-examples, precise naming, and asking the child to say WHY each figure is or isn't the shape.

activities.title: Catch every triangle (varied-case shape hunt)
feedback: When a correct triangle is chosen, confirm the feature: 'Yes — three straight sides, all joined up, so it's a triangle.'

Optional interaction (not required): a correct tap glows green; the caught triangles then slide together and gently morph between one another — huge, tiny, tipped over — while the label 'triangle' stays, making the shared family visible. If used, keep the label fixed so it reads as 'all the same family', not 'one shape turning into another'.
If a curved-sided or unclosed near-miss is chosen, point out the specific feature: 'This side is curved / these lines don't meet, so it isn't a triangle.'
If a long-thin or point-down triangle is skipped, count its three straight sides together and confirm it counts just like the tidy one.
activities.rationale: Recognition by feature is learned by DECIDING across many varied cases and getting feedback tied to the defining property; including non-prototypical and rotated cases from the start targets exactly the figures children wrongly reject, and near-miss non-examples force attention to straightness and closure.
sourceClaims: Young children identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-based) triangle at very high rates (93-96%) but non-prototypical TRIANGLES are much harder: identifying triangle TYPES was hardest (about 48.5% missed the isosceles and 51.2% the right triangle; only ~30.5% got all three), followed by ORIENTATION (rotated triangles), and children rely on 'imposed attributes' such as a horizontal base being treated as if it defined the shape; the recommended remedy is exposing children to typical AND atypical examples plus non-examples in varied sizes, types and orientations.

Children perceive/discriminate shapes and can learn names early, but naming is superficial; the real goal is analysing shapes by defining properties (a triangle must have three sides and be closed) that are invariant over changes in size, orientation and colour, achieved by exposing children to non-prototypical examples and teaching the properties explicitly rather than labels alone.

NCETM lists as common early errors that children think only regular triangles are triangles and only brick-like rectangles are rectangles (shapes defined by their image, not properties) and that squares are only squares when the bottom is horizontal (defined by orientation); it recommends ensuring children see a range of examples of triangles and rectangles in different orientations, sizes, colours and materials.
learnerActions: Look at a field of many shapes that mixes tidy triangles with long-thin, tilted and point-down triangles, plus near-miss non-examples such as a figure with one curved side and three lines that do not quite close.
Tap/pick out every triangle you can find, including the ones that look unusual.
After choosing, say for one of the unusual ones WHY it is a triangle (e.g. 'three straight sides, all joined up').
Say why a near-miss is NOT a triangle (its side is curved, or it isn't closed).
activities.intendedInsight: Sameness of a shape lives in its features — three straight sides and a closed figure — not in its size, proportions, or which way it points. A long, thin, upside-down triangle belongs to the same family as the tidy one.

activities.title: Is it or not? — and how do you know?
feedback: Accept informal language ('pointy', 'fat triangle') as a bridge, then restate precisely: 'Yes — pointy because it has corners where straight sides meet.'
If a child names by resemblance ('it's a roof/mountain'), shift attention to counting straight sides and checking closure by tracing each side with a finger.
Model the reasoning yourself on one case: 'This is a triangle — three straight sides, all joined up.'
When a borderline case is justified correctly, name the feature the child used so it becomes reusable.
activities.rationale: The explicit decide-and-explain routine (drawing shapes and asking children whether each is or is not the shape, and why, using defining properties and correct names) is a recognised early-geometry activity; sorting and picking all of one shape surfaces prototype and orientation errors for the teacher.
sourceClaims: In the Clements & Sarama learning-trajectories approach the early 2-D level is 'Shape Recognizer — Circles, Squares, and Triangles', and a recommended activity is 'Is it or not?' where a teacher draws shapes and children decide whether each is or is not (e.g.) a circle and EXPLAIN why, using defining properties (straight sides, corners) and correct names.

Children perceive/discriminate shapes and can learn names early, but naming is superficial; the real goal is analysing shapes by defining properties (a triangle must have three sides and be closed) that are invariant over changes in size, orientation and colour, achieved by exposing children to non-prototypical examples and teaching the properties explicitly rather than labels alone.
learnerActions: For each figure the teacher shows or draws, decide: is this a triangle (or circle, rectangle, square) — yes or no?

Say out loud which feature makes you sure: count the straight sides, check it is closed, and point to each corner (for rectangles and squares, also check the corners are square corners, and for a square that all four sides are the same length).
Work through deliberately tricky cases: an unclosed figure, a figure with a curved side, a tilted square, and a triangle with no horizontal base.

Sort a mixed set of cut-out shapes into groups and justify the borderline cases. (The cut-outs are thin cards that stand in for the flat shapes we mean — look at the outline, its sides and corners, not the card's thickness.)
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding and explaining — not just naming the obvious prototype — is what reveals and repairs prototype and orientation thinking. The reason ('three straight sides, closed') matters as much as the answer.

activities.title: Turn the same shape (orientation does not change identity)
feedback: If the child calls the tilted square a 'diamond', rotate it back and forth and ask them to count sides and corners each time: 'Same four equal straight sides, four square corners — still a square, just turned.'
Confirm correct reasoning: 'You said the sides didn't change when it turned — that's exactly right.'
Optional: rotate the SAME physical cut-out rather than swapping pictures, so the child sees the one object simply turning.
Reinforce that a triangle does not need a horizontal base to be a triangle.
activities.rationale: Treating orientation as defining ('imposed attributes' such as a horizontal base, or naming a rotated square a 'diamond') is a documented error; rotating a single invariant object directly addresses it by showing the defining features are unchanged.
sourceClaims: NCETM lists as common early errors that children think only regular triangles are triangles and only brick-like rectangles are rectangles (shapes defined by their image, not properties) and that squares are only squares when the bottom is horizontal (defined by orientation); it recommends ensuring children see a range of examples of triangles and rectangles in different orientations, sizes, colours and materials.

Young children identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-based) triangle at very high rates (93-96%) but non-prototypical TRIANGLES are much harder: identifying triangle TYPES was hardest (about 48.5% missed the isosceles and 51.2% the right triangle; only ~30.5% got all three), followed by ORIENTATION (rotated triangles), and children rely on 'imposed attributes' such as a horizontal base being treated as if it defined the shape; the recommended remedy is exposing children to typical AND atypical examples plus non-examples in varied sizes, types and orientations.
learnerActions: Hold one cut-out square and slowly rotate it: at each turn answer 'Is it still a square now? And now?' (The card is a thin stand-in for the flat square — watch its outline, not its thickness.)
Check that the number of straight sides and corners does not change as the shape turns.
Rotate a triangle until its point is at the bottom and confirm it is still a triangle.
Notice that a square turned 45° is still a square. 'Diamond' is an everyday word, not the mathematical name for this shape, so we call it a square.
activities.intendedInsight: Turning a shape does not change what it is; identity is invariant over orientation because the sides and corners stay the same. 'Diamond' is an everyday word, not the mathematical shape name — a rotated square is still a square.

activities.title: Sort-and-justify check (tricky cases)
feedback: Reward the reason, not just the sort: 'Correct — and you knew because it had three straight sides, closed.'
If a tilted square is excluded as a 'diamond', return to rotating the cut-out, counting sides/corners and checking the four sides are equal and the corners are square corners.
Keep illustrations unambiguous — straightness and closure must be visually clear, as drawn shapes can be evocative rather than exact.
If a curvy near-miss is placed with the triangles because it 'looks pointy', retrace its curved side together.
activities.rationale: An include/exclude sort with tricky wrong options built from prototype and orientation errors can surface the exact misconception; because it works as an assessment-style check, keep the defining features unambiguous in any artwork and follow correct answers with a 'why' (sorting alone shows the choice, not whether the child reasoned from features).
sourceClaims: Young children identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-based) triangle at very high rates (93-96%) but non-prototypical TRIANGLES are much harder: identifying triangle TYPES was hardest (about 48.5% missed the isosceles and 51.2% the right triangle; only ~30.5% got all three), followed by ORIENTATION (rotated triangles), and children rely on 'imposed attributes' such as a horizontal base being treated as if it defined the shape; the recommended remedy is exposing children to typical AND atypical examples plus non-examples in varied sizes, types and orientations.

learnerActions: Drag or place figures into 'triangle' and 'not a triangle' groups, where the 'triangle' group must include long-thin and point-down positives and the 'not' group includes a curved-sided near-miss.
Answer 'Which of these are still squares?' when one option is a tilted (correct) square.
For each tricky choice, give the feature-based reason.
Transfer: find another triangle that looks very different from the first but is still a triangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A child who reasons from features will accept non-prototypical positives AND reject near-miss non-examples for the right reason; the 'how do you know' part distinguishes feature reasoning from prototype or object reasoning.

constraints: The learning target is deciding-and-justifying on new, varied cases; a static display showing one shape in many guises (e.g. a wall-card where tapping a fat/thin/tilted/upside-down triangle reveals 'three straight sides — still a triangle') is a useful reference and scaffold but does not rehearse the act of deciding on fresh figures.
Recognition-only responses (tapping or sorting without a stated reason) do not show whether the child reasons from features; always pair the choice with 'how do you know?'
Include non-prototypical and rotated cases from the start — these are exactly the figures children wrongly reject, so leaving them until 'later' hides the misconception.
Accept informal language ('pointy', 'fat triangle') as a bridge but model and expect precise terms ('three straight sides', 'closed', 'corners').
Keep any drawn or on-screen figures clear enough that straightness and closure are unambiguous; illustrations are evocative, not exact.

Paper/card cut-outs have slight thickness and can be held and turned; they are thin models of the flat (ideal, zero-thickness) shape. Use them as approximations and ask the child about the shape REPRESENTED by the outline (its sides and corners), not about the physical card.
'Diamond' should not be used as a 2-D shape name for a rotated square, rhombus or kite; name the actual shape.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source statistics (e.g. ~48.5% missed isosceles, ~51.2% missed right triangles, 93–96% prototype identification) are carried from the cited row claim and have not been re-checked against the original study.

The original row asserted a conversation format 'cannot rehearse the visual decide-and-justify act' and that a third dimension 'adds load and misleads' — these are catalog fit judgements, not established necessity claims, and have been softened to scope: a spoken decide-and-explain routine is in fact used here (the 'Is it or not?' activity is partly verbal), and 2-D focus is chosen because the target shapes are planar, not because other media teach nothing.
The claim that a static image 'cannot teach' the target has been reframed as a scaffold limitation (it does not rehearse deciding on new cases) rather than an absolute.

The original characterised recognition for this age as purely 'perceptual sorting'; that absolute was not propagated. A sort may check or surface classification but does not itself elicit the child's spoken reasoning, which is why every choice is paired with 'how do you know?'.

No arithmetic, force/motion, or physics-modelling content appears in this topic. The only idealisation point is that paper/card cut-outs have slight thickness and model the flat ideal shape; this is stated in the two handling activities and in constraints, and child-facing prompts ask about the shape represented by the outline, never whether the card can be picked up.

probeDeeper: If I turn this triangle upside down, is it still a triangle? How do you know?
Here is a shape with three sides but one of them is bent — is it a triangle? Why not? (counterexample forcing 'straight')
How many straight sides does a triangle have? Point to each one and check it's joined up.
Find me another triangle that looks really different from this one but is still a triangle. (transfer)
assess.correctAnswer: Picks every triangle regardless of size, proportion or orientation (including the long-thin and point-down ones), leaves out the circle, the tilted square and the curved-sided near-miss, and justifies by the defining feature — 'it has three straight sides and it's closed' — not by how it looks or which way it points.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only the 'proper' equilateral, point-up triangle counts as a triangle; long-thin, right, obtuse or point-down ones are rejected ('that's too thin/pointy the wrong way to be a triangle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show many varied triangles together and count the three straight sides on each; run 'is it or not?' with the child saying which feature makes each one a triangle.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is not a triangle — it is too long and thin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks only the tidy horizontal-based triangle from the set and leaves the long-thin and point-down triangles behind; research finds about half of children miss isosceles and right triangles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats orientation as defining ('imposed attribute'): a tilted square is a 'diamond', a triangle 'must' sit on a flat/horizontal base
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the SAME cut-out slowly — 'is it still a square now? and now?' — so the child sees the sides and corners do not change when it turns.
errorPatterns.distractor: That one is a diamond, not a square.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the tilted square (calls it a diamond) or the point-down triangle; reasons from which way it points rather than its sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names by resemblance to a familiar object rather than by features, so a non-triangle that 'looks pointy' is wrongly accepted or a valid triangle that doesn't match the object is rejected
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shift attention from the whole look to counting straight sides and checking the figure is closed; trace each side with a finger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies 'it's a triangle because it looks like a roof/mountain' and then mis-sorts the curved-sided near-miss into the triangle pile.

responseLevels.gap: Names only the prototypical shape; rejects tilted, long-thin or point-down triangles, or calls a tilted square a diamond; justifies by looks or orientation, and may accept a curved-sided near-miss.
responseLevels.full: Identifies each shape across size, proportion and orientation including non-prototypical cases, rejects near-miss non-examples, and justifies by the defining feature ('three straight sides, closed') — transferring the reasoning to a new, unfamiliar example.
responseLevels.partial: Names varied shapes correctly in familiar orientations and can count sides, but still slips on a strongly non-prototypical or rotated case, OR picks correctly yet cannot say why (gives the label without the defining feature).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a mixed set of cut-out shapes including a tidy triangle, a long thin triangle, a triangle turned so its point is at the bottom, a tilted square, a circle, and a near-miss with one curved side. Say: 'Show me all the triangles.' Then point to the point-down triangle and to the curved-sided near-miss in turn and ask: 'How do you know this one is / isn't a triangle?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who recognises by defining features picks the long-thin and point-down triangles AND rejects the curved-sided near-miss for the right reason; a prototype-bound child picks only the tidy triangle, rejects the others, and may accept the curvy one because it is 'pointy'. The 'how do you know' tier is decisive: 'three straight sides, closed' versus 'it looks like a triangle' or 'it points the right way'.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Building & Drawing Shapes
topic.description: Model shapes by building from components (e.g. sticks and clay balls) and by drawing
evidence: Build a triangle from three sticks and three clay balls
Draw a recognisable rectangle
Construct a cube from straws and connectors
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} build or draw a shape they've been shown — for example, making a cube from folded paper or copying a triangle onto dot paper?

pedagogy.summary: Children model shapes two ways: BUILDING them from components (sticks/straws as edges, clay balls/connectors as vertices) and DRAWING them. The procedural work turns attribute knowledge into action — knowing a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners means reaching for 3 sticks and 3 balls and joining them into a CLOSED loop; building a cube means coordinating 12 edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces into a genuine 3-D frame rather than a flat square. It is the doing counterpart of the informal-analysis topic, and it exposes whether a child truly holds a shape's structure. Best taught by naming the attributes and counting the parts before building, insisting on closure, and drawing straight sides on supportive grids.
bestPractices: Name the attributes first and count the components before building ('a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners, so 3 sticks and 3 balls'), then check the finished shape against a real one.
Insist every corner is joined so the figure is CLOSED; an open V is not yet a triangle.
For the cube, build one square face then raise vertical edges to a second square, so children feel a solid is more than a single face (6 faces, not 1).
Support accurate drawing with dotted paper, geoboards or a straight edge, marking each side as it is drawn.
Ask for a non-prototypical version (a long thin triangle, a tall rectangle) so building/drawing is driven by attributes, not a single remembered picture.
keyRepresentations: Sticks/straws (edges) and clay balls/connectors (vertices) for building frames
Geoboard and dotted paper for constructing straight-sided closed figures
A real triangle/cube to compare the built model against
One square face raised into a cube frame to show the 2-D→ 3-D step
commonMisconceptions: Uses the wrong number of components — grabs 4 sticks for a triangle, or the wrong count of straws/connectors for a cube — not matching parts to the shape's attributes.
Leaves the figure OPEN or makes wobbly/curved sides, so the corners don't join into a closed shape.
Builds a cube flat as a single square or a laid-out cross, not raising it into a closed 3-D frame.
Draws only the prototypical wide, horizontal rectangle (or rounds the corners) and cannot draw a tall or tilted one.

learn.summary: Children model shapes two ways: BUILDING them from components (sticks or straws as edges, clay balls or connectors as vertices) and DRAWING them. This procedural work turns attribute knowledge into action — knowing a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners means reaching for 3 sticks and 3 balls and joining them into a CLOSED loop; building a cube means coordinating 12 edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces into a genuine 3-D frame rather than a flat square. It is the 'doing' counterpart of describing and analysing shapes, and it exposes whether a child truly holds a shape's structure. Teach by naming the attributes and counting the parts before building, insisting on closure, and supporting straight drawn sides with grids or a straight edge.

activities.title: Build a triangle from counted components
feedback: If the child grabs 4 sticks, pause and re-count against the named attributes: 'how many sides does a triangle have? So how many sticks?'
If an open 'V' is left, point out the corners do not all join: an open V is not yet a triangle — close the loop.
If sides are wobbly or curved, support straight sides and ask whether a triangle's sides are straight.
For the non-prototypical build: 'Good — a long thin one is still a triangle because it still has 3 straight sides and 3 corners.'
activities.rationale: A polygon is a closed 2-D figure of straight sides meeting at vertices; counting each side and vertex and insisting on closure matches the structure children must coordinate when building. Producing a non-prototypical triangle checks whether the build is attribute-driven rather than copied from a single image.
sourceClaims: A polygon is a closed 2-D shape made of straight sides meeting at vertices; children should count each side/vertex once and are supported by marking each as they go — grounds the 'closed, right number of straight sides' requirement when drawing/building.
learnerActions: Name the attributes aloud first: 'a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners, so I need 3 sticks and 3 balls.'
Count out exactly 3 sticks and 3 clay balls before joining anything.
Join the sticks at the balls into a CLOSED loop so every corner meets.
Check the finished model against a real triangle.
Then make a different triangle — a long thin one — so the build is driven by the attributes, not one remembered picture.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's attributes tell you which parts to gather and how to join them; a triangle must be a closed figure of 3 straight sides meeting at 3 corners, and many different triangles satisfy that.

activities.title: Draw a rectangle (and a non-canonical one)
feedback: If corners are rounded, point out that a rectangle has square corners where two straight sides meet, not curves.
If there is a gap, show the figure is not yet closed and the last corner needs joining.
If only the wide horizontal version is produced, challenge: 'Can you draw a tall thin rectangle?' and confirm it still counts because it is closed, with four straight sides and four square corners.
activities.rationale: Dotted paper, geoboards and a straight edge support accurate straight-sided closed figures; marking each side as it is made helps children track the count. Asking for a non-prototypical rectangle targets the common misconception of drawing only the wide horizontal case. The 'closed, four straight sides and four square corners' description is a deliberately simple age-5-6 working definition rather than a full formal one.
sourceClaims: A polygon is a closed 2-D shape made of straight sides meeting at vertices; children should count each side/vertex once and are supported by marking each as they go — grounds the 'closed, right number of straight sides' requirement when drawing/building.
learnerActions: Draw a recognisable rectangle on dotted paper or a geoboard, marking each side as it is made.
Use a straight edge to keep each of the four sides straight and join the four corners so the figure is closed.
Then make a tall rectangle (longer than it is wide) or a tilted one, not only the wide horizontal version.
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle is a closed figure with four straight sides and four square (not rounded) corners; a tall or tilted rectangle is just as valid as the familiar wide one.

activities.title: Build a cube frame: from one square to a solid
feedback: If straws are laid flat into a single square or a cross/plus shape, show that a cube rises into 3-D — build one square, then raise vertical edges to a second square on top.
If the edge or vertex count is wrong, re-count together against a real cube: 'how many square faces should a cube have? Not 1 — find all six squares.'
Confirm success by checking the frame has 12 edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces (the six square openings) and stands as a solid (an optional screen tally may show the same).
activities.rationale: Properties of 3-D shapes are faces (each a 2-D shape), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where edges meet); a cube has 6 square faces. Handling and marking real solids supports getting these counts right, and the hardest step is coordinating this structure while raising a flat face into a solid — so building one square then raising it directly targets the 'a cube is not just a square' misconception. Note that a stick-and-ball frame is a skeleton: its 6 'faces' are the square openings the edges enclose, not solid surfaces. The built frame (real sticks and balls, which have slight thickness) and any on-screen frame are MODELS of the mathematical cube, whose edges and vertices are ideal and thicknessless; the structure (12 equal edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces), not the material, defines the shape.
sourceClaims: Properties of 3-D shapes are the faces (each a 2-D shape), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where edges meet); a cube has 6 square faces — grounds the edge/vertex/face structure a child must coordinate when building a triangle (3 edges/3 vertices) or a cube from components.

3-D shapes can be described and sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices); handling and marking real solids supports getting these counts right — supports checking a built cube frame against the correct edge/vertex count.
learnerActions: Using sticks that are all the same length, build one square face first from 4 sticks and 4 balls.
Raise 4 vertical sticks from the corners of that square (adding 4 more balls at their tops).
Cap them with a second square on top, so the flat face lifts into a solid frame.
Count the finished frame: 12 edges (sticks), 8 vertices (balls) and the 6 square faces — in a skeleton frame these are the six square openings the edges enclose.
Compare against a real cube and check the counts match.
activities.intendedInsight: A cube is more than a single square: it is a 3-D frame of 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, built by raising one face to a second.

constraints: Building and drawing are active production tasks: the learner must assemble components or draw the figure, not just recognise or tap a finished picture.
Closure is a required outcome, not a stylistic preference: an open figure (an unjoined V, a rectangle with a gap) does not yet count as the shape.

Checking whether a drawing is closed, with four straight sides and four square corners, can confirm the rectangle task, but it does not let a child build a frame or verify edge/vertex counts — use it only as a complement to hands-on building.

Physical sticks-and-balls and clay are central; an optional on-screen snap-together builder (with a live edge/vertex/face tally that only 'sets' when the frame closes, and an open shape that refuses to set) can make closure and counting feel concrete, but is a complement to real materials, not a replacement. Treat both the screen frame and the physical frame as models of the mathematical solid — real sticks and balls have slight thickness, while the ideal cube's edges and vertices are thicknessless.
The cube step (2-D face raised into a 3-D solid) is the hardest to coordinate and benefits most from genuine 3-D handling; a flat picture or 2-D-only tool makes this step harder to feel.
A real triangle and a real cube should be available to compare the built models against.

It is retained for age-appropriateness, with 'square corners' used to rule out rounded ones; fuller right-angle formalism is deliberately deferred.

A stick-and-ball cube is a wireframe with no solid surfaces: its '6 faces' are the square openings bounded by the edges. This modelling approximation is now stated in the cube activity and feedback, not only here.

Original materials describe clay 'balls' and stick 'edges' as approximations of ideal vertices and edges. Real sticks and balls have thickness; the built frame models the mathematical solid rather than being it — stated in the cube activity and constraints as well as here.

The source framed a 3-D interactive as the single 'ideal' and other media as 'poor'/'possible'. Comparative-efficacy and necessity claims are not established by the available sources, so this rewrite presents hands-on building and optional screen models as complementary rather than ranking them.
The original 'adds nothing' dismissal of in-role/conversation formats is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been removed.

probeDeeper: How many sticks did you use? How many corners (balls)? Is that right for a triangle?
Is your shape closed — do all the corners join up?
Can you make a triangle a different way — a long thin one?
Your cube — how is it different from just one square? How many square faces should it have?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) A closed triangle — 3 sticks joined at 3 balls. (2) A recognisable rectangle — a closed figure with four roughly-straight sides and four corners (longer than wide is fine). (3) A cube frame of 12 straws (edges) and 8 connectors (vertices) forming 6 square faces. The child selects the right number of parts and closes the shape, using its attributes to guide the build.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong number of components — grabs four sticks for a triangle, or the wrong count of straws/connectors for a cube — not matching parts to the shape's attributes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the attributes first ('a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners → 3 sticks, 3 balls') and count the parts before building; compare the finished model against a real shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The built shape has the wrong number of sticks (edges) or balls (vertices) for the named shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the figure OPEN or makes wobbly/curved sides, so the corners don't join into a closed shape.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: check that every corner is joined so the shape is closed, and support straight sides with a straight edge or dotted paper.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The sticks don't meet to close the loop; the drawn rectangle has a gap or curved, wandering sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a cube flat as a single square or a laid-out cross, not raising it into a closed 3-D frame.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build one square face, then show it needs vertical edges rising to a second square on top; count that a cube has 6 faces, not 1, and 12 edges.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For the cube, lays straws flat into a square or a plus-shape rather than building up into a solid frame.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the wrong number of components, leaves figures open, or lays a cube flat as a single square; drawings are rounded or unrecognisable.
responseLevels.full: Selects the correct number of sticks/balls or straws/connectors from the shape's attributes, closes the figure with roughly straight sides, builds a genuine 3-D cube frame (12 edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and can produce a non-prototypical version (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Builds and draws recognisable shapes for the familiar prototypical case (a wide rectangle, one triangle) but miscounts components on the cube, leaves gaps, or cannot build/draw a non-canonical version (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three tasks and watch how the child works: (1) 'Use these sticks and balls to make a triangle.' (2) 'Draw a rectangle.' (3) 'Now build a cube with these straws and connectors.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Building and drawing are direct performances of attribute knowledge: a child who knows a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners reaches for 3 sticks and 3 balls and joins them into a closed loop, while one who does not adds extra parts, leaves the figure open, or makes a non-rigid shape. The cube build in particular reveals whether the edge/vertex/face structure is held or whether the child collapses a solid into a single flat square. Watching the making — not asking about it — shows which.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Combining Simple Shapes
topic.description: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes (e.g. two triangles make a rectangle)
evidence: Join two triangles to make a rectangle or larger triangle
Use pattern blocks to fill a hexagon outline
Create a picture or design by combining basic shapes
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} fit smaller shapes together to make bigger ones — like combining two triangles to make a rectangle?

pedagogy.summary: Children compose simple shapes into larger ones — two triangles into a rectangle or a bigger triangle, pattern blocks into a hexagon, basic shapes into a picture. The deep idea is PART-WHOLE: separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity. Clements & Sarama's composition learning trajectory charts the growth from a Piece Assembler (each shape a separate part, trial and error) through the Picture Maker (combines pieces but does NOT anticipate the new shape, matches side lengths not angles) to the Shape Composer (anticipates the fit — 'I know what will fit' — using angles and intentional rotation/flip). Best taught with a graded sequence of pattern-block and tangram puzzles moving from fully-outlined to open, teaching roughly one trajectory level above the child's current one.
bestPractices: Use a graded sequence of pattern-block/tangram puzzles — from fully-outlined (placement shown) to open (child must compose accurately) — as the core activity, pitched about one level above where the child is.
Before each placement ask 'what will fit here?' to grow anticipation, rather than letting the child rely only on trial and error.
When a piece won't seat, talk about the SPACE and its corners/angles — not just the side lengths — to move children off matching side length alone.
Model and encourage rotating and flipping a piece to make it fit; offer a horizontal-base version first if a rotated piece can't be 'seen'.
Name the new whole after combining ('you put two triangles together and made one rectangle') to build the part-whole idea.
keyRepresentations: Pattern blocks with outlined puzzles (e.g. a hexagon to fill) grading to open puzzles
Two identical right triangles to combine into a rectangle or a larger triangle
Tangrams for composing pictures and larger shapes
Rotate/flip actions to seat a piece by matching its corner to the gap
commonMisconceptions: Places shapes separately or by pure trial and error, not anticipating that pieces will combine into a new shape.
Matches side LENGTHS but not ANGLES, so pieces leave gaps/overlaps or a corner won't fit the space (e.g. a square's right angle in a rhombus gap).
Cannot 'see' where a piece goes when it must be rotated off a horizontal base, and doesn't turn it to fit.
Sees the result as still 'two triangles' rather than one new rectangle — misses the part-whole identity of the composite.

learn.summary: Young children (ages ~5–6) learn to compose simple shapes into larger ones — two triangles into a rectangle or a bigger triangle, pattern blocks into a hexagon, basic shapes into a picture. The deep idea is PART–WHOLE: separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity. The Clements & Sarama composition trajectory describes growth from a Piece Assembler (each shape a separate part, trial and error), through a Picture Maker (combines pieces but does NOT anticipate the new shape, matches side lengths not angles), to a Shape Composer (anticipates the fit — 'I know what will fit' — using angles and intentional rotation/flip). The core vehicle is a graded sequence of pattern-block and tangram puzzles moving from fully-outlined to open, pitched about one trajectory level above the child's current one, supported by physical blocks and cut-out triangles.

activities.title: Two triangles become one rectangle
feedback: When the pair fills the outline cleanly, name the whole: 'You put two triangles together and made one rectangle — it's one shape now.'
If the child still calls the result 'two triangles', trace the outside edge of the composite together and ask 'What ONE shape is this now?'
If a triangle won't seat, invite turning or flipping it: 'Try spinning this piece, or flipping it over, so its corner matches the corner of the space.'

An optional on-screen version can let the seam between the two triangles fade and the single rectangle highlight the moment they fill the outline, making the 'two becomes one' instant visible; the insight is in the child constructing and naming the whole, not in the animation.
activities.rationale: Constructing (not just recognising) the composite and naming the new whole targets the part–whole idea directly; asking a prediction first grows the anticipation that distinguishes the Shape Composer level from the trial-and-error Picture Maker.
sourceClaims: At the Picture Maker level children put shapes together using trial and error and 'do not anticipate the creation of the new geometric shape'; they choose shapes by 'general shape' or side length and 'match side lengths (not angles)', so they get frustrated with puzzles needing different angles (e.g. a square whose right angles won't fit). Moving to Shape Composer means combining shapes with anticipation ('I know what will fit') using angles and intentional rotation/flip.
learnerActions: Take two identical right triangles (physical cut-outs and/or an on-screen pair beside a rectangle outline).
Before moving them, answer the prompt 'What ONE shape do you think these will make?'
Arrange them to fill a rectangle outline, turning one triangle (if both start facing the same way, about 180°) so the corners and edges meet with no gaps or overlaps.
Rearrange the same two triangles to make a LARGER triangle by joining matching legs; unless the triangles are isosceles right triangles, you will need to flip one over, not just turn it.
Say aloud what single shape you have made each time: 'I put two triangles together and made one rectangle.'
activities.intendedInsight: Two separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity (part–whole); the same two pieces can compose into different wholes depending on how they are turned, flipped and joined.

activities.title: Fill the hexagon — graded puzzles from outlined to open
feedback: If a block leaves a gap or overlap, point to the SPACE: 'Look at the corner of this gap — does your piece's corner match it?'
When a piece seats cleanly after a deliberate choice, reflect it back: 'You looked at the corner first and knew it would fit.'
If the child relies only on trial and error, keep offering the 'what will fit here?' prompt before each placement rather than marking placements wrong.
An optional on-screen version can snap correct placements and flag gaps/overlaps, and flash a mismatched corner when a wrong-angled piece (e.g. a square's right angle) is dropped into the gap.
activities.rationale: A graded outlined-to-open sequence pitched about one level above the child's current level, with angle-focused talk about the gap, moves children off matching side length alone; multiple solutions reinforce that the whole has several valid compositions.
sourceClaims: At the Picture Maker level children put shapes together using trial and error and 'do not anticipate the creation of the new geometric shape'; they choose shapes by 'general shape' or side length and 'match side lengths (not angles)', so they get frustrated with puzzles needing different angles (e.g. a square whose right angles won't fit). Moving to Shape Composer means combining shapes with anticipation ('I know what will fit') using angles and intentional rotation/flip.
learnerActions: Fill a hexagon with pattern blocks, starting from a fully-outlined puzzle (each block's place shown) and progressing toward an open outline (only the overall hexagon shown).
Before each placement, answer 'What will fit here, and why?'
Find at least two different ways to fill the same hexagon (e.g. two trapezoids; six triangles; a trapezoid plus three triangles).
Check the finished fill for any gaps or overlaps and fix them.
activities.intendedInsight: A whole shape can be composed in more than one way, and a correct fit depends on both side length and the angle of the space being filled.

activities.title: Turning a piece to make it fit
feedback: If the child leaves a gap a rotated piece would fill but only tries it upright, say 'Try turning the piece — it's still the same shape when it's turned.'
Use the horizontal-base version as a stepping stone: 'It fit easily that way — now let's turn it until its corner matches this tilted space.'
Avoid simply showing the answer; let the child do the turning so they feel that rotation preserves the shape.
activities.rationale: Some children cannot 'see' where a piece goes when it is turned off a horizontal base; a matched horizontal-base puzzle plus hands-on turning helps them link rotation to fit while preserving shape identity.
sourceClaims: Practice-based research (Bofferding & Aqazade, 2022, cited on the level page) notes a child sometimes will not 'see' where a square block/tangram can go when it is turned off a horizontal base; comparing a similar puzzle with a horizontal-base square helps.

A common early misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation; letting children handle and rotate cut-outs helps — supports the 'rotate a piece to make it fit' move in composition.
learnerActions: Meet a gap that a square or triangle would fill only when it is rotated off its horizontal base.
First try a matched puzzle where the same piece fits with a horizontal base, then return to the rotated version.
Physically turn the cut-out piece (or rotate the on-screen piece) and watch that turning does not change what the shape is.
Seat the piece once its corner matches the corner of the gap.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape keeps its identity when rotated; turning a piece is a tool for making its corner match the space it must fill.

activities.title: Make a picture from basic shapes
feedback: Ask 'Which shapes did you put together to make this part?' to surface the part–whole structure.
When a child combines pieces into a recognisable larger shape, name it: 'Those two triangles together made a square for the window.'
activities.rationale: Open composition with tangrams extends composing beyond fixed outlines and may give children further practice applying rotation, flipping and part–whole naming in a self-directed context.
learnerActions: Use tangrams or pattern blocks to compose a picture or design (e.g. a house, a rocket, an animal) from basic shapes.
Explain which smaller shapes make up one part of the picture.
Where two pieces together form a familiar larger shape, name that larger shape.
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday pictures and designs are built by combining basic shapes, and the same basic shapes can be put together in many different ways.

constraints: This is a 2-D planar composition task; 3-D composing is a separate, later topic and depth is not used here.

A fixed quiz can check a single known combination but, being fixed, cannot provide the free rotate-and-fit composing or the graded outlined-to-open progression where most of the learning happens; use it only as an occasional spot-check, not the main activity.

On-screen snapping, seam-fade, and angle-flash cues are optional supports that make the mechanism visible; they are not required, and children should still experience physical blocks and cut-outs they can turn and glue.

Trial-and-error placement without anticipation is a normal trajectory level (Picture Maker), not an error to drill or mark wrong; respond by offering puzzles about one level up and prompting 'what will fit here?'.
Teach roughly one trajectory level above the child's current level; pitching too far ahead can cause frustration.
Recognition-only responses (e.g. tapping a correct picture) do not elicit the independent construction this objective requires.
Physical cut-outs and blocks approximate ideal flat figures; treat them as representing the mathematical 2-D shapes composed, not as objects defined by being pickable or by their slight thickness.

errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks a piece whose side is the right length, then it won't seat because the angle is wrong; leaves a gap or forces an overlap (e.g. a square's right angle in a rhombus gap).

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot 'see' where a piece goes when it must be rotated off a horizontal base, and doesn't turn it to fit.

errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves a gap that a rotated square/triangle would fill, but only tries the piece in its upright orientation.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 2-D shapes (age 6+)
topic.description: Identify and describe properties of 2-D shapes including the number of sides and line symmetry in a vertical line
evidence: Count the number of sides of a given 2-D shape
Identify whether a 2-D shape has a vertical line of symmetry
Use properties (number of sides, symmetry) to describe and distinguish between shapes
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count the sides of a shape and say whether it has a line of symmetry — for example, knowing that a rectangle is symmetrical but a scalene triangle is not?

pedagogy.summary: This topic formalises 2-D shape description with two properties: the number of sides, and line symmetry (in Year 2, specifically a vertical line). The conceptual heart is symmetry — and the single idea children must build is that a line of symmetry is a FOLD line where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (mirror images that coincide), NOT merely a line that splits the shape into two same-sized pieces. It is best taught by folding paper cut-outs and using mirrors, so 'the halves match' is something the child physically verifies rather than judges by eye, and by combining side-count and symmetry to describe and tell shapes apart.
bestPractices: Teach a line of symmetry as a FOLD: cut out the shape and fold along the candidate line; it is a line of symmetry only if the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Use mirrors (and mirror-drawing) so children see one half as the reflection of the other — reinforcing 'mirror image', not just 'same size'.
Deliberately test a non-example that has two congruent halves but is NOT symmetric (the diagonal of a non-square rectangle) so children learn congruence is not enough.
Count sides by touching and marking each one; then combine properties ('4 sides AND 2 lines of symmetry') to distinguish shapes such as a square from a non-square rectangle.
Present shapes in varied orientations so a vertical line of symmetry is recognised as a property of the shape, not of the page.
keyRepresentations: Paper/card shape cut-outs for folding along a candidate line
A small mirror (or Mira) placed on the line to check the reflection
Pegboard/dot-paper symmetric-pattern completion (draw the missing mirror half)
Side-by-side square vs non-square rectangle for comparing side-count and number of symmetry lines
commonMisconceptions: Thinks any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry, without checking the halves coincide.
Thinks any line that cuts a shape into two equal/congruent parts is a line of symmetry — e.g. accepts the diagonal of a rectangle because it makes two identical triangles.
Judges 'the halves are the same' by eye/size rather than by folding or mirroring to see if they actually land on each other.
Confuses the vertical line of symmetry with 'any line through the centre' and does not realise a shape can have several (or no) lines of symmetry.

learn.summary: Year 2 learners describe 2-D shapes by number of sides and by line symmetry (specifically a vertical line). The conceptual crux is that a line of symmetry is a FOLD line where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (mirror images that coincide) — NOT merely a line that splits a shape into two same-sized pieces. The decisive non-example is the diagonal of a non-square rectangle: it makes two congruent triangles yet does not coincide on folding. Physical folding of paper cut-outs and mirrors let children verify matching rather than judging by eye; side-count combines with symmetry to tell shapes apart.

activities.title: Fold test: does each half land on the other?
feedback: When the vertical midline fold makes the halves land exactly on each other with no overhang, that IS a line of symmetry.

When you fold the rectangle along its diagonal, a corner pokes out past the edge — the halves do not land on each other, so the diagonal is NOT a line of symmetry even though both triangles are the same size.
If you accepted the diagonal 'because it makes two equal triangles', re-fold and look for the overhanging corner: equal size is not the same as the halves matching.
A square's folds work down the middle, across the middle, AND along both diagonals — fold to find all four.

The paper cut-out has a very slight thickness but stands in for the ideal flat (zero-thickness) mathematical shape. An optional on-screen fold/reflection tool models the same reflection without the thickness — for example recolouring the outline green when the swung half coincides and red when a corner overhangs.
activities.rationale: Folding cut-outs makes 'the halves match' something the child physically verifies rather than judges by eye, and the rectangle diagonal is the targeted non-example that separates congruence from coincidence. The shape used must be a non-square rectangle, since a square's diagonal IS a line of symmetry.
sourceClaims: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves are mirror images that coincide (match exactly); a line dividing a figure into two CONGRUENT parts is not necessarily a line of symmetry — the diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but folding gives a non-matching (kite) result, so congruence is not sufficient.

Common Year 2 misconception: children may think that any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry; remedy is to fold cut-outs so the two halves match (one half a reflection of the other) and to use mirrors.
learnerActions: Cut out a paper/card rectangle (a non-square one).
Fold it along the vertical line down the middle: check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Now fold the same rectangle corner-to-corner along the diagonal and watch what happens to the corners.
Say out loud for each fold whether it is a line of symmetry and why.
Repeat the fold test on other cut-out shapes (square, triangle), hunting for every fold where the halves coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: A line of symmetry is a fold where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (coincide), not just a line that makes two pieces the same size. The diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but a corner overhangs when folded — so congruence is not enough.

activities.title: Mirror check and completing the mirror half
feedback: If the half in front of the mirror plus its reflection looks exactly like the whole shape (with a see-through Mira, if the reflection lines up with the real half behind it), the line is a line of symmetry.
If the reflection does not match the shape's outline, that line is not a line of symmetry even if the two parts are the same size.
When you complete the mirror half on dot-paper, each point should sit the same distance from the line as its partner.
Optionally, a draggable on-screen mirror can sweep across a shape to find every line of symmetry — for a non-square rectangle it finds two, while a square has four.
activities.rationale: Mirrors reinforce 'mirror image' rather than merely 'same size', offering a second concrete test that complements folding.
sourceClaims: Common Year 2 misconception: children may think that any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry; remedy is to fold cut-outs so the two halves match (one half a reflection of the other) and to use mirrors.
learnerActions: Place a small mirror (or Mira) upright along a candidate line on a shape and look at the reflection.
Check whether the reflection in the mirror continues the shape exactly — if it does, the line is a line of symmetry.
On dot-paper or a pegboard, draw/build half of a pattern, then draw or build the missing mirror half so the whole is symmetric.
Describe one half as the reflection of the other, not just 'the same size'.
activities.intendedInsight: One half of a symmetric shape is the mirror image (reflection) of the other; reflecting, like folding, tests whether the halves actually coincide.

activities.title: Count sides and combine with symmetry to tell shapes apart
feedback: Marking each side as you count stops you from double-counting or missing one.
A square has four lines of symmetry; a non-square rectangle has two — so number of symmetry lines, not just side-count, distinguishes them.
If a shape is turned on the page, fold or mirror-test again — a true line of symmetry travels with the shape.
activities.rationale: Combining side-count with symmetry supports the describe-and-distinguish objective, and varied orientations prevent symmetry being tied to the prototypical upright image.
sourceClaims: Early-years/KS1 practice: attend to shape properties (number of sides/corners) and present shapes in varied orientations, sizes and materials rather than a single prototypical image.
learnerActions: Count the sides of a given 2-D shape by touching and marking each side as you count.
Count the lines of symmetry of the same shape by folding or mirroring.
Place a square beside a non-square rectangle and compare both properties: '4 sides AND how many lines of symmetry?'
State how the square differs from the rectangle using BOTH the number of sides and the number of lines of symmetry.

Try the same shapes turned to different angles and fold or mirror-test again to confirm they still have the same lines of symmetry. The lines turn with the shape, so a line that was vertical may now be slanted or horizontal.
activities.intendedInsight: Shapes are described and distinguished by combining properties — a square and a non-square rectangle both have 4 sides, but a square has four lines of symmetry and this rectangle has two. Symmetry is a property of the shape, not of how it sits on the page.

activities.title: Predict-then-fold diagnostic conversation
feedback: Predicting 'yes, they'll match' and then seeing the corner overhang is the moment 'two equal halves' turns into 'the halves must land on each other'.
If you can explain WHY the diagonal fails — the halves don't coincide — you are reasoning by folding/reflecting, not by equal size.

Note the square is different: its diagonal fold DOES make the halves coincide, so a square's diagonal is a line of symmetry while this rectangle's is not — the test is always whether the halves land on each other.
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain exchange is an assessment-aligned diagnostic that exposes the load-bearing congruence-vs-coincidence misconception; it uses the non-square rectangle so the non-example holds.
sourceClaims: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves are mirror images that coincide (match exactly); a line dividing a figure into two CONGRUENT parts is not necessarily a line of symmetry — the diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but folding gives a non-matching (kite) result, so congruence is not sufficient.
learnerActions: Before folding, predict: 'If we fold this non-square rectangle exactly along its diagonal, corner to corner, will the two halves land exactly on top of each other?' Say yes or no first.
Fold along the diagonal and compare what happened to your prediction.
Explain in your own words why two halves being the same size is not enough for a line of symmetry.
Show, by folding, which lines of a square are lines of symmetry and which lines of the rectangle are not.
activities.intendedInsight: Committing to a prediction before folding surfaces whether you are reasoning about matching halves or about equal-sized pieces; the overhang resolves it.

constraints: Line symmetry of a 2-D shape is planar; keep the work flat (folding, mirrors, dot-paper) — adding depth/3-D is not needed for this concept and can distract from the flat fold.

Watching pre-drawn lines of symmetry or tap-to-reveal mirror highlights can show correct examples, but a watch-only display does not let the child test their OWN candidate line or resolve the diagonal misconception through their own folding; treat such displays as a scaffold and still have the child perform a fold or mirror test.

Multiple-choice ('which line is a line of symmetry?') and draw-the-line tasks can check the skill but do not themselves perform the fold, so they do not let the child feel whether the halves coincide; use them to assess, not as the primary teaching of the crux.

Paper/card cut-outs have slight thickness; treat them as a good physical approximation of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) shape. If an on-screen fold/reflection tool is used, note it models the same zero-thickness reflection.

Recognition-only responses (picking a line from options) do not require the learner to construct or verify the fold themselves; include folding, mirroring, or completing a mirror half for independent construction.
The diagnostic non-example must be a NON-SQUARE rectangle: a square's diagonal IS a line of symmetry, so using a square would break the congruence-vs-coincidence contrast.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a cut-out non-square rectangle. 'Predict: if we fold this rectangle exactly along its diagonal, corner to corner, will the two halves land exactly on top of each other? Say yes or no before we fold.' A child who equates congruence with symmetry predicts YES (two identical triangles). Folding reveals NO — a corner overhangs and the shape becomes a kite-like flap. The prediction, and their reaction to the overhang, is the diagnostic: it exposes whether they are reasoning about matching halves or about equal-sized pieces.
probeDeeper: Fold this cut-out rectangle along the middle line. Do the two halves land exactly on top of each other? Now try the diagonal — what happens?
This shape splits into two halves the same size, but they don't match when folded. Is it symmetrical? Why not?

Use both the number of sides AND the number of lines of symmetry to tell me how a square is different from this rectangle.
assess.correctAnswer: The vertical line down the middle IS a line of symmetry — folding along it, the two halves land exactly on top of each other. The diagonal is NOT — folding along it, the two triangular halves do not coincide (a corner overhangs). The check is to fold (or use a mirror) and see whether the halves land on each other, not merely whether they are the same size.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes any line that divides a shape into two equal/congruent parts is a line of symmetry — accepts the rectangle's diagonal 'because it makes two triangles the same'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cut out the rectangle and fold along the diagonal — the halves do not land on each other, a corner overhangs; contrast with folding along the vertical midline where they coincide exactly. Establish: a line of symmetry is a fold where the halves MATCH, not just where the pieces are the same size.
errorPatterns.distractor: The diagonal is a line of symmetry because it splits the rectangle into two equal triangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the diagonal as a line of symmetry and justifies it by the two equal triangles, not by folding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry, without checking that the halves coincide.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the fold-test / mirror-test the habitual check: if the halves don't land on each other it isn't a line of symmetry, wherever the line is drawn.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts a central line automatically ('it goes through the middle') without folding or mirroring to verify.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts any central or halving line as a line of symmetry (including the rectangle's diagonal) and checks only whether the two parts look the same size.
responseLevels.full: Uses the fold/reflection test — the halves must land exactly on each other — to accept the vertical midline and reject the diagonal, explains why two congruent halves are not enough, and combines side-count and symmetry to distinguish shapes (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Correctly identifies the vertical line of symmetry by folding and counts sides, but treats these as separate facts — cannot yet reject the diagonal by reasoning that the halves must coincide, or does not transfer the fold-test to a new shape (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a non-square rectangle with two lines drawn on it: one straight down the middle (vertical) and one from corner to corner (the diagonal). Ask: 'Which of these lines are lines of symmetry for the rectangle? How would you check?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rectangle's diagonal DOES cut it into two congruent triangles, so a child who believes 'any line making two equal parts is a line of symmetry' will accept it. It can only be rejected by fold/mirror reasoning — realising the halves must coincide. That makes it very hard to answer correctly for the wrong reason: the second tier ('how would you check') exposes whether the child reasons by folding/reflecting or by judging equal size.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Composing Shapes
topic.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, quarter-circles) to create composite shapes, and compose new shapes from the composite shape
evidence: Combine two triangles to form a rectangle or larger triangle
Put together half-circles and quarter-circles to form circles or new shapes
Decompose a composite shape and describe which simpler shapes make it up
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use flat shapes like triangles and rectangles to fit together and make a new larger shape — like a puzzle?

pedagogy.summary: Composing 2-D shapes — combining triangles, squares, trapezoids and half-/quarter-circles into composite shapes and finding new shapes within them — develops through Clements & Sarama's trajectory from unsystematic Piece Assembly, through trial-and-error Picture Making, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION and substituting equivalent pieces. It is taught best with outline (puzzle) tasks engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, prompting children to choose pieces by side length and angle rather than general appearance, and asking them to decompose a composite and name the simpler shapes that make it up.
bestPractices: Use outline puzzles engineered to require the next level of thinking (e.g. remove one internal guide line to push from Piece Assembler to Picture Maker).
Nudge from trial and error to anticipation: 'Can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
Have children choose pieces by attributes — matching side lengths and angles — and use turns and flips intentionally.
Ask children to decompose the composite ('what smaller shapes make this up?') and to find new shapes within it (two triangles make a square; two half-circles make a circle).
Pitch tasks one level beyond the child's current level and fade support — this out-performed jumping straight to the target level (Clements et al. 2019, effect size .55).
keyRepresentations: Pattern blocks and tangram pieces
Outline puzzle cards of increasing difficulty
Two triangles composing a square or larger triangle; half-circles composing a circle
Angle-and-side-length matching between a gap and a piece
commonMisconceptions: Assembles by trial and error with no advance plan and does not anticipate the new shape (an expected early trajectory level, not a fault).
Chooses pieces by general shape only, not by matching angles and side lengths, so pieces do not fit the gap.
Sees the composite as one whole and cannot decompose it into the simpler shapes it is made from.

learn.summary: Children compose 2-D shapes — combining triangles, squares, trapezoids, and half-/quarter-circles into composite shapes and finding new shapes within them. The goal is to move along Clements & Sarama's trajectory: from unsystematic trial-and-error assembly (Piece Assembler), through trial-and-error picture making, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — choosing a piece because its angle and side length will fit, using turns and flips intentionally, and decomposing a composite back into the simpler shapes that make it up. The core teaching medium is manipulating flat pieces into outline (puzzle) tasks engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, with immediate fit/misfit feedback.

activities.title: Fill the outline with the right pieces
feedback: If the child places pieces at random until one fits and cannot say in advance which will fit: this is an expected early trajectory level, not an error — do NOT mark it wrong. Offer a puzzle just one step ahead (for example, remove a single internal guide line) and ask 'Can you see what will fit before you place it?'
If the child grabs a triangle of the wrong size or angle that won't fit: say 'This gap has a slanted edge — which piece has an edge that matches it?' and compare edges and corners before placing.
When a piece snaps into place because its angle and side matched, name it: 'You picked that because its edge was the same length as the gap.'
activities.rationale: Outline puzzles engineered to require the next level of thinking, with pieces chosen by angle and side length and intentional rotation/reflection, are the tasks through which this trajectory was researched. Pitching one level beyond the child's current level and fading support is the recommended progression.
sourceClaims: Shape composition progresses from the Piece Assembler and Picture Maker levels (building by unsystematic trial and error, choosing pieces by general shape or side length) to the Shape Composer level (composing with anticipation, choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and using rotations and reflections intentionally); outline puzzles are engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, and instruction one trajectory level ahead out-performed skipping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Give the child flat shape pieces (for example, pattern blocks, tangram pieces, or cut-out triangles, squares, rectangles, trapezoids, half-circles and quarter-circles) and an outline puzzle card that those pieces can cover exactly. Standard pattern blocks and tangrams do not include half-circles or quarter-circles, and tangrams have no trapezoid, so add cut-out pieces for any shapes the set lacks.
As they work, ask them to say which shape they are using and why.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Will this piece fit this gap? How do you know?' — encouraging a prediction from the gap's edges and corners.
When a piece doesn't fit, have them compare the gap's edge length and corner angle to the piece, then choose one that matches.
Let them use turns and flips to make a piece fit, naming what they did ('I flipped it so the slanted edge lines up').
activities.intendedInsight: A piece can be chosen in advance by matching its side length and angle to the gap, rather than by trying pieces at random until one happens to fit.

activities.title: Same pieces, different shapes
feedback: If the child treats each arrangement as unrelated, overlay or re-join the same two right-angled triangles in front of them to show the square and the larger triangle come from the same pieces.
Praise the moment they predict a new shape before building it: that is composing with anticipation.
activities.rationale: Composing new shapes from the same component pieces, using rotation and reflection intentionally, is explicitly required by the trajectory and the grade-1 standard. The square/larger-triangle example only holds for congruent right-isosceles triangles, so pieces are chosen accordingly.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 geometry requires pupils to compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles and quarter-circles) to create a composite shape, and to compose new shapes from the composite shape.

Shape composition progresses from the Piece Assembler and Picture Maker levels (building by unsystematic trial and error, choosing pieces by general shape or side length) to the Shape Composer level (composing with anticipation, choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and using rotations and reflections intentionally); outline puzzles are engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, and instruction one trajectory level ahead out-performed skipping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Using two congruent right-isosceles (tangram-style) triangles, have the child join them along their long (hypotenuse) edges to form a square. Then have them rejoin the same two triangles along one of the shorter equal edges, mirrored so the two right-angle corners sit side by side, to form a larger triangle instead. Joining them along a shorter edge with one triangle turned the other way makes a parallelogram, which is another new shape worth naming. (Note for the adult: two equilateral pattern-block triangles would instead make a rhombus, not a square, so choose right-isosceles triangles for this square example.)
Have them put two half-circles together to form a circle, and explore what else the pieces can make.
Ask: 'You made a square from two triangles — can you make a different shape with those same two pieces?'
activities.intendedInsight: The same pieces can compose different shapes depending on how they are turned and joined — composing is a deliberate, reversible act.

activities.title: Find the shapes hiding inside
feedback: If the child names only the whole composite and cannot show its parts, lift and overlay the pieces to reveal the two right-angled triangles inside the square, then hunt together for 'shapes hidden within shapes'.
Confirm when they both name a part and show where it sits in the whole.
activities.rationale: Decomposing the composite and naming its component shapes is a listed objective in the row's own evidence and directly addresses the misconception that a composite is one undifferentiated whole. Neither cited source claim directly attests to decomposition, so no source claim is attached here.
learnerActions: Show the child a completed composite shape and ask 'Which smaller shapes are hiding inside this?'
Have them lift and separate the pieces to reveal, for example, that the square is made of two right-angled (right-isosceles) triangles or the circle of two half-circles.
Ask them to name each component shape as they take the composite apart, then rebuild it.
activities.intendedInsight: A composite shape is built from — and can be pulled apart into — simpler named shapes; seeing the whole does not mean you can only see the whole.

activities.title: Reference and post-check (supporting activities)
feedback: If a child can match or name parts but still fits pieces by trial and error, return to the hands-on outline puzzles — matching checks recognition, not the composing action.
Use the spoken prediction to surface anticipation, then have the child actually place the piece to confirm.
activities.rationale: A static decomposition display supports naming parts but does not exercise the act of fitting pieces; a matching/sequence check can verify which pieces make a shape but not the composing action; a spoken prediction can prompt anticipation but the manipulative act carries the learning. These supports are useful alongside, not instead of, hands-on composition.
learnerActions: As a reference, show a composite alongside a reveal of its decomposition ('this is made of two triangles') to support naming the parts.
As a post-check after hands-on building, have the child match composites to the component pieces that make them, or sequence which pieces make a given shape.
Use a short spoken prediction before a build: 'Which piece will fit here, and why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Naming and matching parts consolidates vocabulary and checks understanding, but the composing skill itself is built through the hands-on fitting activities above.

constraints: The core skill is a manipulative, spatial act: children must physically (or on-screen) fit, turn, and flip pieces into outlines. Recognition-only tasks (matching a composite to its parts, naming shapes) check understanding but do not elicit the independent act of composing.
A static composite with a tap/reveal of its decomposition is a reference and naming aid; it cannot exercise choosing and fitting pieces.
This is a planar concept; it needs a flat working surface (physical blocks or a 2-D screen). A 3-D rendering is not needed and can distract from the flat composition being learned.
Spoken prediction ('which piece will fit?') is valuable for eliciting anticipation but should accompany actual placement, not replace it.
Trial-and-error assembly with no advance plan is an expected early trajectory LEVEL, not a fault to be marked wrong; respond by offering a puzzle one step ahead and fading support.

Engineer puzzles to require the next level of thinking (e.g. remove one internal guide line at a time) and pitch one level beyond the child's current level; the cited study reports this out-performed jumping straight to the target level (effect size .55).
For the 'two triangles make a square' example, use congruent right-isosceles (tangram-style) triangles; two equilateral pattern-block triangles form a rhombus, not a square.

Decomposition ('find the shapes hiding inside') is drawn from the row's objective, evidence and misconception list; neither sources[].claim directly attests to decomposition, so the decomposition activity carries no source claim.
