assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are pattern-block pieces — triangles, squares, trapezoids and some half-circles and quarter-circles. Cover this outline puzzle exactly using the pieces, and as you work tell me which shapes you are using. Then show me two triangles making a square, and tell me one other shape you could make from the pieces.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Defining attributes of shapes
topic.description: Distinguish defining attributes of shapes (e.g. triangles are closed and three-sided) from non-defining attributes (e.g. colour, orientation, overall size)
evidence: Build and draw shapes that possess defining attributes
Identify that a shape remains a triangle regardless of its size, colour, or orientation
Explain why a given shape is or is not a particular type based on its defining properties
topic.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that what makes a shape a triangle is having 3 sides and 3 corners — not its colour or which way it's pointing?

pedagogy.summary: This is the pivotal move from recognising shapes by how they LOOK to defining them by their PROPERTIES. A DEFINING attribute is one a shape must have (a triangle: three straight sides, closed; a square: four equal straight sides and four right-angle corners); a NON-DEFINING or 'imposed' attribute is incidental (colour, size, overall orientation, sitting on a horizontal base). Children routinely treat imposed attributes as if they were defining — rejecting a rotated square as a 'diamond', or a long-thin or point-down triangle as 'not a real triangle'. It is taught by explicitly contrasting varied examples with non-examples, foregrounding the invariant defining feature, rotating/resizing the same shape to show identity is preserved, and asking children to explain WHY a shape is or is not a given type.
bestPractices: Explicitly separate 'must-have' (defining) from 'doesn't-matter' (non-defining) attributes: a triangle is ANY closed figure with three straight sides — colour, size and which way it points do not matter.
Contrast varied examples with carefully chosen near-miss non-examples (three sides but one curved; three straight lines that don't quite close) so the defining feature is isolated.
Make non-prototypical and rotated cases the main event — long-thin, right, obtuse and point-down triangles, tilted squares — because these are where imposed attributes get mistaken for defining ones.
Rotate and resize the SAME shape and ask 'is it still a…?' so the child sees the defining attributes stay constant while orientation and size change.

Have children BUILD or DRAW a shape to a defining spec ('draw a triangle that looks different from mine') and JUSTIFY why borderline figures are included or excluded — the reasoning is the assessment.
keyRepresentations: 'Must-have versus doesn't-matter' attribute contrast
Example / near-miss non-example sets (curved side; not closed)
The same shape rotated and resized to show invariance
Tracing each side and checking 'straight' and 'closed'
commonMisconceptions: Treats ORIENTATION as defining (an 'imposed attribute'): a rotated square is a 'diamond'; a triangle 'must' have a horizontal base — about 15% of children reject even a prototypical triangle once it is rotated.
Treats shape type as defined by its image/prototype: only 'regular' triangles or brick-like rectangles count; long-thin, right and obtuse triangles are rejected.
Thinks size or colour can change a shape's identity (a very big or a red triangle is 'a different shape').
Accepts a near-miss non-example (a curved-sided or unclosed 'triangle') because it resembles the prototype — ignoring 'straight' and 'closed'.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds move from recognising shapes by how they look to defining them by their properties. A defining attribute is one a shape must have (a triangle: three straight sides, closed; a square: four equal straight sides and four right-angle corners); a non-defining ('imposed') attribute is incidental (colour, size, overall orientation, sitting on a horizontal base). Children routinely treat imposed attributes as defining — rejecting a rotated square as a 'diamond', or a long-thin or point-down triangle as 'not a real triangle'. The core moves are: contrast varied examples with carefully chosen near-miss non-examples, foreground the invariant defining feature, rotate/resize the same shape to show identity is preserved, and ask children to explain WHY a shape is or is not a given type.

activities.title: Triangle studio: what can change, what cannot
feedback: When a learner tilts or resizes and still calls it a triangle: 'Yes — you changed how it looks, but you kept three straight sides joined up, so it is still a triangle.'
When a side is bent: 'Now one side is curved, so it is no longer a triangle — a triangle needs every side straight.'
When a corner is pulled open: 'The outline doesn't join up all the way round now, so it is not closed — that's why it stopped being a triangle.'
If a learner expects colour or size to matter: 'Watch the label — making it red or huge changed nothing. Those are "doesn't-matter" attributes.'
activities.rationale: Separating defining from non-defining attributes is learned by observing what CAN change (size, orientation, colour) while the shape stays the same, and what CANNOT (exactly three sides, straightness, closure). A live manipulable where only the invariant features control the label makes that contrast concrete. Live recolouring, size sliders, draggable vertices, and a label that flips with a highlighted broken feature are optional ways to make the mechanism visible, not required components.
sourceClaims: Understanding requires analysing shapes by their DEFINING properties (a triangle must have three sides and be closed; a square is a sub-class of rectangles) and grasping that these properties are invariant over changes in size, orientation and colour — children must be able to explain why a figure is a triangle even when it is not prototypical; over-reliance on prototypical shapes in books and toys is a root cause, so adults should expose children to non-prototypical examples and teach the defining properties explicitly.

Children rely on 'imposed attributes' — attributes that are not formal (sides, corners, lengths) but just match how the prototype looks, e.g. that a triangle has a horizontal base — and treat them as if defining; about 15% failed to identify a prototypical triangle once its orientation changed, non-prototypical triangle TYPES (isosceles, right) were hardest (about half missed), and the remedy is experiencing typical and atypical examples plus non-examples.
learnerActions: Drag the three corners of a triangle to stretch it into different types (long-thin, right, obtuse) and tilt it to any angle, checking after each change whether it is still a triangle and saying why (if the three corners are dragged into one straight line, it flattens and is no longer a triangle).
Use size and colour controls to make the triangle big, small, and recoloured, and confirm the label 'triangle' stays the same because three straight sides and closure have not changed.

Break the shape on purpose: bend one side into a curve, or drag a corner apart so the outline no longer closes, and watch the label flip to 'not a triangle' with the non-straight side or the open gap highlighted.
State in your own words which attributes can be 'thrown around' with no effect (colour, size, orientation) and which changes end it (for example a curved side or an open corner).
activities.intendedInsight: Size, colour and orientation can swing wildly while a shape keeps its identity, but the instant a side curves or a corner opens it stops being a triangle — this makes defining versus non-defining attributes directly visible.

activities.title: Is it or not? — and explain why
feedback: For a correctly accepted point-down triangle: 'Right — turning it upside down didn't change the three straight sides, so it is still a triangle.'
For a correctly rejected curved-sided figure: 'Yes, and the reason matters: one side isn't straight, so it fails the test even though it looks pointy.'
If a learner rejects the long-thin triangle: 'Count the sides — three straight sides, closed. Being long and thin is a "doesn't-matter".'
If a learner calls the tilted square a 'diamond': 'Check the sides and corners — four equal straight sides and four square corners. Turning it didn't change those, so it is still a square.'
activities.rationale: An include/exclude judgement with distractors drawn directly from the orientation and prototype errors targets the misconception, and requiring a stated reason builds recognition on properties rather than prototypes. Note that choosing correctly is easier to elicit than justifying, so the reason should be treated as the main evidence of understanding, not the correct selection alone.
sourceClaims: The Clements & Sarama trajectories use an 'Is it or not? — and explain why' activity in which children decide whether a drawn figure is or is not a given shape and justify it by defining properties (straight sides, corners), building recognition on properties rather than prototypes.

NCETM lists as common errors that children define shapes by their image (only regular triangles / brick-like rectangles count) and by their orientation (a square is only a square with a horizontal base), and recommends ensuring children see a range of examples of the same shape in different orientations, sizes, colours and materials, and can 'recognise a range of triangles and say how they know what they are'.
learnerActions: Decide for each drawn figure whether it is or is not a given shape: non-prototypical positives (long-thin triangle, point-down triangle, tilted square) and near-miss negatives (one curved side, an open/unclosed corner).

For every decision, justify it by naming the defining property — e.g. 'three straight sides, all joined up' or 'that side isn't straight' — rather than 'it looks like one' or 'it points the right way'.
Compare a figure with one resized/recoloured and state whether anything that matters has changed.

Trace a finger along each side of a borderline figure to test 'how many sides?', 'is every side straight?' and 'is it joined up all the way round?' (and, for a square, 'are all four sides equal and all four corners square?')
activities.intendedInsight: Membership of a shape category depends on invariant defining properties, and the reason given — not just the yes/no — shows whether a child is reasoning from properties or from the prototype.

activities.title: Shape detective: argue back
feedback: When the child cites a defining attribute: 'Good argument — four equal sides and square corners. The character gives in.'
If the child relies on how it points: 'The character will keep insisting — which way it points is a "doesn't-matter". Tell them about the sides and corners instead.'
When the child spots a missing feature: 'Exactly — you named what's broken, not just that it looks odd.'
activities.rationale: Because this topic is fundamentally about giving reasons, a dialogue that keeps demanding justification and offers counterexamples can rehearse the explanation skill; a dialogue checks whether a child can produce the reason but does not by itself make the shape change visible. For this age the decision still benefits from seeing the shape change, so pair the discussion with a visible or physical rotation rather than relying on talk alone.
sourceClaims: Understanding requires analysing shapes by their DEFINING properties (a triangle must have three sides and be closed; a square is a sub-class of rectangles) and grasping that these properties are invariant over changes in size, orientation and colour — children must be able to explain why a figure is a triangle even when it is not prototypical; over-reliance on prototypical shapes in books and toys is a root cause, so adults should expose children to non-prototypical examples and teach the defining properties explicitly.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who holds up a rotated square and insists 'that's a diamond, not a square', arguing back from the four equal sides and square corners.
Answer repeated 'how do you know it's a triangle?' challenges, citing a defining attribute each time until the character concedes.
Handle thrown counterexamples — a curved-sided or unclosed figure — by explaining exactly which defining feature is missing.
Defend why size and colour changes do not change the shape's name.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to defend a classification out loud with the defining attribute, against a plausible prototype-based objection, is the goal — the reasoning is what is being learned.

activities.title: Build and draw to a defining spec
feedback: For a valid non-prototypical drawing: 'That looks very different from mine, but you kept three straight sides closed up — so it really is a triangle.'
For an open-cornered build: 'Right now it isn't closed. What would you do to join it up all the way round?'
If the child only draws the tidy prototype: 'Try one that is long and thin or points downward — can you still make it a real triangle?'
activities.rationale: Constructing and drawing to a defining specification, plus justifying borderline cases, requires independent production rather than recognition, and the justification doubles as assessment. A paper or stick build has real thickness and is an approximation of the ideal flat shape; treat the cut-out as standing for the mathematical shape being discussed, not as the shape itself.
sourceClaims: NCETM lists as common errors that children define shapes by their image (only regular triangles / brick-like rectangles count) and by their orientation (a square is only a square with a horizontal base), and recommends ensuring children see a range of examples of the same shape in different orientations, sizes, colours and materials, and can 'recognise a range of triangles and say how they know what they are'.
learnerActions: Draw a triangle that looks completely different from a given one but is still a triangle (e.g. long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down), then explain why it still counts.
Build shapes from sticks or strips to a spec such as 'three straight sides, joined up all the way round'.
Make a near-miss on purpose (leave a corner open, or use a bendy side) and say what would have to change to fix it.
Turn your own cut-out shape, and compare it with a larger or smaller version, checking aloud that the defining attributes stay the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Producing a novel valid example — and justifying it — shows the child can apply the defining properties rather than only recognise a tidy prototype.

activities.title: Must-have versus doesn't-matter reference
feedback: When a learner places 'orientation' under doesn't-matter: 'Correct — which way it points doesn't change what it is.'
When a learner places 'three straight sides' under must-have: 'Yes — remove that and it stops being a triangle.'
activities.rationale: A clear reference contrasting must-have and doesn't-matter attributes helps children name criteria, and a sort can check whether a child classifies an attribute correctly; a sort does not by itself elicit deciding on NEW borderline figures, which is where the learning happens — so use it alongside judging and building tasks rather than on its own.
learnerActions: Reveal a shape's must-have attributes (three straight sides, closed) and its doesn't-matter attributes (colour, size, orientation) shown greyed out, and read which column each feature belongs to.
Sort a few new attributes into 'must-have' or 'doesn't-matter' using the panel as a guide.
After consulting the panel, decide a fresh borderline case and say which column your reason came from.
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping an explicit two-column picture of defining versus incidental attributes supports children in checking their reasoning against the right criteria.

constraints: Target age 6–7; conceptual geometry about 2-D attributes. Avoid introducing a third dimension/solids for this planar objective, since it adds load and can mislead toward solids.

Treat classification choices (triangle / not a triangle, square / diamond) as scaffolds: the stated reason, not the yes/no, is the real evidence, because a correct choice can come from the prototype alone.
Static reference panels and sorts support but cannot by themselves rehearse deciding on new borderline cases; include tasks where the child decides and justifies fresh figures.
Make non-prototypical and rotated cases the main event (long-thin, right, obtuse, point-down triangles; tilted squares), because these are where imposed attributes get mistaken for defining ones.
Choose near-miss non-examples deliberately: three sides but one curved, or three straight lines that don't quite close, so the defining feature is isolated.

Physical cut-outs and stick builds have real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat shape; ask about the mathematical shape represented, and distinguish the cut-out from the shape it represents.
Interaction examples (draggable vertices, colour/size controls, a label that flips with the broken feature highlighted) are optional ways to make the mechanism visible, not mandatory mechanisms.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a triangle resting on its base. Before turning it, ask the child to PREDICT and commit to a reason: 'If I turn it upside down so the point is at the bottom, will it still be a triangle — yes or no, and why?' A prototype/orientation-bound child predicts 'no, it becomes a different shape'. Then slowly rotate it and ask them to explain what they see: the sides and corners are unchanged, so it is still a triangle. The reason stated BEFORE turning is the diagnostic part — it reveals whether orientation is being treated as defining.
probeDeeper: If I make this triangle much bigger, or colour it red, is it still a triangle? Why? (invariance over size and colour)
Here are three straight sticks laid down but not joined at the corners — is that a triangle? Why not? (counterexample — closure)
This shape has one curved side — what would I have to change to make it a real triangle? (counterexample — straightness)
Draw me a triangle that looks completely different from this one but is still a triangle. (transfer / build to a defining spec)
assess.correctAnswer: The long-thin and point-down figures ARE triangles (three straight sides, closed) whatever their proportions or orientation; the curved-sided figure is NOT (a side isn't straight); the rotated square IS still a square (four equal straight sides, four right-angle corners) — turning it does not change what it is. Reasons cite the defining attributes, not the look or the base.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats orientation as defining (an 'imposed attribute'): a rotated square is a 'diamond'; a triangle 'must' sit on a horizontal base
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the SAME cut-out slowly — 'is it still a square now? and now?' — so the child sees the four equal sides and square corners do not change as it turns; name orientation as a 'doesn't-matter'.
errorPatterns.distractor: That one is a diamond, not a square.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the point-down triangle or the tilted square, reasoning from which way it points rather than from its sides and corners.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the prototype image as defining: only a 'regular' triangle counts, so a long-thin, right or obtuse triangle is rejected as 'not a proper triangle'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show many varied triangles and count the three straight sides on each; state that being long, thin or tilted is a 'doesn't-matter' as long as the three straight sides are closed up.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is not a triangle — it is too long and thin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the long-thin triangle as 'too thin to be a triangle' while accepting only the tidy one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the defining feature and accepts a near-miss non-example by resemblance — a curved-sided or unclosed 'triangle' is called a triangle because it looks pointy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put it beside a real triangle and run a finger along each side — 'is EVERY side straight? is it joined up all the way round?' — so straightness and closure become the test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the curved-sided figure is a triangle; does not check that every side is straight and the figure is closed.

responseLevels.gap: Judges by look or orientation — rejects point-down or long-thin triangles, calls the tilted square a diamond, and/or accepts the curved-sided non-example; reasons from resemblance.
responseLevels.full: Includes non-prototypical and rotated examples, excludes near-miss non-examples, and justifies by the invariant defining attributes (three straight sides and closed; four equal sides and right-angle corners for a square), explaining that size, colour and orientation don't matter — and transfers by drawing a novel valid example.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts varied triangles in familiar orientations and may state 'three sides', but still trips on a strongly rotated or atypical case, OR names the defining feature without applying it to the borderline figure (says 'three sides' yet still rejects the point-down triangle) — has the parts but doesn't yet coordinate them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child three figures in turn: a long, thin triangle; a triangle turned so its point is at the bottom; and a near-miss with one gently curved side. For each ask 'Is this a triangle? How do you know?' Then show a square rotated 45° and ask 'Is this a square, or something else? Why?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has separated defining from imposed attributes accepts the long-thin and point-down triangles, rejects the curved one for the RIGHT reason ('that side isn't straight'), and keeps the rotated square a square. A prototype/orientation-bound child rejects the point-down triangle or the tilted square ('that's a diamond') and may accept the curvy one because it 'looks like' a triangle. The 'how do you know' tier is decisive: 'three straight sides, closed' versus 'it looks like one' or 'it points the right way'.

sources.claim: Children rely on 'imposed attributes' — attributes that are not formal (sides, corners, lengths) but just match how the prototype looks, e.g. that a triangle has a horizontal base — and treat them as if defining; about 15% failed to identify a prototypical triangle once its orientation changed, non-prototypical triangle TYPES (isosceles, right) were hardest (about half missed), and the remedy is experiencing typical and atypical examples plus non-examples.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 2-D shapes (age 7+)
topic.description: Draw 2-D shapes and make 3-D shapes using modelling materials; recognise 3-D shapes in different orientations and describe them
evidence: Draw a triangle, rectangle, pentagon, or hexagon accurately
Construct a cube or cuboid from modelling materials (e.g. straws and connectors)
Recognise a 3-D shape (e.g. a pyramid) when it is rotated or seen from a different angle
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a cube to look at, can they draw it on paper — and then make a cube-shaped model from modelling clay or construction materials?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to draw 2-D shapes accurately, to make 3-D shapes from modelling materials (e.g. straws for edges and connectors for vertices), and to recognise a 3-D shape when it is rotated or seen from a different angle. Two procedural strands matter: constructing a solid correctly requires coordinating its edge/vertex/face structure (a cube needs 12 equal edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and orientation recognition requires naming a shape by properties that stay the same under rotation. The central obstacle is orientation dependence — children anchored to a canonical view judge a rotated or point-down solid to be 'a different shape'. Best taught by handling and rotating real solids, and by building frames while counting edges and vertices.
bestPractices: Build 3-D frames from straws (edges) and connectors (vertices), counting how many of each are needed first (a cube: 12 edges, 8 vertices) and checking equal straw lengths so faces are square.
Let children physically rotate a solid — point-up, on its side, point-down, viewed from above — and re-name it each time, so the name is seen to be invariant to orientation.
Name solids by their properties (a pyramid has triangular faces meeting at an apex) rather than by a single remembered picture, so rotation doesn't change the name.
Draw 2-D shapes on dotted paper/geoboards, marking each side as it is drawn to keep the count and closure accurate.
Connect nets and faces to the built solid, so each face is seen as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model.
keyRepresentations: Straws-and-connectors (or clay balls and sticks) for building edge/vertex frames
A real solid to grab and rotate through many orientations
Dotted paper / geoboard for accurate 2-D drawing
Nets that fold into the solid, linking 2-D faces to the 3-D shape
commonMisconceptions: Does not recognise a solid (or 2-D shape) in an unfamiliar orientation — calls a rotated or point-down pyramid 'a different shape' or 'not a pyramid'.
Builds the wrong frame — incorrect number of edges/vertices, or unequal edges so the faces are not square (a wonky frame or a cuboid when a cube was asked for).
Draws 2-D shapes inaccurately — non-closed, curved-sided, or with the wrong number of sides.
Treats a shape's name as tied to its usual position, so turning it seems to change what it is.

learn.summary: Children (age 7-8) learn to draw 2-D shapes accurately, build 3-D solids from modelling materials, and recognise a 3-D shape as the same shape when it is rotated or seen from a new angle. Two procedural strands matter: constructing a solid correctly requires coordinating its edge/vertex/face structure (a cube has 12 equal edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and orientation recognition requires naming a shape by properties that stay the same under rotation. The central obstacle is orientation dependence: a child anchored to a canonical view judges a rotated or point-down solid to be 'a different shape'. The curriculum calls for making 3-D shapes from modelling materials, so hands-on building, rotating real solids, and careful drawing on dotted paper/geoboards are the core activities; on-screen builders and spinners are useful complements, and recognition tasks can check outcomes but do not by themselves elicit construction.

activities.title: Build a cube frame from straws and connectors
feedback: If the frame has the wrong number of straws or connectors, re-establish the target first (12 edges, 8 vertices) and rebuild, counting each piece as it is added.

If the faces are not square, check that all straws are equal length and that the corners are right angles; unequal straws give a cuboid or an irregular frame rather than a cube, and even equal straws can lean into diamond-shaped faces unless the frame is squared up.
Compare the built frame side by side with a real cube-shaped solid to spot missing or extra edges.
activities.rationale: Properties of 3-D shapes are faces (flat 2-D surfaces), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where edges meet); handling real solids and marking each feature supports accurate counting and grounds the structure a child must coordinate when building a cube.
sourceClaims: Properties of 3-D shapes are the faces (flat 2-D surfaces), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where two or more edges meet); handling real solids and marking each feature supports accurate counting — grounds the edge/vertex/face structure a child must coordinate when building a cube.
learnerActions: Before building, predict and count how many edges (straws) and vertices (connectors) a cube needs, and state the target: 12 edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces.
Build the cube frame, snapping straws (edges) onto connectors (balls of clay or plastic joints for vertices).

Check that every straw is the same length and that the corners are square (right angles, not leaning), because equal straws alone can still give a squashed frame with diamond-shaped faces; then compare the finished frame against a real cube-shaped solid.
Point to and count the edges, vertices and faces on the completed frame to confirm the structure.
Try building a cuboid with edges of different lengths as a contrast and describe how it differs from the cube (not all edges equal, so some faces are rectangles that are not squares).
activities.intendedInsight: A cube is defined by its structure — 12 equal edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces — and building it requires coordinating that structure rather than approximating a box shape.

activities.title: Rotate a solid and keep naming it
feedback: If the child renames a point-down or sideways shape, hand them the same object and let them rotate it continuously so they see it never changed into something else.
Redirect naming to invariant properties (triangular faces meeting at an apex) rather than to a remembered picture of its usual position.
The point-down pyramid is often a hard case — linger there and ask the child to name the faces they can see and feel.
activities.rationale: Young children often treat orientation as a defining feature and may reject a rotated shape as not matching their prototype; rotated or non-standard triangles are commonly among the harder 2-D cases, and similar orientation dependence can affect 3-D solids such as a point-down pyramid. The suggested remedy is to present and handle shapes in varied orientations and to name by properties.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is that children may not recognise a 2-D shape when it is presented in a different orientation; the remedy is to let children handle and rotate cut-outs to explore how a shape looks in different orientations, and to touch the sides and vertices as they count.

Young children treat orientation as a defining feature (e.g. rejecting a rotated shape), an 'imposed attribute' matching the prototype; a rotated isosceles triangle is the hardest case, with even a prototypical triangle missed by ~15% once rotated. Remedy: present shapes in varied orientations.
learnerActions: Hold a real pyramid (or cube) and physically turn it: point-up, on its side, point-down, and viewed from directly above.
At each orientation, say what the shape is and how you know, naming it by its properties (e.g. 'a pyramid has triangular faces meeting at an apex').
State explicitly whether the name changed when the shape turned, and explain why it should not.
Repeat with a cuboid laid on different faces, confirming it is the same solid each time.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's name comes from properties that do not change when it is rotated or viewed from a new angle; turning a solid does not make it a different shape.

activities.title: Draw 2-D shapes accurately on dotted paper or a geoboard
feedback: If the figure is not closed, return to the starting dot and count sides until the path closes.
If a side is curved, redraw it as a straight segment between two dots.
If there are too few or too many sides, re-count aloud while re-drawing, marking each side as it is placed.
activities.rationale: Marking each side as it is drawn and using dotted paper/geoboards supports accurate counting and closure; varying size while keeping the name reinforces that the name derives from invariant properties, not appearance. This strand follows the pedagogy's stated best practice; no cited source directly establishes its efficacy.
learnerActions: Draw named 2-D shapes (triangle, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon) on dotted paper or a geoboard.
Count and mark each side as it is drawn, keeping track so the figure closes with the right number of straight sides.
After drawing, re-count the sides and check the shape is closed and has straight (not curved) edges.
Draw the same shape again at a different size and confirm it keeps its name (a bigger hexagon is still a hexagon).
activities.intendedInsight: An accurate 2-D shape is a closed figure with the correct number of straight sides; its name depends on properties such as closure, side count and, for shapes like rectangles, right angles, not on size.

activities.title: Link nets and faces to the built solid
feedback: If the child cannot see a face as a 2-D shape, lay the net flat and trace one face, then fold it back into place on the solid.
Count the faces on both net and solid to confirm they match.
Note that a folded card net is a thin physical approximation of the ideal solid, which has zero-thickness faces — it stands in for the mathematical shape it represents.
activities.rationale: Connecting nets and faces to the built solid lets each face be seen as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model, reinforcing the face/edge/vertex structure. This activity extends the pedagogy's stated best practice; no source directly establishes its efficacy.
learnerActions: Fold a net into a solid, then identify each face as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model.
For a built cube frame, point out where each square face sits between four edges.
Match the faces on the net to the faces on the solid, naming the 2-D shape of each (square, triangle).
activities.intendedInsight: Each face of a solid is a 2-D shape, so 2-D and 3-D shape knowledge connect: a cube's faces are squares, a pyramid's faces include triangles.

activities.title: On-screen builder and spinner (complementary digital practice)
feedback: If the digital frame will not close, use the tally to find which count is short and add or correct that feature.
After watching the point-down pyramid keep its name on screen, re-do the same rotation with a real wooden pyramid to confirm it feels the same.

A recognition choice (e.g. 'which picture is the same pyramid rotated?') can check whether orientation is understood, but follow it with an actual build or rotation task, since choosing does not show the child can construct or turn a solid themselves.
activities.rationale: Both hard parts are spatial — coordinating edge/vertex/face structure while building and seeing a shape as the same under rotation — and interactive builders with a live tally plus a grab-and-spin solid can make these visible. A flat projection only approximates free 3-D construction and rotation, so physical materials remain central; comparative efficacy is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Using a construction tool, snap virtual edges onto vertices to build a cube; watch a live tally of edges, vertices and faces update as you work.
Notice that a lopsided attempt with unequal edges does not resolve into a correct cube until the structure matches 12 edges, 8 vertices and six square faces.
Grab and spin an on-screen pyramid through point-up, on-its-side, point-down and top-down views, reading a label that continues to name it 'a pyramid' in every orientation.
Where possible, pair each on-screen task with the matching physical build or real solid so the hands confirm the screen.
activities.intendedInsight: A live edge/vertex/face tally and free rotation make the structure and its invariance under rotation visible; the digital model complements, and does not replace, handling real solids.

constraints: The curriculum requires making 3-D shapes from modelling materials, so children should build frames and turn real solids, not only watch or tap.

Recognition tasks (multiple-choice 'which is the same shape rotated?', or picking a drawn path) can check outcomes but do not let a child build a frame or freely rotate a solid, so they must not replace construction and manipulation.

On-screen builders and spinners are useful complements but approximate true 3-D construction and free rotation in a flat projection; pair them with real straws, clay/connectors and a wooden solid where possible.

Paper and card cut-outs and straw frames have real thickness; treat them as physical approximations of the ideal mathematical solid (whose faces have zero thickness), and treat any zero-thickness screen model as a model of the solid it represents.

Name shapes by invariant properties (for 2-D: closure, number of straight sides and, where relevant, angles such as a rectangle's right angles; for 3-D: faces/edges/vertices and how they meet), not by a single remembered picture or usual position.
The point-down pyramid is often a particularly demanding orientation case for recognition and deserves extra attention.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The dotted-paper/geoboard drawing activity and the nets activity derive from the pedagogy's stated best practices; no cited source directly establishes their efficacy, so both carry sourceClaims [].

In 'Rotate a solid and keep naming it', the Oak claim cited is about 2-D shapes in different orientations; it is applied here to 3-D solids by analogy. The orientation-invariance principle transfers and is independently supported by the EJMSTE finding, but no cited source tests this specifically for 3-D solids at this age.

The cited ~15% miss rate for a rotated prototypical triangle and the 'rotated isosceles triangle is hardest' finding come from a single study (Yeşil Dağlı & Halat, 2016) and are reported as claimed, not independently re-verified here.

The original recommendation leaned heavily on a specific 3D interactive and asserted a flat medium 'cannot' teach these spatial skills; that comparative/necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been softened to a complement with stated affordances and limits.

The original marked a static tap-to-reveal image and an in-role conversation as poor fits because they do not support active production; this is retained as the narrow observable point that recognition-only or role-play formats do not themselves elicit independent construction, without claiming they teach nothing.

The source claim about faces as 'flat 2-D surfaces' is strictly true for polyhedra like cubes and pyramids but not for curved solids; the activities here concern polyhedra, so the claim is applied appropriately.

probeDeeper: Turn the pyramid so it points downwards. Is it still a pyramid? How do you know?
Your cube frame — how many straws (edges) did you use? How many corners? Should a cube have that many?
Draw the same shape again but a different size. Is it still a hexagon?
I'll lay the cuboid down on a different face — is it a different shape now?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) A closed, six-sided, straight-edged figure. (2) A cube built from 12 equal straws (edges) and 8 connectors (vertices), giving 6 square faces. (3) Identifies it as the same pyramid in every orientation — a shape's name does not change when it is rotated or viewed from a different angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to recognise a solid (or 2-D shape) in an unfamiliar orientation — says a rotated or point-down pyramid is 'a different shape' or 'not a pyramid'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Let them handle and physically rotate the solid so they see it is the same object throughout; name it by properties (triangular faces meeting at an apex) that do not change with orientation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When the pyramid is turned point-down or laid on its side, the child renames it or says it is no longer a pyramid.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds the wrong frame — incorrect number of edges/vertices, or unequal edges so the faces are not square (a wonky frame or a cuboid when a cube was asked for).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the target structure first — a cube needs 12 edges and 8 vertices — and check equal straw lengths for square faces, comparing the frame against a real cube.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws 2-D shapes inaccurately — non-closed, curved-sided, or the wrong number of sides.

topic.name: Recognising and drawing shapes by attributes
topic.description: Recognise and draw shapes having specified attributes (e.g. a given number of angles or equal faces); identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes

Identify all quadrilaterals in a set of mixed shapes

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given instructions like "draw a shape with 5 sides" or "draw a shape with all equal angles," can they draw it correctly?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to recognise and DRAW shapes that satisfy a specified attribute (e.g. exactly five sides, a given number of angles) and to identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons and hexagons within a mixed set. The procedural work is building or selecting to a property — a pentagon is any closed figure with five straight sides — rather than reproducing a memorised prototype. The central obstacle is the prototype effect: children draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, 'textbook' version and miss irregular or rotated members of the class. Best taught by generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute, and hunting for ALL members (including non-prototypical ones) in mixed sets.
bestPractices: Define each shape class by its attribute (a hexagon is ANY closed shape with 6 straight sides / 6 vertices) and check drawn shapes against it.
Demand and celebrate IRREGULAR and rotated examples — 'draw a different pentagon that doesn't look like that one' — to break the single-prototype image.
Give mixed 'find them all' sets that include irregular, tilted and near-miss shapes so identifying a class means applying the attribute, not matching a picture.
Model counting and marking each side/vertex once when drawing or checking, so the side-count is accurate.
Use dotted paper, geoboards or a peg grid to support accurate drawing of straight-sided closed figures.
keyRepresentations: Geoboard / pegboard and dotted paper for constructing polygons to a target side-count

learn.summary: Children learn to draw and identify polygons by their defining attribute — a pentagon is ANY closed figure with five straight sides whose sides do not cross each other, not one memorised 'textbook' shape. The core obstacle is the prototype effect: learners draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base version and miss irregular, tilted or rotated members of a class. Guidance centres on generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute (side/vertex count, closed, straight-sided, sides not crossing), and hunting for ALL members in mixed sets that include non-prototypical and near-miss shapes. Accurate side/vertex counting is scaffolded by marking each once.

activities.title: Build a polygon to a target side-count
feedback: If the shape has the wrong number of sides, recount together, marking each side exactly once from a clear start point; dotted paper or pegs keep sides straight.
If only a regular/symmetrical version is produced, prompt: 'Make one that is squished, tilted, or spiky but still has five straight sides' and affirm that it counts just as much.
If the figure has a gap or a curved/bulging edge, check it against the attributes aloud: is it closed? is every side straight?
Celebrate an irregular valid solution explicitly so the learner sees it is as correct as the neat one.
activities.rationale: Constructing to an attribute is an active production task that confronts the prototype effect directly; demanding varied and irregular examples is intended to break the single-image definition. Counting sides, checking closure (whether by the learner, an adult, or an optional live side-counter) and visibly accepting ANY valid (including irregular) shape are intended to make the defining attribute the thing being rewarded.
sourceClaims: A polygon is a 2-D shape made of three or more straight sides that meet at vertices; children are taught to identify and sort polygons by number of sides/vertices, using varied examples (all sides/vertices the same, some the same, all different). A common misconception is inaccurate counting of sides/vertices from losing track of the start point; remedy is to mark each side/vertex once as it is counted.

The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.
learnerActions: Given an instruction such as 'build a shape with exactly five straight sides', construct the figure on dotted paper, a geoboard, or a peg/rubber-band grid.
Count and mark each side (and vertex) once as it is drawn, so the total is checked rather than guessed.
Ensure the figure CLOSES and that every side is straight before declaring it finished.
When one valid shape is made, draw 'a different pentagon that does NOT look like the first one' — a long, spiky, or irregular one.
Compare a regular and an irregular example of the same class side by side and state why both satisfy the attribute.
activities.intendedInsight: A polygon class is defined by its attribute (number of straight sides meeting at vertices, closed figure with sides that do not cross), invariant to size, orientation and regularity — not by matching a single remembered prototype.

activities.title: Find them all in a mixed set
feedback: If an irregular or tilted member is skipped, draw attention to it and recount its sides together; attending to the awkward four-sided shape is intended to loosen the prototype grip as the learner sees the squished one also counts.
If a shape is included or excluded by its name/look alone (e.g. 'that's a diamond, not a quadrilateral'), redirect to counting the four straight sides.
If counting on an irregular shape loses track, model starting at one vertex and marking each side once around the figure.
activities.rationale: A 'find them all' set that deliberately contains non-prototypical and near-miss shapes is designed to require attribute-based classification and to surface the prototype misconception; it is hard to fake because the regular example alone is insufficient to complete the task.
sourceClaims: Young children over-rely on a prototypical exemplar: 93-96% identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-base) triangle but far fewer accept atypical types (only ~30.5% identified all three of scalene/right/isosceles) or rotated versions; a non-formal attribute matching the prototype (e.g. horizontal base) is treated as defining ('imposed attribute'). Remedy: typical + atypical examples and non-examples.

The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.
learnerActions: From a mixed set that includes regular, irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples, mark EVERY member of a named class (e.g. 'circle all the quadrilaterals').
For each shape marked or skipped, justify by counting sides/vertices and checking closed + straight-sided, not by its name or look.
Deliberately inspect the awkward shapes — a long thin tilted four-sided shape, a dented pentagon — and decide membership by the attribute.
Explain why a square is a quadrilateral, and why a 'diamond' is also a quadrilateral regardless of its orientation.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying a class means applying its attribute to every candidate, including irregular and rotated ones, rather than recognising a familiar picture.

activities.title: Name, draw and justify by attribute
feedback: If the count is wrong, recount marking each side/vertex once; dotted paper keeps the sides straight.
If both drawings look the same, ask for a genuinely different-looking version with the same number of sides.
Accept and praise any closed, straight-sided figure with the correct count regardless of regularity.
activities.rationale: Requiring a spoken/written justification by attribute, plus a deliberately varied second example, checks that the class is defined by count rather than appearance.
sourceClaims: The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.

A polygon is a 2-D shape made of three or more straight sides that meet at vertices; children are taught to identify and sort polygons by number of sides/vertices, using varied examples (all sides/vertices the same, some the same, all different). A common misconception is inaccurate counting of sides/vertices from losing track of the start point; remedy is to mark each side/vertex once as it is counted.
learnerActions: Draw a named polygon (e.g. a hexagon) and explain how you know it is one by counting its six straight sides and six vertices/angles.
Produce a second example of the same name that looks clearly different from the first.
State the defining attributes in your own words ('a hexagon is any closed shape with six straight sides that do not cross each other').
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying class membership by the attribute count — and producing a non-prototypical second example — demonstrates the definition is understood, not just a remembered shape.

constraints: Tasks must require active drawing/construction and selection, not tap-to-reveal recognition: a static labelled picture can show examples but does not itself let the learner build or choose, and active production and selection are where the prototype misconception can surface.
Mixed 'find them all' sets must include irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples; a set of only regular shapes cannot discriminate attribute-use from picture-matching.

Any 'draw a pentagon' response format should be paired with a side-count check (counting/marking by the learner or an adult), since free drawing alone does not reliably verify the exact number of straight sides.

A fixed single-answer format under-rewards the many-different-valid-answers goal; whatever format is used, multiple distinct correct shapes (including irregular ones) must be treated as equally valid.

A live side-counter, closure check, and visible acceptance of any valid shape (e.g. a highlight on a correct irregular pentagon, a pulse on a missed tilted quadrilateral) are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete, but are optional illustrations, not required technology.

The topic is primarily 2-D polygon drawing and identification; the single 'cubes' reference does not require a 3-D spatial environment. If cube identification is added, ask about the mathematical solid REPRESENTED on a thin card (which itself has slight thickness and can be held), not whether the physical card can be picked up.
Scaffolds (dotted paper, geoboards, peg grids) support accurate straight sides and counting but should not become the only medium; plain drawing and physical shape sorting are also valid.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 2-D shapes (age 8+)
topic.description: Identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations; recognise line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry
evidence: Find all lines of symmetry in a rectangle, square, and equilateral triangle
Determine whether a given shape has a line of symmetry when rotated
Identify which shapes in a set have exactly one line of symmetry
Determine how many lines of symmetry a regular hexagon has
Draw all lines of symmetry for a given figure
Identify which figures from a set are not line-symmetric
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a picture of a butterfly or a star shape, can they draw the line (or lines) where you could fold it exactly in half so both sides match?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn that a line of symmetry is a fold line: a line about which one half of a figure maps exactly onto the other. They find ALL such lines in a shape, recognise shapes that have none, and — crucially — do this whatever the shape's orientation. The defining idea is the fold-and-match test, not a counting rule: a rectangle has two lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of opposite sides), not four, and its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding along a diagonal leaves the halves misaligned. Symmetry is a structural property to be tested, never read off the number of sides.
bestPractices: Define a line of symmetry operationally — fold along it and the two halves must coincide exactly; teach children to check by drawing round a shape, cutting it out and folding (mindful that careless cutting distorts the result) (NCETM).

Actively confront the 'lines of symmetry = number of sides' over-generalisation: because early examples are usually regular shapes, children conclude a rectangle has 4 lines — give many NON-regular shapes and have them test each candidate line by folding (NCETM).
Use the rectangle as the anchor counterexample: its 2 real lines (vertical and horizontal through side-midpoints) versus its 2 falsely-assumed diagonals, disproved by folding corner-to-corner.

Present shapes in varied orientations — tilted and rotated, not just upright — so symmetry is judged by structure, not by whether a mirror line happens to be vertical; move the mirror line around (geoboard + elastic band) rather than always drawing it on upright pictures (NCETM).
Teach patterns before shapes — children recognise symmetry in patterns more readily — then progress to naming and drawing lines on shapes (NCETM).
Sort shapes by symmetry (Carroll/Venn: 'no lines', 'exactly one line', 'more than one line') to build precise vocabulary and expose non-symmetric cases.
keyRepresentations: Fold test — physically folding a cut-out shape so halves coincide (the definition made concrete)
Geoboard with an elastic band as a movable mirror line
Mira/mirror placed on a candidate line to see if the reflection completes the shape
Rectangle-versus-square comparison showing 2 lines vs 4
Carroll/Venn sorting by number of lines of symmetry
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — so a rectangle is given 4 lines instead of 2 (over-generalised from regular shapes).
Treating a diagonal of a rectangle (or other non-square) as a line of symmetry, when folding along it shows the halves do not match.
Only recognising a line of symmetry when it is vertical/upright, missing symmetry in tilted or rotated shapes.
Thinking every shape must have at least one line of symmetry (not recognising asymmetric shapes).

learn.summary: Children learn that a line of symmetry is a fold line: a line about which one half of a figure maps exactly onto the other. The defining idea is an operational fold-and-match test, not a counting rule. A non-square rectangle has two lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of opposite sides), not four, and its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding corner-to-corner leaves the halves misaligned (a square, the special rectangle, has 4 lines including its diagonals). Children find ALL lines in a shape, recognise shapes with none, and judge symmetry whatever the shape's orientation. The activities use physical folding of cut-out shapes and movable mirror lines to confront the common 'lines = number of sides' over-generalisation, with item-based and tappable-image formats as complementary assessment and illustration.

activities.title: Fold-and-match test with a drawn candidate line
feedback: When halves coincide exactly, the line is a true line of symmetry; where corners or edges miss, it is not — e.g. an optional green overlay for a match and red where halves fail to meet makes this vivid.
If a learner marks 4 lines on the rectangle, have them fold each: the two diagonals fail, leaving 2 true lines.

If a learner says a diagonal 'cuts it in half so it counts', fold corner-to-corner and look at the corners — 'cuts in half' is not the same as 'folds onto itself'; the two triangles are congruent but do not land on each other under the fold.
If a learner only finds symmetry when a line is upright, keep the shape tilted and fold along the sloping line to show symmetry belongs to the shape, not the page.

A paper or card cut-out has slight thickness and may be imperfectly cut; treat the fold result as testing the ideal flat shape it represents, and re-check a near-miss in case it is only a cutting artefact.
activities.rationale: The misconception lives in the child's own proposed line, so letting them test their OWN candidate lines by folding gives the felt refutation of the counting rule. Physical cut-and-fold, or a model that folds across a drawn line, makes the operational definition concrete; varied orientations prevent the 'symmetry must be upright' habit.
sourceClaims: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.

Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
learnerActions: Start with a cut-out or on-screen rectangle. Draw where you think each fold line (line of symmetry) should be, and say why before testing.
Fold (or let a screen model fold) one half across each drawn line and check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Deliberately try a diagonal corner-to-corner: fold along it and watch the far corners — they miss each other, so it is NOT a line of symmetry.
Confirm the vertical and horizontal lines through the side midpoints: these fold to an exact match, so the rectangle has 2 lines, not 4.
Tilt or rotate the shape (e.g. 30-40 degrees) and re-check the same lines are still there without turning the page upright.
Progress to non-regular polygons and a few asymmetric shapes (answer: 0 lines), testing every candidate line by folding.
activities.intendedInsight: A line of symmetry is whatever survives the fold-and-match test, not whatever a count-the-sides rule predicts; symmetry is a structural property of the shape independent of its orientation.

activities.title: Movable mirror line on a geoboard or with a mirror
feedback: If the reflected image does not line up with the existing half, the mirror is not on a line of symmetry — move it and try again.
When completing a half-shape, check the finished figure folds onto itself along the given line.
Careless cutting distorts a cut-out, so a near-miss fold may be a cutting artefact — re-check with a mirror or a cleaner cut-out.
activities.rationale: A movable mirror line decouples symmetry from page orientation and lets children explore many candidate positions; starting from patterns matches the reported ease ordering. Completion tasks rehearse the Year 4 objective of completing a symmetric figure about a specific line.
sourceClaims: Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
learnerActions: Use a geoboard with an elastic band (or a Mira/mirror laid on a candidate line) as a movable mirror line.
Move the mirror line around the shape rather than always drawing it on an upright picture; check whether the reflection completes the shape.
Begin with symmetric patterns before moving to named shapes, recognising symmetry in patterns first.
Complete the missing half of a shape given a specific line of symmetry.
activities.intendedInsight: A mirror line can sit anywhere, and reflection across the right line reproduces the shape; recognising symmetry in patterns builds toward naming and drawing lines on shapes.

activities.title: Sort shapes by number of lines of symmetry
feedback: A shape with no line of symmetry is a valid answer — not every shape is symmetric.

If a learner says the rectangle has 4 lines like the square because both have 4 sides, test the rectangle's diagonals by folding to show it has exactly 2 lines (still in 'more than one line', like the square, but with a different count).
Use the regular hexagon (6 lines, 6 sides), equilateral triangle (3 lines, 3 sides) and rectangle (2 lines, 4 sides) side by side to pin down exactly when the side-count rule works.
When a learner justifies a placement only by counting sides, ask them to fold a candidate line — the regular cases and the rectangle then separate clearly.
activities.rationale: Sorting builds precise vocabulary and brings non-symmetric and non-regular cases into view, which supports attacking the over-generalisation from regular shapes; a sort checks classification but does not itself elicit folding, so each placement is justified by the fold-and-match test. Comparing triangle, square, rectangle and hexagon isolates why the counting rule is only sometimes valid.
sourceClaims: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.

learnerActions: Sort a set of shapes into 'no lines', 'exactly one line', and 'more than one line' using a Carroll or Venn arrangement.
Include non-regular and asymmetric shapes so cases with zero lines appear.
For each shape, justify its placement by the fold-and-match test rather than by counting sides.
Compare an equilateral triangle (3 lines), a square (4 lines), a rectangle (2 lines) and a regular hexagon (6 lines), and discuss when 'lines = sides' holds and when it breaks.
activities.intendedInsight: Symmetry must be tested per shape; 'lines = number of sides' holds only for regular shapes, so the equilateral triangle, square and regular hexagon match their side counts while the (non-regular) rectangle has fewer lines than its 4 sides.

activities.title: Check items and tappable-line illustration (assessment and support)
feedback: For the rectangle item, the answer is 2; choosing 4 signals the count-the-sides rule and choosing the diagonals signals the 'cuts in half' error — both are refuted by folding.

On a tilted shape that does have a line of symmetry, a 'no symmetry' answer usually means the learner is only looking for upright lines; re-test by folding along a sloping line (a tilted asymmetric shape genuinely has 0 lines).
The tappable overlay shows which fixed lines match, but it reveals pre-drawn lines rather than the learner's own guess, so pair it with hands-on folding of a candidate line the learner proposes.
activities.rationale: Items offering 4 and the diagonals as tempting wrong answers help separate the heuristic from the method, because the two give different answers for a rectangle. A tappable fold-reveal illustrates the idea and supports learners, but because it presents fixed lines it does not let the child test their own proposed line, where the misconception actually lives. Recognition items assess the concept but do not themselves generate the fold-and-match evidence the learner must produce.

learnerActions: Answer short items: 'How many lines of symmetry does this rectangle have?' (with 4 and 'the diagonals' as tempting wrong options), draw all lines on a given figure, decide whether a statement about a tilted shape is true or false, and sort shapes by number of lines.
Include at least one tilted shape and one asymmetric shape in any set.
As a lighter support, tap each drawn line on a static shape to reveal a fold overlay showing match or mismatch, and open a flap asking 'does the diagonal work?' answered by the mismatched fold.

constraints: Define a line of symmetry operationally: fold along it and the two halves must coincide exactly. Teach checking by drawing round a shape, cutting it out and folding — but note careless cutting distorts the result, so a near-miss may be a cutting artefact.
Actively confront the 'lines = number of sides' over-generalisation with many NON-regular shapes; do not rely only on regular shapes, which breed the misconception.

Use the rectangle as the anchor counterexample (2 real lines vs 2 falsely assumed diagonals) and contrast with equilateral triangle (3), square (4) and regular hexagon (6) to show the side-count rule holds for regular shapes only.
Present shapes in varied orientations (tilted and rotated), judging symmetry by structure, not by whether a mirror line happens to be vertical.

A paper or card cut-out has slight thickness and can be imperfectly cut; treat it as an approximation of the ideal flat shape whose exact halves coincide, and reason about the mathematical shape it represents rather than the physical card.
Recognition and multiple-choice items assess the concept but do not, by themselves, generate the fold-and-match evidence the learner must produce; pair them with hands-on or learner-proposed folding.

A tappable-line reveal shows fixed, pre-drawn lines; it illustrates the idea but does not let a child test their own candidate line, so use it as support alongside active folding, not as a replacement.
This is planar (line/reflective) symmetry of 2-D shapes; keep away from 3-D planes of symmetry and depth, which are a different topic.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a paper rectangle. Ask them to PREDICT how many lines of symmetry it has and to mark where, saying WHY before folding. Then have them fold along each marked line and OBSERVE which folds make the halves coincide. The prediction of 4 (or of a working diagonal) is violated when the diagonal fold leaves the corners apart — the child then EXPLAINS that only the vertical and horizontal folds match, so there are 2.
probeDeeper: 'You folded along the vertical line and the halves matched. Now fold along a diagonal — what happens to the corners?' (counterexample that refutes the diagonal directly).
'A square has 4 lines of symmetry. Why does this rectangle have fewer, even though both have 4 sides?' (forces reasoning about equal vs unequal sides, not the counting rule).

'A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry — the same as its number of sides. So is "lines = sides" a good rule? When does it work and when does it break?' (tests understanding of WHY the rule holds for regular shapes only).
Rotate the rectangle 40°: 'Does it still have lines of symmetry? Show me where, without turning the page.' (orientation-independence).
assess.correctAnswer: Two lines of symmetry — one vertical and one horizontal, each through the midpoints of opposite sides. The child justifies each by the fold-and-match test (folding along the line, the two halves land exactly on each other) and explains that the diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding corner-to-corner leaves the halves misaligned.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides, so a rectangle 'has 4' ('four sides, four lines')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold the rectangle along each proposed line; the diagonals fail. Contrast with the square (4) and a regular hexagon (6) to show the rule holds ONLY for regular shapes, and have the child test many non-regular shapes.
errorPatterns.distractor: 4 lines of symmetry — one for each side
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States 4 lines for the rectangle; applies a counting rule rather than folding; often confident because it worked on squares and regular shapes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a diagonal of the rectangle as a line of symmetry (fold corner-to-corner)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold along the diagonal and look at the corners — they do not meet; the two triangles are congruent but reflected the wrong way. Establish that 'cuts it in half' is not the same as 'folds onto itself'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The two diagonals are also lines of symmetry
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws one or both diagonals as lines of symmetry and claims the halves 'match'; has not actually tested the fold, or judges by the line 'splitting it in two' rather than by congruent reflection.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only recognises a line of symmetry when it is vertical/upright, missing symmetry in a tilted or rotated shape
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep the shape tilted and use a mirror/fold along a sloping line; show symmetry is a property of the shape, not of the page orientation. Revisit vertical-only symmetry from Year 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a rotated shape (surfaced by a follow-up), finds no line or only a would-be vertical one; needs to turn the shape upright before spotting symmetry.

responseLevels.gap: Counts lines of symmetry as the number of sides (rectangle = 4), includes diagonals, and/or only looks for a vertical line; cannot justify by folding.
responseLevels.full: Identifies all and only the true lines of symmetry by the fold-onto-itself test, rejects the rectangle's diagonals with a corner-mismatch justification, finds symmetry regardless of orientation, and explains that 'lines = sides' holds for regular shapes only — transferring correctly to non-regular and asymmetric shapes.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the two true lines by folding on an upright shape but cannot fully justify why the diagonals fail, or reverts to the counting rule on an unfamiliar shape, or misses symmetry when the shape is tilted. assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show an upright rectangle (clearly not a square). Ask: 'How many lines of symmetry does this rectangle have? Draw each one. Then tell me: how do you KNOW each line you drew is a line of symmetry — and how would you decide whether a line is NOT one?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rectangle is the decisive shape: a child using the 'lines = number of sides' rule answers 4 (adding the two diagonals), while a child using the fold-and-match test answers 2 — the heuristic and the correct method give DIFFERENT answers here, so the response separates them. topic.description: Understand that shapes in different categories may share attributes defining a larger category; classify quadrilaterals (rhombuses, rectangles, squares) and draw examples of quadrilaterals not in those subcategories

pedagogy.summary: By Y4, children move from naming shapes by look (van Hiele level 1) to reasoning about defining properties (level 2), and start the class-inclusion idea (level 3): a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) because it has every property a rectangle needs plus the extra property of four equal sides. The obstacle is prototype/partition thinking — a child sorts each shape into exactly one box and rejects a square as a rectangle because it doesn't look like the 'long' rectangle they picture. Teaching works by shifting the question from 'what does it look like?' to 'what tests must it pass?', so category membership is decided by properties, not appearance.
bestPractices: Define categories by an explicit checklist of properties (rectangle = 4 right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) and let children TEST a shape against the checklist rather than judge by eye
Use nested/overlapping Venn or set diagrams so a shape can visibly sit in two categories at once — this attacks the partition assumption that each shape belongs to exactly one box
Deliberately include non-prototypical examples: a square, a rectangle tilted 45°, a very-nearly-square rectangle, so 'rectangle' is not welded to the long-oblong prototype
Contrast examples with non-examples: ask children to draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, forcing them to reason about which properties are absent
Insist on justification in the child's own words ('it is a rectangle because...') — knowing the shared properties is the point, not the yes/no answer
keyRepresentations: Property checklist / definition card for each category (right-angle marks, equal-side tick marks, parallel arrows)
Nested Venn diagram: quadrilaterals ⊃ rectangles ⊃ squares, with rhombuses overlapping so square sits in the intersection
A 'stretchy' square that can be pulled into an oblong rectangle or squashed to a rhombus, showing square as the special case where both hold
Set-square and ruler to physically verify right angles and equal sides
commonMisconceptions: A square is not a rectangle — they are two different, separate kinds of shape (exclusive/partition thinking)
A rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square cannot be one (oblong prototype; the unequal-sides attribute is wrongly treated as defining)
A shape can only belong to one category, so it cannot be a rectangle AND a square at the same time
A square turned 45° is a 'diamond', not a square (orientation bound to the prototype)

activities.title: Sort and stretch: does the shape pass the rectangle tests?
feedback: When a learner says a square is 'too square' to be a rectangle, walk the rectangle checklist together item by item; if it passes every test, the square belongs in the 'rectangle' ring without leaving 'square'.

If a learner thinks a rectangle must have two long and two short sides, show a run of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square, confirming each passes the same tests — length is not a defining property.

If a learner accepts the shared properties yet still won't let one shape be in two categories, offer everyday inclusion analogies (a spaniel is a dog AND an animal at once) and more nested-set practice rather than drilling the yes/no fact.
Reinforce justification: the point is naming the shared properties ('four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel'), not the bare yes/no answer.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable surface lets children test a shape against a visible checklist and watch labels attach or drop as properties change — making 'membership by property, not appearance' concrete. A stretch tool that keeps the 'rectangle' label while dropping the 'square' badge, and nested rings that show one shape in two boxes at once, directly address partition and oblong-prototype thinking. Optional interaction examples (draggable handles, a checklist that ticks green as each test passes, snapping to the deepest qualifying region) make the mechanism tangible but are not mandatory.

learnerActions: Take a plain quadrilateral and adjust its corners until all four angles are right angles (check with a set-square); confirm whether opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Run the rectangle checklist item by item — '4 right angles? ✓ opposite sides equal and parallel? ✓' — and place the shape inside the 'rectangle' ring of a nested diagram when it passes all tests.

Now, starting from a rectangle with all four sides equal (a square), pull one pair of opposite sides longer while keeping all four right angles, so the shape stays a rectangle but is no longer a square; then shorten them, still keeping the right angles, until all four sides are equal again and watch it move into the innermost 'square' region nested inside 'rectangle', which is nested inside 'quadrilateral'.
Say out loud, in your own words, why the SAME shape can sit in two boxes at once ('it is a rectangle because... and also a square because...').
Repeat with a rhombus checklist to see the square also sits inside 'rhombus' where the rings overlap.
activities.intendedInsight: Category membership is decided by which property tests a shape passes, not by how it looks; a square passes every rectangle test, so a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) — and one shape can belong to two nested categories at once.

activities.title: Predict, test, explain with a real square
feedback: A correct answer is 'yes — a square is a rectangle: it has four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel, plus its four sides happen to be equal, so it is a special rectangle.'
If a learner judges by appearance ('it's too square-looking') and cannot state the defining properties, build the checklist together and test item by item.
For 'a square turned 45° is a diamond', confirm turning a shape does not change which property tests it passes, so it is still a square and still a rectangle.

When asked to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle, the learner should discover this is impossible: every square passes all the rectangle tests, so no such shape exists — whereas a rectangle that is not a square CAN be drawn. Noticing this one-way asymmetry is the sign of real property-based understanding.
Treat 'it can be a square OR a rectangle but not both' as a maturing class-inclusion stage, not a false fact; give more nested-set experience rather than correction drills.
activities.rationale: A predict–test–explain routine with a physical square, set-square and ruler makes the diagnostic reasoning visible and lets children verify right angles and equal sides themselves. Asking for the reason, not just the answer, discriminates property-based reasoning from a lucky 'yes' backed only by 'both have four sides'.

Check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler: four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel?

Answer probing questions: Does it matter how long the sides are? Is a square turned to look like a diamond still a square and still a rectangle? Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?
Decide whether a square is also a special rhombus, and justify.

The asymmetry — you can draw a rectangle that is not a square, but not a square that is not a rectangle — is the tell of genuine understanding.

activities.title: Draw the exceptions and defend the claim
feedback: Accept a non-example only when the learner shows a defining property is missing for each category it must be excluded from. Some missing properties exclude only some categories: 'no right angles → not a rectangle or square' still leaves rhombus open, so also check 'the four sides are not all equal → not a rhombus or square'. One missing property can exclude all three: rectangles, rhombuses and squares all have both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so a shape without two pairs of parallel sides (e.g. a kite or trapezium) is none of them.
Accept the inclusion claim only when the learner cites the defining properties the square passes, not just that 'it looks like one' or 'both have four sides'.
If a learner cannot produce a non-prototypical rectangle, offer tilted and nearly-square examples and have them verify each against the checklist.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples with non-examples forces attention to defining versus non-defining attributes, and justification in the child's own words is the learning target. An in-role classifier who presses 'but it doesn't look like a rectangle — why does it still count?' surfaces and names the reasoning; dialogue here supports the property inspection rather than replacing it.
