learnerActions: Draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, and say which defining property it is missing for EACH of those three categories.
Draw a rectangle that is not a square.
Explain to a sceptical 'shape detective' why a square still counts as a rectangle even though it doesn't look like a long oblong, citing the defining properties it passes.
Sort a mixed set of quadrilaterals (including a square, a 45°-tilted rectangle, and a nearly-square rectangle) into a nested/overlapping Venn, justifying each placement by properties.

constraints: Target concept is property-based classification and class inclusion, not shape naming; always require justification by defining properties, not a bare yes/no.

A scored sort/multiple-choice can assess whether a child accepts the inclusion (e.g. 'Is a square a rectangle?' with distractor 'No, they are different shapes') but does not by itself let the child feel a square pass the tests; use it to check, not to build, the insight.

A static tap-to-reveal Venn or hierarchy is a useful summary/reference showing where a square sits, but because nothing recomputes the child cannot TEST a shape's membership; best used after hands-on testing rather than as the primary route.

Distinguish an ideal zero-thickness plane figure from physical card/cutouts, which have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat cutouts as approximations of the represented flat shape and ask about the mathematical shape represented, not whether the physical card can be picked up. Quadrilateral classification is a planar, 2D property idea, so a third spatial dimension is not needed here (a limit of relevance, not evidence that any one medium is superior).
Treat the one-box (class-inclusion) stage as developmental: give more nested-set and everyday-inclusion experience rather than drilling the fact.
Set-square/ruler verification and recolouring/ticking checklists are optional supports to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.

assess.correctAnswer: Yes — a square is a rectangle. A rectangle needs four right angles and opposite sides that are equal and parallel; a square has all of those, plus its four sides happen to be equal too, so it is a special kind of rectangle.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a rectangle property checklist together and test the square against it item by item; use a nested Venn so the child sees the square can sit inside 'rectangle' without leaving 'square'. Reteach in place — this is the target concept.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a square and a rectangle are different kinds of shape
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no' and, on the reason tier, treats square and rectangle as separate named categories rather than comparing properties

errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate defining properties (right angles, opposite sides equal/parallel) from typical appearance; show a range of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square so the prototype loosens. Revisit shape-property work.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides

pedagogy.summary: Classifying figures by their line properties is the procedural core of van Hiele level 2: instead of sorting shapes by overall look, the child TESTS each figure for a property — are these two sides parallel? do these two meet at a right angle? is there a 90° angle in this triangle? — and sorts on the result. The skill is applying a reliable CHECK (sliding or extending a ruler, using a set-square or the corner of a page) rather than eyeballing. Two obstacles dominate: confusing the words parallel and perpendicular, and treating a non-defining feature — line length, or horizontal/vertical orientation — as if it decided the classification, because textbook examples almost always show equal-length parallel lines in standard orientation.
bestPractices: Teach a physical CHECK for each relation: parallel = the gap stays constant / the lines never meet (slide a ruler between them or extend them); perpendicular / right angle = test with a set-square or the square corner of a card
Show parallel and perpendicular lines of DIFFERENT lengths, thicknesses and orientations, so pupils sort on the property rather than the appearance (NCETM)
Use 'nearly' examples — lines that are almost-but-not-parallel, a triangle with an almost-right angle — so a checking method is genuinely needed; obvious examples let pupils guess by eye
Ask pupils to DRAW a line parallel or perpendicular to a given one, and to draw a right triangle in a non-standard orientation — producing, not just spotting
Present right triangles rotated and in scalene form so 'right triangle' is defined by the 90° angle, not by a horizontal-and-vertical-legs prototype
keyRepresentations: Set-square or the square corner of a card as a right-angle checker; a ruler slid between two lines to test constant distance
Carroll and Venn sorting grids with criteria ('has parallel sides', 'has a right angle', regular/irregular)
A dynamic pair of lines whose length and orientation vary while the parallel/perpendicular relation is held or broken
Sets of triangles varied by orientation and side length — some right-angled, some not
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the vocabulary — mixes up 'parallel' and 'perpendicular'
Thinks parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by always-equal-length textbook examples)
Only recognises parallel/perpendicular when the lines are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs
Fails to recognise a right triangle when it is rotated or looks scalene (right-angle-legs prototype)

learn.summary: Help 9-10 year olds classify 2-D figures by TESTING line properties (parallel sides, perpendicular sides, right angles in triangles) rather than sorting by overall appearance. The core skill is applying a reliable physical check — sliding or extending a ruler to confirm a constant gap for parallel lines, and using a set-square or the square corner of a card to confirm a 90 degree angle — and then sorting on the result. A single figure may carry more than one property (a rectangle has parallel sides AND right angles), so each property is decided by its own independent check. Two obstacles dominate: confusing the words 'parallel' and 'perpendicular', and treating non-defining features (unequal line length, or horizontal/vertical orientation) as if they decided the classification, because typical textbook pictures show equal-length parallel lines in standard orientation.

activities.title: Sort the tray: test every figure before you bin it
feedback: If a learner rejects the tilted unequal-length pair, saying the lines are 'not the same length so not parallel', show two parallel lines of very different lengths and slide the ruler between them — parallel means the gap stays constant / the lines never meet, and length does not matter.

If a learner only accepts horizontal or vertical parallels or an upright right triangle, slowly rotate the same figure and let them watch the ruler gap stay constant or the set-square still fit — the property is preserved when you turn the figure.

If a learner accepts the slowly-converging pair as parallel by eye, have them measure the gap straight across at each end to see that it changes, and extend both lines in the direction they close up to show they would meet (if the meeting point is off the page, the changing gap is still the evidence), showing the eyeball guess was wrong.

If a learner is unsure where the rectangle belongs, have them run the two checks separately — slide the ruler for the constant gap and fit the set-square in a corner — and see that it passes both, so it is recorded as having parallel sides AND a right angle.

If a learner swaps the words, re-anchor each to its check: parallel lines run alongside and never meet (the ruler gap holds); perpendicular lines cross at a right angle (the set-square fits the corner). Have them name the relation while performing the check.
activities.rationale: Classifying by property is a doing-and-checking skill at the heart of this objective; building figures that defeat eyeballing (unequal-length tilted parallels, near-parallels, rotated right triangles) is intended to require a genuine check rather than a glance, which can help counter the equal-length and horizontal-orientation prototypes. Testing each property independently keeps multi-property figures like rectangles coherent.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective 'Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines, and properties of rectangles'; misconceptions = pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/thicknesses and orientations, use 'nearly' examples that force a checking method, and ask pupils to DRAW a line parallel/perpendicular to a given one

Children reason from prototypes and impose non-defining/salient attributes (e.g. orientation, a horizontal base) as if defining, and reject non-prototypical or rotated examples of a shape category — the mechanism behind not recognising a rotated right triangle
learnerActions: Lay out a mixed tray of shapes and lines including a pair of parallel lines of clearly DIFFERENT lengths tilted off horizontal, a pair that looks parallel but slowly converges, a right-angled triangle rotated so neither leg is horizontal or vertical, a rectangle, and a non-right triangle.

For each pair of sides, test for parallel: slide a ruler along one side keeping it touching, and check whether the gap to the opposite side stays the same, measuring straight across (at right angles to the lines) at two or more places, including near both ends where the lines lie alongside each other, or extend both lines to see whether they would meet.
For each corner you suspect is a right angle, drop a set-square or the square corner of a card into the corner and check whether it fits exactly against both sides.

Record each figure by property, testing the two properties independently: does it have a pair of parallel sides? does it have a right angle / is it a right triangle? A figure may pass BOTH tests (a rectangle has parallel sides AND right angles), just one, or neither — note what each check shows rather than forcing it into a single exclusive box, and only decide after the check, not after a glance.

Say out loud, for at least three figures, which check you used and what it showed (for example: 'I slid the ruler and the gap never changed, so these sides are parallel even though one line is longer' or 'the rectangle passed both — parallel sides and a right-angle corner').
activities.intendedInsight: A property, not the look of a figure, decides the category: a tilted, unequal-length pair is just as parallel as a tidy horizontal pair, and a rotated triangle is still a right triangle if a corner tests at 90 degrees. Properties are independent, so a figure can have both (a rectangle), one, or neither. The question shifts from 'does it look like the book example?' to 'does it pass the test?'

activities.title: Draw it, don't just spot it
feedback: If the learner's 'parallel' line visibly converges on checking, point to where the gap changes and ask them to redraw keeping the ruler's reported gap constant.
If the 'perpendicular' line fails the set-square, show the gap between the card's square corner and the line and have them adjust until it fits.
If the learner only draws an upright right triangle, ask them to draw one more tilted so no side is straight across or straight up, then confirm the 90 degree corner is still present.
activities.rationale: Construction tasks require the learner to generate the property themselves and check their own work; because recognising ready-made examples does not by itself elicit production, a drawing task adds evidence that the learner can produce the property, and drawing in non-standard orientations directly targets the orientation prototype.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective 'Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines, and properties of rectangles'; misconceptions = pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/thicknesses and orientations, use 'nearly' examples that force a checking method, and ask pupils to DRAW a line parallel/perpendicular to a given one
learnerActions: Given a line drawn at an angle (not horizontal or vertical), draw a second line parallel to it, then check your own drawing by sliding a ruler to confirm the gap is constant.
Given another angled line, draw a line perpendicular to it, then check with a set-square or square corner that the crossing is a right angle.
Draw a right triangle that stands on its point or sits at an angle, so that neither of the two shorter sides is horizontal or vertical; mark the right angle and verify it with the set-square.
Swap drawings with a partner and test each other's lines and triangle with the ruler and set-square, reporting whether each one passes.
activities.intendedInsight: Producing parallel and perpendicular lines, and a right triangle in a non-standard orientation, is evidence the learner holds the defining property rather than copying a familiar picture.

activities.title: Sorting grids for mixed properties
feedback: If a learner cannot place a rectangle in the 'both' cell, have them separately test a pair of sides for the constant gap and a corner for 90 degrees, then see both tests pass.
If placements are made by appearance, ask them to demonstrate the check for one figure in each cell before moving on.
activities.rationale: Carroll/Venn-style grids make the independence of the two properties explicit and reveal whether a learner can hold more than one criterion at once, which a single-bin sort does not require.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory content: pupils use the properties of rectangles and recognise/use parallel and perpendicular lines; classify shapes by their properties
learnerActions: Set up a two-way sorting grid: one axis 'has parallel sides / no parallel sides', the other 'has a right angle / no right angle'.
Place each figure from a mixed set into the correct cell, including shapes that belong in the cell with BOTH parallel sides and a right angle (such as a rectangle).
For each placement, state the check you used and keep the ruler and set-square to hand so you can re-test any figure a classmate questions.
activities.intendedInsight: Properties combine: a figure can have parallel sides, a right angle, both, or neither, and each property is decided by its own independent check.

activities.title: Quick reference card for the two words
feedback: If a learner relies on the card to decide a figure's classification, redirect them to run the check on the figure itself, since the card only reminds them what the words mean.
activities.rationale: A static reference may support vocabulary recall and self-correction, but because nothing on it recomputes for a specific figure, it should sit alongside — not replace — the hands-on checking that carries the concept.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective 'Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines, and properties of rectangles'; misconceptions = pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/thicknesses and orientations, use 'nearly' examples that force a checking method, and ask pupils to DRAW a line parallel/perpendicular to a given one
learnerActions: Keep a small reference card where pointing to a pair of sides shows 'parallel: always the same distance apart, never meet' and pointing to a corner shows the 90 degree square for 'perpendicular / right angle'.
Use the card to settle vocabulary disputes during the sorting and drawing tasks, then return to the physical check to confirm the actual figure.
activities.intendedInsight: A quick visual anchor helps keep 'parallel' and 'perpendicular' straight, but naming is not the same as verifying — the figure in front of you still has to pass the ruler or set-square test.

constraints: The classification skill is a doing-and-checking action: learners must physically test figures (slide/extend a ruler, apply a set-square or square card corner), not only name or recognise properties.

Include figures that defeat eyeballing — a tilted pair of parallel lines of unequal length, a slowly-converging near-parallel pair, and a right triangle rotated off the horizontal-and-vertical-legs position — because obvious upright examples let learners guess by appearance.

Treat the two properties as independent and test each on its own: a figure such as a rectangle can have both parallel sides and right angles, so do not force figures into a single exclusive bin — record each property separately or use a two-way grid.

Tasks that only ask learners to select or drag pre-made figures into categories test the classification outcome but do not require the learner to perform the ruler/set-square check, which is the actual skill; pair any such recognition task with hands-on checking or construction.
A reference poster or card supports vocabulary but does not let the learner verify an individual figure; treat it as a summary aid after hands-on work, not as the main activity.
Spoken discussion can rehearse the vocabulary and reasoning but does not itself perform the manual test; use talk to accompany checking rather than replace it.
This objective concerns parallel and perpendicular relations within flat 2-D figures; parallel/perpendicular in three dimensions is a later, distinct idea and is not required here.

The ruler, set-square and square card corner are physical approximations with real thickness; use them as practical checking tools, and keep the focus on the relation they reveal (constant gap, 90 degree corner) rather than on the tool itself.

probeDeeper: How did you CHECK that these two lines are parallel — what did you do to be sure they never meet?
These two lines are different lengths — can they still be parallel? How do you know?
I'll turn this right triangle so it stands on its point — is it still a right triangle? Show me how you can tell.
Here are two lines that look parallel but slowly get closer together — how would you find out for certain?
assess.correctAnswer: The child uses a physical check — slides or extends lines to confirm two sides stay the same distance apart (parallel), and applies the set-square/paper corner to confirm a 90° angle — and sorts on the result: places the tilted, unequal-length pair with the parallels, rejects the slowly-converging pair, and identifies the rotated triangle as a right triangle regardless of its orientation.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the vocabulary — swaps 'parallel' and 'perpendicular', e.g. calls a right-angle corner 'parallel' or a pair of parallel sides 'perpendicular'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor each word to its check and image: parallel lines run alongside and never meet (slide the ruler, the gap holds); perpendicular lines cross at a right angle (set-square clicks). Rehearse naming while checking.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the parallel label to lines meeting at 90° or vice-versa; uses the two words interchangeably while sorting

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks parallel lines must be the SAME LENGTH — rejects a genuinely parallel pair because the two lines are unequal in length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show parallel lines of very different lengths and thicknesses; define parallel by constant distance / never meeting, tested by sliding a ruler or extending them — length is irrelevant (NCETM).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Excludes the tilted, unequal-length pair from the parallel set, giving a length reason ('they're not the same length, so they can't be parallel')

errorPatterns.pattern: Orientation-bound — only accepts parallel/perpendicular when the lines are horizontal or vertical, and does not recognise a right triangle once it is rotated off a horizontal-and-vertical-legs position
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the same figures slowly so the child sees the property is preserved under turning, and test the right angle with the set-square in any orientation (prototype/imposed-attribute: orientation wrongly treated as defining).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts the tilted parallel pair and the rotated right triangle as 'not parallel' / 'not a right triangle'; only the upright examples are accepted

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by eye without testing — calls an almost-90° angle 'a right angle' or the slowly-converging pair 'parallel' because they look right
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the check with the 'nearly' examples where eyeballing fails — obvious examples do not need a method, near ones do (NCETM).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the near-right angle or the converging pair without sliding/extending or applying the set-square

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by overall appearance or the equal-length/horizontal prototype; rejects the tilted unequal-length parallels and the rotated right triangle; uses 'parallel' and 'perpendicular' interchangeably; does not apply a check.
responseLevels.full: Tests each figure with a reliable method (constant distance / extend for parallel; set-square for right angles) and sorts on the property regardless of length or orientation — correctly placing the tilted unequal-length parallels, rejecting the converging pair, and identifying the rotated right triangle; explains the check and transfers to a new mixed set.
responseLevels.partial: Applies a check to the obvious, upright examples and classifies them correctly, but reverts to appearance on the tilted/unequal or rotated items, or is unsure which word is which — can list the properties but does not reliably test every figure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a mixed set of shapes and lines. Include: (i) a pair of parallel lines of clearly DIFFERENT lengths, tilted off horizontal; (ii) a pair that looks parallel but slowly converges; (iii) a right-angled triangle rotated so neither leg is horizontal or vertical; and (iv) a rectangle and a non-right triangle. Give the child a set-square or the square corner of a card and say: 'Sort these — which have parallel sides, and which have a right angle or are right triangles — and show me how you check each one.' Say nothing about method; watch what they DO.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The items are built so that eyeballing fails and only a check succeeds. A child who sorts by property uses the tools and gets the tilted unequal-length pair and the rotated right triangle right; a child ruled by the equal-length/horizontal prototype rejects the tilted unequal pair ('they're different lengths / not straight across') and misses the rotated right triangle; a child who confuses the words applies the wrong test to the wrong figure. Watching the checking action — not asking 'what does parallel mean?' — reveals which.

topic.name: Regular and irregular polygons
topic.description: Distinguish between regular and irregular polygons based on reasoning about equal sides and equal angles
evidence: Classify a set of polygons as regular or irregular
Explain that a regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and 5 equal angles
Identify that a rectangle is irregular (equal angles but not all equal sides) unless it is a square
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a stop sign (regular octagon) and a wonky eight-sided shape, can they explain which is regular and which is irregular — and why?

pedagogy.summary: A polygon is regular only when it meets TWO conditions at once — all sides equal AND all angles equal; failing either makes it irregular. Because the concept is a conjunction, the characteristic error is applying just ONE criterion, usually the more salient 'all sides equal', so a rhombus (four equal sides, unequal angles) gets wrongly called regular; less often a rectangle (four equal angles, unequal sides) does. The square is the pivotal case — the one quadrilateral that satisfies both. Teaching succeeds when children habitually check BOTH sides and angles and can name a shape that passes one test but fails the other. A secondary trap is everyday language: hearing 'regular' as 'ordinary/tidy' and 'irregular' as 'odd-looking'.
bestPractices: State regularity as a conjunction and always check BOTH conditions: equal sides AND equal angles; a shape that fails either is irregular
Use the rhombus and the (non-square) rectangle as the key teaching cases — each satisfies exactly one condition — to break the single-criterion habit
Contrast with the square, the quadrilateral that satisfies both, so children see why it, and not the oblong rectangle or the non-square rhombus, is regular
Include many-sided and non-standard-orientation examples, and avoid only ever showing regular shapes, so 'regular' is not welded to a symmetric-looking prototype (NCETM)
Separate the mathematical meaning of regular/irregular from the everyday meaning
keyRepresentations: A two-column check applied to each shape: sides equal? (tick/cross) | angles equal? (tick/cross)
A regular pentagon/hexagon/equilateral triangle beside their irregular counterparts (an irregular pentagon, a rhombus, an oblong rectangle)
Sorting / Carroll cards: 'regular polygon', 'irregular polygon', 'equal sides but not equal angles', 'at least one right angle' (NCETM)
The rhombus (sides tick, angles cross) and the rectangle (angles tick, sides cross) flanking the square (both tick)
commonMisconceptions: Regular = equal sides only — ignores the equal-angles condition, so a rhombus is wrongly called regular
Regular = equal angles only — so a non-square rectangle is wrongly called regular
'Regular' means an ordinary/symmetrical/tidy-looking shape and 'irregular' means an odd or random-looking one (everyday-language interference)
Assumes a polygon has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides — over-generalised from only ever seeing regular examples (NCETM)

learn.summary: A polygon is regular only when it satisfies TWO conditions simultaneously: all sides equal AND all angles equal. Failing either makes it irregular. The characteristic error is applying only one criterion — usually the more salient 'all sides equal' — so a rhombus (four equal sides, unequal angles) is wrongly called regular; less often a non-square rectangle (four equal angles, unequal sides) is. The square is the pivotal quadrilateral that passes both. Teaching succeeds when children habitually check BOTH sides and angles and can name a shape that passes one test but fails the other. A secondary trap is everyday language: hearing 'regular' as 'ordinary/tidy' and 'irregular' as 'odd-looking'.

activities.title: The two-key lock: checking both conditions on a changing shape
feedback: When a rhombus is placed and only the sides indicator is green: 'All four sides are equal — but look at the angles indicator. Two angles are acute, two obtuse, so the angles are NOT all equal. Failing either condition makes it irregular.'

When a non-square rectangle is placed: 'All four angles are equal right angles — but the sides are not all the same length, so it is still irregular. It mirrors the rhombus, which fails on the other condition.'
When the square passes both: 'Both equal sides AND equal angles — this is the one quadrilateral that turns both keys, so it is regular.'
If a child predicts the rhombus is regular: 'That uses only the sides. Run the angle check too before deciding.'
activities.rationale: The core difficulty is that regularity is a conjunction while learners latch onto a single salient attribute. Letting a learner reshape one figure and watch a rhombus and a rectangle each fail on a DIFFERENT condition makes the two-part rule felt rather than merely recited.
sourceClaims: A regular polygon has sides all of equal length AND each interior angle equal; an irregular polygon has sides that are not all equal OR angles that are not all equal OR both — so failing EITHER condition makes a polygon irregular (hence a rhombus with equal sides but unequal angles, and an oblong rectangle with equal angles but unequal sides, are both irregular)

Children reason from prototypes and impose a single salient attribute as if it defined a category, rather than checking the full set of defining properties — the mechanism behind judging regularity on equal sides alone
learnerActions: Work with an adjustable polygon (3–8 sides) that can be reshaped, with two visible condition indicators overhead — 'all sides equal' and 'all angles equal' — and a 'REGULAR' badge that lights only when BOTH indicators are green.
Start with a square: confirm both indicators are green and the badge reads REGULAR.

Skew the square so it leans into a rhombus — the tool keeps all four sides equal — and watch the sides stay equal (green) while the angles become unequal (red), so the badge drops to IRREGULAR even though every side is still the same length.

Straighten the rhombus back into a square, then stretch it along one direction into a long rectangle: watch the angles stay as four right angles (green) while the sides are no longer all equal (red) — still IRREGULAR.

Take named shapes from a gallery (rhombus, oblong rectangle, square, regular pentagon, irregular pentagon) and place each onto the checker, predicting first whether it will be regular and which condition (if any) it fails.
Attempt a 'make it regular' challenge that only succeeds when both conditions hold at once.
activities.intendedInsight: Regularity is a conjunction: equal sides alone, or equal angles alone, is not enough — the badge is a two-key lock, and only a shape that turns both keys (the square among quadrilaterals) is regular.

activities.title: Sorting with regular/irregular criteria
feedback: If a shape is sorted by look: 'Decide with the two columns, not how neat it looks — a tilted regular pentagon is still regular, and a neat oblong rectangle is still irregular.'
If the rhombus is placed with the regular group: 'Check the angle column. Sides tick, angles cross — it belongs with the irregular shapes.'
Confirm correct discrimination: 'You separated the rhombus (sides only) from the rectangle (angles only) from the square (both) — exactly the three cases that break the single-criterion habit.'
activities.rationale: When continually shown regular shapes, pupils over-generalise (for example assuming the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides). Sorting against explicit regular/irregular criteria, and avoiding only-regular examples, directly counters that over-generalisation. A sort can check and build classification but does not itself elicit a spoken explanation or hands-on manipulation.
sourceClaims: Year 4 objective 'Classify polygons ... whether or not they are regular, symmetry properties'; when continually shown regular shapes, pupils over-generalise (e.g. assume the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides); remedy = sorting cards with regular/irregular criteria and avoid presenting only regular examples

Children reason from prototypes and impose a single salient attribute as if it defined a category, rather than checking the full set of defining properties — the mechanism behind judging regularity on equal sides alone
learnerActions: Sort a mixed set of polygons into 'regular' and 'irregular' groups, including many-sided shapes and shapes shown in non-standard orientations (e.g. a tilted regular pentagon).

Use a two-way sort with the criteria 'all sides equal?' and 'all angles equal?', giving four groups: 'equal sides but not equal angles', 'equal angles but not equal sides', 'both equal', and 'neither equal'. Place the rhombus, oblong rectangle, square and regular/irregular pentagons.
For each shape, apply a two-column check: sides equal? (tick/cross) | angles equal? (tick/cross), and only call it regular when both columns tick.
Deliberately include an odd-looking regular shape and a tidy-looking irregular shape so that appearance is decoupled from the definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying by explicitly checking both conditions — not by overall appearance or by sides alone — and recognising that 'regular' is not welded to a symmetric-looking prototype.

activities.title: Produce a shape that passes one test but fails the other
feedback: If only one counterexample is produced: 'You have the sides-only case — now make an angles-only case (a long rectangle) to show you can fail either condition.'
If the square/rhombus contrast is explained by sides alone: 'Both do have four equal sides. The difference is the angles: the square's four angles are equal, the rhombus's are not.'
Confirm: 'You produced a shape that passes each test separately and explained the square as the one that passes both — that is the full definition in use.'
activities.rationale: Reciting the criteria without applying them is a common partial state; asking learners to construct cases that pass exactly one condition requires active use of both criteria and surfaces whether the definition is genuinely held. Recognition or sorting alone does not require this independent production.
sourceClaims: A regular polygon has sides all of equal length AND each interior angle equal; an irregular polygon has sides that are not all equal OR angles that are not all equal OR both — so failing EITHER condition makes a polygon irregular (hence a rhombus with equal sides but unequal angles, and an oblong rectangle with equal angles but unequal sides, are both irregular)
learnerActions: Draw a shape with all equal sides that is NOT regular (e.g. a rhombus), and label why: equal sides, unequal angles.
Draw a shape with all equal angles that is NOT regular (e.g. an oblong rectangle), and label why: equal angles, unequal sides.
Explain in words why a square is regular but a rhombus is not, even though both have four equal sides.
State the rule by completing: 'a regular polygon has equal ___ and equal ___', then use it to classify a new shape not seen before.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to construct counterexamples (equal sides only; equal angles only) shows the learner holds and can apply the full two-part definition, not just recite it.

activities.title: Shape inspector dialogue: always ask the second question
feedback: If a verdict is given after one condition: 'Before deciding, say what the angles do. Only then can you call it regular or irregular.'
On everyday-language slips: 'Neat or odd-looking does not decide it — a tilted regular pentagon looks unusual but is regular; a tidy oblong is irregular.'
activities.rationale: Articulating reasoning can surface the single-criterion error, and explicitly separating the mathematical meaning from the everyday meaning addresses language interference. This supports classification work rather than replacing hands-on checking of shapes.
sourceClaims: Children reason from prototypes and impose a single salient attribute as if it defined a category, rather than checking the full set of defining properties — the mechanism behind judging regularity on equal sides alone
learnerActions: Take the role of, or respond to, a 'shape inspector' who accepts 'regular' only after BOTH conditions are confirmed.
When the learner offers 'the sides are equal', the inspector presses: 'The sides are equal — but what about the angles?' before any verdict is reached.
Talk through the rhombus and the rectangle, each time naming which single condition passes and which fails.
Separate the everyday sense ('regular' = ordinary/tidy) from the mathematical sense by discussing a deliberately odd-looking regular shape and a tidy-looking irregular one.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising both checks — and resisting a verdict until the second condition is examined — can make the single-criterion habit visible and correctable through talk.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reference chart of near-twins
feedback: 'The regular pentagon meets both conditions; its irregular twin fails at least one. Name which condition each near-twin fails.'
activities.rationale: A fixed reveal-chart cannot recompute as a learner alters a shape, so it serves as a reference/summary rather than a place to test a shape the learner changes; it is best used alongside the manipulable and construction activities.
sourceClaims: A regular polygon has sides all of equal length AND each interior angle equal; an irregular polygon has sides that are not all equal OR angles that are not all equal OR both — so failing EITHER condition makes a polygon irregular (hence a rhombus with equal sides but unequal angles, and an oblong rectangle with equal angles but unequal sides, are both irregular)
learnerActions: Use a reference chart pairing each regular shape with its irregular near-twin: a regular pentagon beside an irregular pentagon, a square beside a rhombus, a square beside an oblong rectangle.

Reveal for each shape which conditions it meets — e.g. regular pentagon: '5 equal sides AND 5 equal angles'; rhombus: 'equal sides, but NOT equal angles → irregular'; oblong: 'equal angles, but NOT equal sides → irregular'.
Use the chart as a summary to confirm or check answers after sorting or constructing shapes.
activities.intendedInsight: A compact reference reinforces that each irregular near-twin fails a specific named condition, consolidating the conjunction rule.

constraints: Regularity requires checking BOTH conditions together: equal sides AND equal angles. A shape failing either is irregular — do not let 'all sides equal' alone stand as the test.
Use the rhombus (sides only) and the non-square rectangle (angles only) as the discriminating cases, flanking the square (both), so the single-criterion habit is broken from both directions.
Include many-sided and non-standard-orientation examples, and do not present only regular shapes, so 'regular' is not welded to a symmetric-looking prototype.
Explicitly separate the mathematical meaning of regular/irregular from the everyday meaning (tidy vs odd-looking); appearance must not decide classification.
Keep tool manipulations geometrically coherent: a rhombus demonstration must hold all four sides equal (a shear/skew) rather than imply a single-corner drag that would change side lengths.
A reveal/reference chart is a summary scaffold: it does not recompute when a learner changes a shape, so it cannot replace activities where the learner tests shapes they alter.

Sorting or multiple-choice items can check the rule but do not require the learner to construct a counterexample; include production tasks (drawing/labelling a shape that passes one test and fails the other) for full mastery.

Regularity is a planar property of sides and angles; adding a third spatial dimension is not needed to teach it. This is a scope note, not a claim that any representation is incapable of teaching the concept.
Dialogue can surface the single-criterion error and is a useful accompaniment to hands-on checking and sorting of shapes; its efficacy relative to those activities is untested.

The original design note described 'dragging one corner' of a square to form a rhombus while sides stay equal — geometrically impossible, since moving a single vertex changes side lengths. Activity 1 was reworded to a shear/skew in which the tool keeps all four sides equal, preserving the intended 'sides equal, angles unequal' demonstration.

Geometry self-check: a rhombus has four equal sides with two acute and two obtuse angles (fails the angle condition); a non-square rectangle has four equal right angles with unequal sides (fails the side condition); a square satisfies both. Among quadrilaterals only the square is regular. No arithmetic or force/motion content is present.
'Rhombus' and 'rectangle' are used in the non-square sense throughout, matching the age 9–10 pedagogy; note that technically a square is itself a special rhombus and rectangle.

probeDeeper: You've checked the sides — now check the ANGLES. Are all four angles the same size? So is it regular?
Here is a long rectangle. All four of its angles are equal right angles — is it a regular polygon? Why or why not?
Draw me a shape with all equal sides that is NOT regular. Now draw one with all equal angles that is not regular.
Why is a square regular but this rhombus is not, when both have four equal sides?
assess.correctAnswer: No — it is irregular. A regular polygon must have BOTH all sides equal AND all angles equal; this rhombus has four equal sides but its angles are not all equal (two acute, two obtuse), so it fails the angle condition and is irregular. Only when a rhombus's angles are also all equal — making it a square — is it regular.

errorPatterns.pattern: Regular = equal sides only — 'yes, it's regular, all four sides are the same', ignoring that the angles are not equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the angle check explicitly — run BOTH conditions on the rhombus so the child sees it passes sides but fails angles; contrast with a regular pentagon and with the square. Reteach in place: applying the second criterion IS the target.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it is regular, because all four sides are equal
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'regular' and, on the reason tier, cites only the equal sides; does not mention the angles

errorPatterns.pattern: Regular = equal angles only — surfaces on a rectangle: 'yes, regular, all four corners are the same', ignoring the unequal sides
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run both conditions on the rectangle — equal angles tick, equal sides cross -> irregular; pair it with the rhombus (the mirror case) and the square (both tick).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Under the rectangle probe, calls an oblong rectangle regular, citing its equal (right) angles

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Regular' means an ordinary/tidy shape and 'irregular' means an odd or random-looking one (everyday-language interference)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the maths meaning from the everyday one; give a deliberately odd-looking but regular example (a regular pentagon tilted) and a tidy-looking irregular one (an oblong rectangle) so appearance is decoupled from the definition.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it is a neat, even shape, so it is regular
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies by look — 'it's a neat/even/normal shape' or 'it's not a weird shape' — rather than by the sides-and-angles conditions

responseLevels.gap: Calls the rhombus regular citing equal sides only, or judges by look ('it's a normal/diamond shape'); does not use the angle condition and cannot say why a rectangle is irregular.
responseLevels.full: Judges the rhombus irregular because, although its sides are equal, its angles are not — applying BOTH conditions; explains that a regular pentagon has 5 equal sides AND 5 equal angles, identifies the rectangle as irregular (equal angles, unequal sides) and the square as the regular quadrilateral, and can produce a shape that passes one condition but fails the other.
responseLevels.partial: Can recite that a regular polygon needs equal sides 'and equal angles' and gets the rhombus right once prompted to check the angles, but does not apply both conditions spontaneously and cannot handle the rectangle (angles-only) case or explain why the square is the regular quadrilateral — lists the criteria without using them to classify new cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a rhombus — a 'diamond' with four equal sides but two acute and two obtuse angles (NOT a square). Ask: 'Is this a regular polygon?' Then, whatever they answer: 'How do you know? What makes a polygon regular?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rhombus is chosen because it satisfies exactly the salient condition (equal sides) and fails the hidden one (equal angles). A child holding the full two-part definition says 'no, irregular' and cites the unequal angles; a child running the sides-only rule says 'yes, regular — all four sides are equal', exposing the missing angle condition on the reason tier. A 'no' backed only by 'it's a diamond, not a normal shape' reveals the everyday-meaning error rather than mastery.

sources.claim: A regular polygon has sides all of equal length AND each interior angle equal; an irregular polygon has sides that are not all equal OR angles that are not all equal OR both — so failing EITHER condition makes a polygon irregular (hence a rhombus with equal sides but unequal angles, and an oblong rectangle with equal angles but unequal sides, are both irregular)
sources.source: Third Space Learning — GCSE Maths, Regular Polygon & Irregular Polygon guides

sources.claim: Year 4 objective 'Classify polygons ... whether or not they are regular, symmetry properties'; when continually shown regular shapes, pupils over-generalise (e.g. assume the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides); remedy = sorting cards with regular/irregular criteria and avoid presenting only regular examples
sources.source: NCETM — 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' (Shape section, polygon-classification objective)

sources.claim: Children reason from prototypes and impose a single salient attribute as if it defined a category, rather than checking the full set of defining properties — the mechanism behind judging regularity on equal sides alone
sources.source: Yesildag-Hasancebi & Halat (2016), prototype and imposed-attribute obstacles in shape classification, EJMSTE 12(2)

sources.claim: Year 5 statutory content: pupils distinguish between regular and irregular polygons based on reasoning about equal sides and equal angles
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 5 Geometry — properties of shapes)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 2-D shapes (age 10+)
topic.description: Draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles, using a ruler and protractor accurately
evidence: Draw a triangle with sides 5 cm, 7 cm and an included angle of 60°
Construct a rectangle with given length and width using a ruler and set square
Draw a regular pentagon given the side length and interior angle
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to draw a triangle with sides of 5 cm and 7 cm with a 40° angle between them, can they use a ruler and protractor to draw it accurately?

pedagogy.summary: At age 10-11 (UK Y6) children construct 2-D shapes to a specification using a ruler and protractor — e.g. a triangle from two sides and an included angle, or a regular polygon from side length and interior angle. This is a precision motor-and-procedure skill layered on angle-measuring: the accuracy of the final figure exposes whether the sub-skills are secure. The dominant failure points are protractor-specific — reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (drawing the supplement of the intended angle), and misplacing the protractor's centre on the vertex or its zero-line along the drawn side — plus the ruler habit of measuring from the ruler's physical end instead of its zero mark. The remedy is a disciplined routine (estimate the angle first to choose the right scale; centre-on-vertex, zero-line-on-line; ruler zero on the endpoint) taught explicitly and rehearsed, alongside checking that the figure closes and sides are equal.
bestPractices: Estimate before measuring: decide whether the target angle is bigger or smaller than a right angle, then pick the protractor scale whose reading agrees — the single most reliable guard against the dual-scale supplement error

Drill the placement routine explicitly: protractor centre-hole on the vertex dot, zero-line exactly along the existing side, count up from the 0 on the arm you laid down; a single-scale or numberless protractor removes the scale ambiguity while the routine is learned
Teach ruler measurement from the zero mark, not the end of the ruler; mark the point then join, rather than eyeballing a length

Sequence the construction: draw the base first with the ruler, then set each given angle at its endpoint, then rule the rays to meet — and check the figure CLOSES; a non-closing triangle signals an accumulated placement/scale error
For regular polygons, connect side length and the (interior or exterior) turn angle so children construct by repeating an equal side and an equal turn, checking equal sides and equal angles
keyRepresentations: Protractor with the estimate-first rule (is it more or less than 90°?) to disambiguate the two scales
Single-scale or numberless protractor for the placement-learning phase
The 'centre-on-vertex, zero-on-line' placement diagram
Base-then-angles construction sequence for a triangle (SAS-style)
Side-and-turn model for constructing regular polygons
commonMisconceptions: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing the supplement (e.g. 60° instead of 120°)
Places the protractor's centre off the vertex or its zero-line off the side, so every angle is a few degrees out or the ray does not start at the vertex
Measures length from the physical end of the ruler rather than the zero mark, adding the end-margin to each length
Treats a 'nearly closing' triangle as correct rather than a signal of accumulated error
Draws sides to look right rather than to the measured length, or turns an inconsistent amount at each corner of a regular polygon

learn.summary: For children aged 10-11 (UK Year 6) learning to construct 2-D shapes to a specification with a ruler and protractor: a triangle from a base and the two angles at its ends (Angle-Side-Angle), a triangle from two sides and an included angle (Side-Angle-Side), a rectangle from length and width, or a regular polygon from side length and turn angle. This is a precision procedural skill layered on angle measuring. The accuracy of the finished figure is itself the evidence: measuring its sides and angles against the specification (and, for rectangles and regular polygons, checking whether it closes) exposes whether the sub-skills are secure; an ASA or SAS triangle will close even when it is inaccurate, so closure alone proves little there. There are three dominant, well-documented failure points — two protractor-specific plus one ruler habit: reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (so the supplement is drawn, e.g. 140° for 40°), and misplacing the protractor (centre off the vertex, zero-line off the drawn side); and, separately, measuring length from the ruler's physical end rather than its zero mark. The remedy taught here is a disciplined, rehearsed routine: estimate the angle first to choose the right scale, centre-on-vertex with zero-line-on-line, ruler zero on the endpoint, then check the finished figure by measuring its sides and angles (and closure, for rectangles and polygons).

activities.title: Construct a triangle from a base and two base angles (ASA-style)
feedback: If the triangle fails to close or looks badly wrong, check whether you read the supplement (e.g. 140° where 40° was wanted): re-estimate 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' and choose the scale whose number agrees.
If every angle is a few degrees out or a ray does not start at the vertex, re-seat the protractor: centre hole on the dot, zero-line exactly on the line.
If the base comes out systematically long, check you measured from the ruler's zero mark and not its physical end (the other two sides are set by the angles, so check those angles too).

A triangle whose measured angles (40°, 65° and a third angle of about 75°) and 7 cm base all match within tolerance is good evidence the routine held together; closing alone proves little, because the two rays will meet for almost any guessed angles that add up to less than 180°.
activities.rationale: Construction is a procedural doing-skill: building placement-and-scale judgement requires the child to actually set the angles and measure the sides, and re-measuring the finished triangle (the two set angles, the 7 cm base and a third angle of about 75°) turns the figure into immediate self-assessment of the coordinated routine.
sourceClaims: UK Y6 statutory: pupils 'draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles'; the wider programme expects accurate use of a ruler to the nearest millimetre and measuring/drawing angles with a protractor.

Documented protractor difficulties: on a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with WHICH scale to read (drawing the supplement), and with placing the vertex and baseline correctly; a numberless/single-scale protractor and estimate-first strategies reduce these errors (Exeter 2002 work cited).
learnerActions: Rule a base exactly 7 cm long, placing the ruler's zero mark (not its physical end) on the starting point, then mark and join.
At the left endpoint, before reading, decide: is the 40° angle smaller or bigger than a square corner (right angle)? Use that estimate to pick which of the two protractor scale numbers to read.
Place the protractor with its centre hole on the vertex dot and its zero-line exactly along the base, count up from the 0 on the arm laid along the base, mark 40°, and rule the ray.
Repeat at the right endpoint to set a 65° angle and rule the second ray so the two rays meet.

Check the triangle against the specification: re-measure the 40° and 65° angles and the 7 cm base, then measure the third angle, which should be about 75° (the angles of a triangle add up to 180°). If an angle is out by more than about 2°, or the two rays spread apart and never meet (a sign that a supplement such as 140° was drawn), find where the placement or scale error crept in.
activities.intendedInsight: The two scales of a dual-scale protractor offer supplementary numbers (e.g. 40 and 140); your own estimate of whether the angle is bigger or smaller than a right angle is what picks the correct one. Careful placement and measuring from zero are what make the figure match its specification. (A base with an angle set at each of its two ends is an angle-side-angle construction.)

activities.title: Isolate placement with a single-scale or numberless protractor
feedback: If angles are consistently off by a small amount, the zero-line is probably not flush with the side or the centre hole is off the dot — re-seat and remeasure.
When placement feels automatic, test yourself by switching back to the dual-scale tool and estimating first.
activities.rationale: Removing scale ambiguity isolates the placement routine so it can be rehearsed deliberately; the cited misconception work notes numberless/single-scale protractors reduce these specific errors while the routine is learned.
sourceClaims: Documented protractor difficulties: on a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with WHICH scale to read (drawing the supplement), and with placing the vertex and baseline correctly; a numberless/single-scale protractor and estimate-first strategies reduce these errors (Exeter 2002 work cited).
learnerActions: Using a numberless or single-scale protractor, practise seating it: centre hole on the vertex dot, zero-line exactly along the existing side, every time.
Measure and draw several given angles, focusing only on placement while the scale-reading ambiguity is removed.
Once placement is automatic, return to a dual-scale protractor and reintroduce the estimate-first scale choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Separating the placement sub-skill from the scale-reading sub-skill lets each become secure before they must be coordinated.

activities.title: Construct a regular polygon by repeating an equal side and an equal turn
feedback: If the pentagon does not close, check whether you turned an inconsistent amount at some corners or drew a side to look right rather than measuring it.
If sides differ in length, re-measure each from the ruler's zero mark rather than judging by eye.
activities.rationale: Connecting side length to a repeated turn gives children a constructive model of regularity and a built-in check (equal sides, equal turns, closure).
sourceClaims: UK Y6 statutory: pupils 'draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles'; the wider programme expects accurate use of a ruler to the nearest millimetre and measuring/drawing angles with a protractor.
learnerActions: Draw a regular pentagon with sides of 4 cm by ruling an equal side, then setting an equal turn at each corner, and repeating.

Use the same angle at every corner: for a regular pentagon each interior angle is 108° (equivalently an exterior turn of 72°, since 360° ÷ 5 = 72°); with a protractor, measure 108° inside the shape from the side just drawn. The side length (4 cm) does not change these angles.
After drawing, check that all five sides are equal in length and all corners turn by the same amount, and that the figure closes back to the start.
activities.intendedInsight: A regular polygon is built from a repeated equal side and an equal turn; keeping both consistent is what makes it regular and makes it close.

activities.title: Knowledge check on scale choice and placement (supporting check)
feedback: If you pick the supplement, re-apply 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' and choose the number that agrees.
Correctly spotting a misplaced protractor means you know the placement rule; now apply it with real tools on paper.
activities.rationale: A recognition check can surface whether the scale and placement rules are understood, but it cannot by itself elicit or assess actual drawing accuracy; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on construction.
sourceClaims: Documented protractor difficulties: on a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with WHICH scale to read (drawing the supplement), and with placing the vertex and baseline correctly; a numberless/single-scale protractor and estimate-first strategies reduce these errors (Exeter 2002 work cited).
learnerActions: Given an angle, state which of the two protractor scale readings is correct and why (estimate against a right angle first).
Spot a misplaced protractor in a picture (centre off the vertex, or zero-line off the side) and say what is wrong.
Estimate an unlabelled angle as bigger or smaller than a right angle before any reading is given.
activities.intendedInsight: The decisions behind a correct construction — scale choice and correct placement — can be reasoned about explicitly, which supports but does not replace actual drawing.

constraints: This is a hands-on motor-and-procedure skill: it must be practised with real ruler-and-protractor construction on paper (as the Y6 programme requires). Recognition-only checks (which scale, spot the misplacement) support reasoning but do not elicit the actual drawing accuracy that is the target skill.
A labelled picture or reference card can display the placement routine but cannot by itself build the placement-and-scale judgement; treat it as a reminder, not the main teacher.

A draggable on-screen ruler and protractor is an optional scaffold for the judgement (scale choice, placement, closure check) and should be paired with real tools so the physical motor skill develops alongside; it is not a substitute for drawing on paper.
Accept an accuracy tolerance of roughly ±2° and ±2 mm for a successful construction at this age.

The estimate-first rule ('bigger or smaller than a right angle?') resolves the supplement ambiguity only when the target angle is not itself close to 90°; for angles near a right angle, placement and careful reading carry more of the load.

A triangle built from a base plus an angle at each of its ends is an angle-side-angle (ASA) construction; a triangle built from two sides and the angle between them is side-angle-side (SAS). Name the construction accurately rather than conflating the two.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row labelled the base-and-two-angles construction 'SAS-style' in its keyRepresentations; this is incorrect — a base with an angle at each end is an angle-side-angle (ASA) construction. The activity and summary have been corrected to ASA; SAS is retained only to describe the separate two-sides-and-included-angle evidence item.

An optional interactive scaffold was described in the source (protractor snaps/glows when centred, both scale numbers ghost-appear with a 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' prompt, ruler enforces measuring from zero, green tick when the figure closes). These are retained as illustrative affordances, not mandatory mechanisms.

The source asserted '3D adds nothing' and that a static image 'cannot teach' the skill; these have been softened to scoped limits (planar construction; a picture is a reminder not a teacher) rather than universal claims, since catalog ratings do not establish necessity or comparative efficacy.

The example triangle (base 7 cm, 40° and 65°) and pentagon (4 cm sides) are internally consistent: 40+65+75=180, so the third angle is 75°, a valid closing triangle. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated examples.
Two error patterns in the original row routed to a reteach prerequisite; prerequisite routing is a platform concern and is not reproduced in learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: Before you read the protractor — is this angle going to be more or less than 90°? So which of the two numbers can it be?
Your triangle didn't quite close — where do you think the error crept in?
Why did you start measuring from there and not from the very end of the ruler?
For the pentagon, how did you know how far to turn at each corner to keep the sides and angles equal?
assess.correctAnswer: Lays the ruler's zero (not its end) on the start point and rules a 7 cm base; places the protractor centre on each base endpoint with the zero-line along the base, reads the correct scale to mark 40° and 65°, and rules the two rays to meet, producing a closed triangle accurate to about ±2° / ±2 mm; constructs the pentagon with equal 4 cm sides and an equal turn at each corner.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing the supplement of the intended angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Install the estimate-first rule: 'is this bigger or smaller than a square corner?' then choose the scale whose number agrees; rehearse on a single-scale/numberless protractor until scale choice is automatic
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Marks 140° where 40° was asked (or 120° for 60°), so the angle drawn is the supplement and the triangle is badly wrong or fails to close

errorPatterns.pattern: Misplaces the protractor — centre off the vertex or the zero-line off the drawn side — so angles are consistently a few degrees out or the ray does not start at the vertex
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explicit 'centre-hole on the dot, zero-line on the line' routine, checked each time; use a numberless protractor to isolate placement from scale-reading
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Each measured/drawn angle is off by a small consistent amount, or the ray begins away from the vertex; the triangle nearly-but-not-quite closes

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures length from the physical end of the ruler rather than the zero mark, adding the end-margin to each side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground ruler use: align the zero mark (not the end) with the endpoint, mark, then join; verify a couple of lengths back against the ruler
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sides come out systematically long by the ruler's end-margin, or lengths are judged by eye rather than measured from zero

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place the protractor or ruler reliably — reads whichever scale, measures from the ruler end — and the figures do not close or match the given dimensions.
responseLevels.full: Constructs the specified figure accurately and repeatably: estimates before reading to pick the right scale, aligns centre-on-vertex and zero-on-line, measures from the ruler's zero, and self-checks that the triangle closes and the polygon's sides and angles are equal.
responseLevels.partial: Draws each element correctly in isolation but with recurring slips — sometimes the wrong scale, or the triangle nearly closes — able to measure but not yet to coordinate the whole construction to the given spec (has the parts but not their relational assembly).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a ruler and a protractor in front of the child. Say: 'Draw a triangle with a base of 7 cm, an angle of 40° at the left end of the base and an angle of 65° at the right end. Then draw a regular pentagon with sides of 4 cm.' Watch how they place the protractor, which scale they read, where they start the ruler, and whether the triangle closes — do not talk them through it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The finished figure is the evidence: a child with the skill produces a closing, correctly-scaled triangle because they estimated-then-read the right scale and aligned centre-on-vertex, zero-on-line; a child without it draws the supplementary angle (wrong scale) or a non-closing, mis-sized figure. You cannot fake a closing triangle by guessing.
