topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Classifying shapes by properties
topic.description: Compare and classify geometric shapes based on their properties and sizes; understand that attributes belonging to a category also belong to all subcategories; classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
evidence: Explain why all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares
Place quadrilaterals in a hierarchy diagram showing subset relationships
Identify properties shared by all parallelograms and explain why rhombuses and rectangles are special cases
topic.assessmentPrompt: If someone asks {{name}} "is a square also a rectangle?", can they explain why the answer is yes — because a square has all the properties of a rectangle plus equal sides?

pedagogy.summary: By Y6 children should reach van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction): not just that a square is a special rectangle, but a full quadrilateral hierarchy where attributes flow downward — anything true of a parallelogram is automatically true of a rhombus, rectangle and square, because each is a special parallelogram. The two load-bearing ideas are (a) attribute inheritance (a subcategory has every property of its parents plus extra) and (b) the ASYMMETRY of class inclusion: all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares. Persistent obstacles are exclusive/oblong-prototype thinking carried up from KS2, and treating 'all A are B' as if it were symmetric ('so all B are A'). Teaching succeeds when children build and defend the hierarchy from properties rather than from appearance.
bestPractices: Make attribute inheritance explicit: a rhombus is a parallelogram with all sides equal, a rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles, a square is both — so a square inherits every parallelogram property (opposite sides parallel, diagonals bisect each other) automatically
Draw the hierarchy as a family tree / nested sets and have children justify each subset link ('why is every rectangle a parallelogram?') from properties
Confront the asymmetry directly with the two statements 'all squares are rectangles' vs 'all rectangles are squares' and demand the reason for which is true
Use everyday class-inclusion analogies (every spaniel is a dog and an animal, but not every dog is a spaniel) to make the one-directional logic intuitive
Ask for defining vs shared properties: what do ALL parallelograms share, and what EXTRA property makes each special case — forcing the necessary/sufficient distinction
keyRepresentations: Quadrilateral hierarchy diagram (family tree) with quadrilateral ⊃ parallelogram ⊃ {rhombus, rectangle} ⊃ square
Nested Venn sets showing rhombus and rectangle overlapping, with square in the intersection
Property table: rows = shapes, columns = properties (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals) showing how ticks accumulate down the hierarchy
A parallelogram with adjustable angles and side lengths that becomes a rhombus, rectangle, or square as constraints are added
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'all squares are rectangles' as symmetric — concluding 'so all rectangles are squares' (or that both are equally true/false)
Reversing the subset direction — thinking a rectangle is a special square rather than a square a special rectangle
Exclusive/oblong prototype persisting from KS2: a 'real' rectangle must be longer than it is wide, so a square is not a rectangle at all
Not applying inheritance: agreeing a rhombus is a parallelogram in words, but not granting that it therefore has all parallelogram properties (e.g. opposite sides parallel, diagonals bisecting)

learn.summary: Year 6 learners (ages 10-11) build the quadrilateral hierarchy from properties rather than appearance, grasping two load-bearing ideas: attribute inheritance (a subcategory has every property of its parents plus an extra constraint) and the asymmetry of class inclusion (all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares). The target understanding is the van Hiele informal-deduction level (level 3 when levels are numbered from 1, level 2 when numbered from 0): learners justify and defend subset links from properties, overcoming the exclusive/oblong prototype formed in earlier school years and the tendency to treat 'all A are B' as symmetric.

activities.title: Build the shape by adding properties
feedback: If a learner builds a square but denies it is a parallelogram, point back to the property table: it has opposite sides parallel, so it meets the parallelogram definition.

If a learner expects removing 'right angles' from a rectangle to leave it a rectangle, show that the 'rectangle' label depends on that very property — removing it moves the shape up to plain parallelogram.

When a learner sees the reverse challenge is impossible, name the insight: 'all rectangles are parallelograms but not all parallelograms are rectangles' (just as all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares) is something you bumped into, not a rule to memorise.
activities.rationale: Adding and removing defining properties and watching a shape's position in the hierarchy change makes attribute inheritance and the one-directional asymmetry concrete and reasoned rather than memorised. A live constraint model with linked hierarchy diagram, nested Venn sets and a ticking property table is an optional way to make the mechanism visible; the same reasoning can be done with paper cut-outs and a drawn family tree.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
At van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction) students can explain why all squares are rectangles; the levels progress from visual to descriptive to relational reasoning
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: Start with a general 'floppy' quadrilateral and switch on one property at a time: make opposite sides parallel, add right angles, make all sides equal.

Watch how the shape changes and where it belongs: making opposite sides parallel turns it into a parallelogram; adding right angles makes it a rectangle; instead making all sides equal makes it a rhombus; doing both makes it a square.

After each change, record in a property table which properties the shape now has (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals), noticing that these ticks accumulate as you go down each branch of the family tree.

Attempt the reverse challenge: try to make a rectangle that is NOT a parallelogram, and explain why you cannot — four right angles force each pair of opposite sides to be parallel (two sides that are both perpendicular to the same side are parallel), so every rectangle automatically meets the parallelogram definition.
Place the finished square, rhombus and rectangle onto a family-tree (hierarchy) diagram and into nested Venn sets, saying why the square sits inside BOTH the rhombus and rectangle regions.
activities.intendedInsight: A square inherits every property of the parallelogram, rhombus and rectangle because it is a special case of each; adding an extra constraint moves a shape DOWN the hierarchy, and the inheritance runs one way only — removing the extra property moves back up, but you cannot have a rectangle that is not also a parallelogram.

activities.title: Defend the asymmetry: which statement is true?
feedback: If a learner picks statement (2), use nested sets: the square set sits INSIDE the rectangle set, so square→rectangle always holds but rectangle→square does not.

If a learner rejects statement (1) because 'a rectangle must be longer than it is wide', show rectangles ranging from very long to square and test each against the definition (right angles, parallel opposite sides) rather than its typical look.
If a learner treats both statements as equally true or false, return to the spaniel/dog/animal analogy to feel the direction of the inclusion.
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the two statements and demanding a property-based reason surfaces whether the learner treats inclusion as symmetric, reverses the direction, or holds the oblong prototype — each error leads to a distinct, identifiable answer, so this both teaches and discriminates reasoning.
sourceClaims: 'All squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rectangle a special parallelogram? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
Children impose non-defining attributes and reason from prototypes, causing them to reject inclusive relationships between quadrilaterals
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: Consider two statements: (1) all squares are rectangles, (2) all rectangles are squares. Decide which is true and which is false.

Justify the choice from properties: a square has every property a rectangle needs (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) PLUS all four sides equal, so every square qualifies as a rectangle; a rectangle only becomes a square when it also has equal sides, which most do not.
Test the everyday analogy: every spaniel is a dog and every dog is an animal, but not every animal is a dog — explain how this one-directional logic matches squares and rectangles.
Attempt counterexamples: draw a rectangle that is NOT a square, a parallelogram that is NOT a rectangle, and try to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle (explaining why the last is impossible).
activities.intendedInsight: Class inclusion is one-directional: 'all A are B' does not mean 'all B are A'. The subset asymmetry follows from the extra defining property, not from which shape is more familiar.

activities.title: Shared versus extra properties across the parallelogram family
feedback: If a learner agrees in words that a rhombus is a parallelogram but lists its properties in isolation, build the property table so the shared parallelogram properties are seen carrying down to every special case.
If a learner cannot name the EXTRA property for a rhombus or rectangle, prompt: 'What does this shape have that a general parallelogram need not have?'
Praise reasoning that distinguishes a property ALL members share from the extra property that makes a case special.
activities.rationale: A property table makes inheritance visible and forces the necessary/sufficient distinction, addressing the misconception where learners grant category membership in name but withhold the inherited properties. A tap-to-reveal hierarchy with properties highlighted in parent nodes is one optional consolidation reference once the idea is understood.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: List the properties that ALL parallelograms share (opposite sides parallel and equal, diagonals bisect each other).

For each special case, state the extra property that defines it compared with a general parallelogram: a rhombus adds all sides equal, a rectangle adds right angles, and a square adds both (or just one extra property compared with a rhombus or a rectangle).
Fill a property table (rows = shapes, columns = properties) and confirm that each subcategory keeps every shared parallelogram property and adds its extra constraint.
Transfer the reasoning to a new or less familiar shape: given its properties, say where it belongs in the hierarchy and why, and which properties it inherits.
Justify a subset link in words, e.g. 'why is every rectangle a parallelogram?', using shared properties rather than appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: Every special parallelogram inherits all the shared parallelogram properties and adds extra defining constraints (one for a rhombus or a rectangle; two for a square, which is one more than a rhombus or a rectangle); this separates necessary/shared properties from the extra property or properties that name each shape.

activities.title: Convince the shape sceptic
feedback: If the learner argues from appearance ('it just looks like one'), the sceptic should ask which defining properties are met.
If the learner accepts the reverse ('every rhombus is a square'), ask for a rhombus that is not a square as a counterexample.
Reward justifications that cite shared and extra properties explicitly.
activities.rationale: Dialogue that demands property-based justification can surface reasoning and press the asymmetry, and can complement structural work done with diagrams and manipulatives.
sourceClaims: At van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction) students can explain why all squares are rectangles; the levels progress from visual to descriptive to relational reasoning
learnerActions: Respond to a sceptic who accepts a hierarchy claim only when it is justified from properties: 'Convince me a square belongs inside the rhombus family.'
Answer the follow-up pressure: 'Then is every rhombus a square?' — explaining why the reverse does not hold.
State, for each claim, which properties make it true and which extra property the reverse would require.
Use a counterexample when the sceptic over-generalises (e.g. produce a rhombus that is not a square).
activities.intendedInsight: Being made to articulate and defend each subset link, and to expose the reverse as false, consolidates property-based justification over appearance-based classification.

activities.title: Classify and check the hierarchy
feedback: If a shape is misplaced, ask which defining property is missing or extra for the region chosen.
For the true/false item, if the reversal is chosen, revisit the nested sets showing the square set inside the rectangle set.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching and a well-built true/false item check that reasoning is secure and are well suited to confirming the hierarchy and asymmetry. Recognition and correct placement alone do not require the learner to construct the inheritance, so use these alongside or after construction and reasoning work.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
learnerActions: Drag or place a set of quadrilaterals into nested regions of a hierarchy, putting the square in the intersection of the rhombus and rectangle sets.
Match each shape (parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square) to its extra defining property.
Answer a true/false question on the asymmetry — 'Which is true: all squares are rectangles, or all rectangles are squares?' — and spot the reversal as a wrong option.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and correct placement confirm the hierarchy is stable, including the asymmetry and each shape's extra defining property.

constraints: Build and defend the hierarchy from properties, not from appearance; the oblong/prototype view ('a rectangle must be longer than it is wide') must be directly confronted, not reinforced.

Classification, matching and true/false items check that the hierarchy is secure but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the inheritance insight; use them to confirm understanding alongside or after construction and reasoning work.

A tap-to-reveal hierarchy/property table is a useful reference once the idea is understood, but it does not let the learner add or remove constraints to feel a shape descend the hierarchy; pair it with construction activities.
Dialogue with a sceptic supports property-based justification; the structural subset relationships can be seen clearly in a diagram, nested sets or manipulative, so pair dialogue with those.

Optional interactive features (live constraint handles, animated descent down the tree, updating nested Venn sets, a ticking property table, tap-to-reveal nodes) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; paper cut-outs and a drawn family tree can serve the same reasoning (a paper cut-out has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal flat quadrilateral it represents).
Keep class-inclusion attention one-directional: contrast 'all squares are rectangles' with 'all rectangles are squares' as genuinely different claims, not as a reversible rule.

Use 'equal diagonals' (true of rectangles and squares, not of general parallelograms or rhombuses) as the distinguishing property-table column so ticks genuinely accumulate; keep 'diagonals bisect each other' as a shared parallelogram property, not as an accumulating column.

The original claimed a scored linear quiz 'tests the reasoning rather than building the inheritance insight' and that dialogue 'supports rather than delivers'; these have been reframed as narrow affordances/design cautions, not proven efficacy or medium-superiority claims.
The National Curriculum (Year 6 Geometry) source is marked verified:false in the row; treat that citation with caution.

If using physical cut-outs to model quadrilaterals, note that paper has slight thickness and only approximates an ideal plane figure; discuss the represented flat shape, not whether the card can be handled.

The property-table column was changed from 'diagonals bisect each other' (a shared parallelogram property that does not accumulate) to 'equal diagonals' (parallelogram ✗, rhombus ✗, rectangle ✓, square ✓) so the accumulation observation stays coherent; the bisecting property is retained as a shared parallelogram property.

probeDeeper: 'What do ALL parallelograms have in common? What extra property makes a rhombus special? A rectangle?' (tests inheritance and the necessary/sufficient distinction)

'You said a square is a rectangle — is a square also a rhombus? Is it a parallelogram? Why?' (transfer down two branches of the hierarchy)

'Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square, and a parallelogram that is NOT a rectangle? Could you ever draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?' (counterexamples; the last is impossible — the asymmetry made concrete)
assess.correctAnswer: Statement (1) is true, statement (2) is false. A square has every property a rectangle needs (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) plus the extra property that all four sides are equal, so every square qualifies as a rectangle. A rectangle only becomes a square when it gains that extra property of equal sides, which most rectangles do not have — so not every rectangle is a square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the subset direction — picks 'all rectangles are squares' as the true one (treats the more familiar/larger category as the special case)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use nested-set and property-table work to show which set contains which: the square set sits INSIDE the rectangle set, so going square→rectangle always holds but rectangle→square does not. Revisit classifying by parallel/perpendicular-line properties.
errorPatterns.distractor: Statement (2) is the true one — all rectangles are squares
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses statement (2) and, on the reason tier, argues that a rectangle 'is a kind of square' or that the two claims are interchangeable

errorPatterns.pattern: Oblong-prototype exclusion persisting from KS2 — 'a square isn't a rectangle at all because a rectangle has to be longer than it is wide', so (1) is judged false
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate defining properties from typical appearance; show rectangles ranging from very long to square and test each against the definition. Reground in property-based classification.
errorPatterns.distractor: Neither is true — a square is not a rectangle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects statement (1) and, on the reason tier, defines a rectangle by its unequal-sides look rather than its right angles and parallel opposite sides

errorPatterns.pattern: Inheritance not applied — agrees a rhombus/rectangle is a parallelogram in name, but does not grant that it therefore has all parallelogram properties, and describes rhombus/rectangle as unrelated to the parallelogram family
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the property table so shared parallelogram properties (opposite sides parallel and equal, diagonals bisect) are seen to carry down to every special case, with each subcategory adding exactly one extra constraint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Under the parallelogram probe, lists a rhombus's or rectangle's properties in isolation and cannot say what EXTRA property each adds to a shared parallelogram base

responseLevels.gap: Picks the wrong statement or says both are equally true/false; or rejects 'all squares are rectangles' on appearance. Cannot use defining properties to reason about inclusion.
responseLevels.full: Picks statement (1) and explains the asymmetry from properties — a square has all a rectangle's properties plus equal sides, so every square is a rectangle but only equal-sided rectangles are squares; places quadrilaterals correctly in a hierarchy, states the properties all parallelograms share, and explains rhombus and rectangle as parallelograms each adding one extra property, transferring the reasoning to a new shape.
responseLevels.partial: Picks statement (1) and can say a square is a special rectangle, but lists shared/defining properties without using them to explain the asymmetry, and cannot apply inheritance to the parallelogram family (does not identify what extra property makes a rhombus or rectangle special, or transfer to a new case).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell the child: 'Here are two statements — (1) all squares are rectangles, and (2) all rectangles are squares. One is true and one is false.' Ask: 'Which one is true? And how do you know — what makes it true and the other one false?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands one-directional class inclusion picks statement (1) and explains the asymmetry via the extra property. A child treating inclusion as symmetric, or reversing the direction, picks (2) or says both are true/false. A child still holding the oblong prototype rejects (1) outright ('a square isn't a rectangle'). Each faulty reasoning route lands on a different, identifiable answer, and the reason tier separates a memorised 'square is a special rectangle' from genuine grasp of WHY the reverse fails.

pedagogy.summary: Naming the parts of a circle (radius, diameter, circumference) and knowing the diameter is twice the radius is taught best by grounding each term in its DEFINING PROPERTY — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a line through the centre from edge to edge, the circumference is the distance all the way round — rather than by rote labels. Drawing and measuring many circles of different sizes and tabulating radius against diameter lets pupils discover the invariant d = 2r for themselves, and practising the conversion in BOTH directions guards against the pervasive radius/diameter swap.
bestPractices: Anchor each term in its defining property: a radius touches the centre; a diameter passes through the centre; the circumference is the perimeter (distance around).
Draw and measure several circles of different sizes and tabulate radius vs diameter, so pupils see d = 2r holds at every scale.
Practise conversion in both directions — diameter from radius AND radius from diameter — and monitor for confusion between the two (NCTM).
Label parts on circles in varied positions and surface the longest-chord property (the diameter is the longest line across).
Provide a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and require pupils to use the terms when they reason.
keyRepresentations: A labelled circle: centre, radius, diameter, circumference
Radius vs diameter vs an off-centre chord, contrasted
A radius/diameter table across several circle sizes
String wrapped round a circle to show the circumference as a length
commonMisconceptions: Swaps radius and diameter, or substitutes a diameter where a radius is needed — the 'half/twice' error (NCTM).
Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or draws a radius/diameter that does not reach or pass through the centre.
Applies the conversion in the wrong direction (doubles when it should halve), or thinks the radius equals the diameter.

learn.summary: Pupils (age 10–11) learn to name and identify the radius, diameter and circumference of a circle by their DEFINING PROPERTIES — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a straight line from edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across), and the circumference is the distance all the way around — and to apply d = 2r in both directions. The core work is drawing and measuring many circles, tabulating radius against diameter so the invariant d = 2r is discovered rather than told, and practising conversion both ways to guard against the pervasive radius/diameter swap. Several complementary media (dynamic manipulation, paper-and-string measurement, a labelled reference, and a short conversion check) each support a different part of this objective.

activities.title: Measure many circles and discover d = 2r
feedback: If a pupil's pairs don't come out close to double, check that the diameter was drawn through the centre and that both were measured along a straight line — an off-centre line is shorter and will break the pattern.
Prompt: 'Does your doubling pattern still hold for your biggest circle and your smallest circle?' to surface that the relationship is scale-independent.
If a pupil writes the names interchangeably, ask them to point to where each line starts and ends relative to the centre.
activities.rationale: Grounding each term in its defining property and tabulating radius against diameter across sizes lets pupils see d = 2r hold at every scale, which the curriculum expects pupils to know and the geometry research links to moving beyond naming toward defining properties.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter and circumference, and know that the diameter is twice the radius; the non-statutory guidance expresses this as d = 2 × r.

Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Draw several circles of clearly different sizes (small, medium, large).
For each circle, mark the centre, draw a radius from the centre to the edge and a diameter from edge to edge through the centre.
Measure the radius and the diameter of each circle and record them in a two-column table (radius | diameter).
Look across the table and describe the pattern you notice between the radius and the diameter.
State the relationship in your own words and as d = 2 × r.
activities.intendedInsight: Across every size of circle, the diameter is exactly twice the radius. Pupils' own measurements will come out close to double, allowing for small measuring errors, so they can see the pattern holding for themselves rather than memorising a rule.

activities.title: Which line is longest? Predict then measure
feedback: Many pupils pick a long-looking slanted line; after measuring, point out that the through-centre line always wins, which is why the diameter is defined by the centre, not by looking long.
If a pupil labels an off-centre chord a diameter, have them check whether it passes through the marked centre.
Fold a paper circle in half (and again) to locate the centre, then confirm which drawn lines actually pass through it.
activities.rationale: Predicting before measuring makes the reasoning visible and the counterexample (an off-centre chord) directly tests the through-centre defining property rather than surface appearance, countering prototype-based reasoning.
sourceClaims: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: On a circle with the centre marked, draw several straight lines from edge to edge — some passing through the centre and some not.
Before measuring, PREDICT which line is the longest and write down why you think so.
Measure each line and compare with your prediction.
Decide which lines pass through the centre (diameters) and which do not (other chords), and explain the difference using the word 'centre'.
activities.intendedInsight: The longest straight line across a circle is always the one through the centre — the diameter — so a line that misses the centre is a shorter chord, not a diameter. The pre-stated reason is what reveals a pupil's thinking.

activities.title: Convert both ways and reason aloud
feedback: Worked check: a radius of 4.5 cm gives a diameter of 9 cm because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). A diameter of 10 cm gives a radius of 5 cm because the radius is half the diameter.
If a pupil gives 2.25 cm as the diameter of a 4.5 cm radius, they halved instead of doubling — return to the measured table showing the diameter is always the larger, doubled value.
Require the pupil to name which quantity is which before computing, so a radius isn't treated as a diameter.
activities.rationale: Practising conversion in both directions and requiring reasoning with correct vocabulary targets the flagged radius/diameter confusion and supports fluent, justified use of the terms.
sourceClaims: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Given a radius (e.g. 4.5 cm), work out the diameter and state how you did it.
Given a diameter (e.g. 10 cm), work out the radius and state how you did it.
For each, say in words whether you doubled or halved and why.
Use a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and use the correct term in each explanation.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting diameter-from-radius and radius-from-diameter are different directions of the same relationship; knowing which to double and which to halve, with a reason, prevents the half/twice swap.

activities.title: Feel the circumference as a length
feedback: If a pupil calls a straight line across the circle 'the circumference', have them trace the edge with a finger: the circumference is the whole way round.
Compare the straightened string length with the diameter drawn straight across to reinforce that they measure different things.
activities.rationale: A tactile wrap-and-straighten activity is intended to make the circumference concrete as a go-around length, addressing the confusion between circumference and a straight measurement across. Proposed as a hands-on scaffold; its effectiveness is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Wrap a length of string once around the edge of a circle, mark where it meets, then straighten it against a ruler to measure the distance around.
Run a finger all the way around the edge and say in your own words what the circumference is.
Contrast this with a straight line drawn across the circle and explain why the circumference is not a straight line.
activities.intendedInsight: The circumference is the distance all the way around the edge — a curved length — not a straight line across the circle.

activities.title: Dynamic circle: watch d = 2r hold as the circle resizes (optional screen scaffold)
feedback: Live readout feedback: as the pupil stretches the circle, the diameter reading stays at twice the radius (the last digit may differ slightly if the display rounds), so the relationship can be observed across scales.
When a dragged line misses the centre and is refused the 'diameter' label, prompt: 'What do you need to change so it becomes a diameter?'
Pair this with the paper-and-ruler measuring so the relationship is grounded in real measurement, not only an on-screen readout.
activities.rationale: A dynamic, draggable model lets the invariant be experienced across many sizes in quick succession and can enforce the through-centre property via snapping/labelling; a static labelled reference states d = 2r but cannot show it varying. Offered as a complement to, not a replacement for, hands-on measuring; its efficacy relative to other media is not established here.
sourceClaims: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Drag a point to make the circle bigger and smaller and watch a live readout of the radius and the diameter.
Notice whether the diameter readout always shows twice the radius as the size changes.

Drag the endpoint of a line inside the circle; observe that it is labelled 'diameter — the longest line across' only when it passes through the centre, and is refused the label when it misses the centre.
Say what stays the same (d = 2r) and what must be true for a line to be a diameter (it passes through the centre).
activities.intendedInsight: The 2× relationship is invariant across every size, and only a through-centre line earns the name 'diameter' — both the invariant and the defining property made visible together.

activities.title: Labelled circle reference (supporting scaffold)
feedback: Reveal-on-tap can confirm each term's defining property as a reference, but d = 2r is stated here, not discovered — use it alongside the measuring activity.
Varying the position of the labelled parts guards against pupils only recognising a standard horizontal diameter.
If a pupil can label a standard diagram but slips on a slanted or off-centre line, return to the defining-property test (does it pass through the centre?).
activities.rationale: A clear labelled reference with varied positions supports the vocabulary and surfaces the longest-chord property; presenting shapes in varied positions counters prototype-based recognition. This is a reference scaffold and cannot by itself build the measured discovery of the invariant.
sourceClaims: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.

Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Study a labelled circle showing centre, radius, diameter and circumference.
Reveal or read each term's defining property: radius = centre to edge; diameter = edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across); circumference = the distance all the way round.
Label parts yourself on circles drawn in varied positions and orientations, including ones where the diameter is slanted.
Match each term to its definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Each circle part is identified by its defining property and position relative to the centre, not by a fixed picture orientation.

constraints: A static labelled diagram or reveal-on-tap reference states d = 2r but does not let pupils see it vary across sizes; pair it with hands-on drawing and measuring so the invariant is genuinely discovered.

A label/match/slider conversion check can verify vocabulary and the d = 2r computation but does not by itself build the defining-property understanding; use it as a check after the measuring and reasoning activities.
Recognition-only responses (matching terms to a standard diagram) do not elicit independent construction; require pupils to draw, measure, convert both ways, and justify.
Present diameters and radii in varied positions (including slanted and non-standard) so pupils do not over-rely on a horizontal prototype.
Always insist pupils state WHY (which line passes through the centre, whether they doubled or halved); the reason is what distinguishes understanding from a lucky guess.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a 3-D environment as 'adding nothing' for a planar concept. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A planar concept is naturally well-served by 2-D media, but no universal 'adds nothing' claim is made here.

The source stated conversation is 'poor' for this concept. This is not a general pedagogical law; spoken justification is used throughout (predict-and-explain, reason-aloud conversion) as part of teaching, not only assessment. The medium-ranking boilerplate was removed.
The 'diameter is the longest line across (longest chord)' property is stated correctly for a circle and is used as a measurable, verifiable prediction task.

Self-audit of the worked conversions: radius 4.5 cm → diameter 9 cm (2 × 4.5) is correct; the distractor 2.25 cm correctly models halving instead of doubling; diameter 10 cm → radius 5 cm is correct. No arithmetic errors found.

The circumference string activity and the circumference-vs-straight-line confusion it targets come from the pedagogy/assessment material, not from the cited sources; its sourceClaims were set to [] and the rationale hedged accordingly, as no source establishes the method's effectiveness.
All sourceClaims were re-checked to be verbatim copies of the three original sources[].claim strings; this addresses the prior validation failure caused by a non-matching claim string.

assess.poeTask: Draw several straight lines from edge to edge across a circle, some through the marked centre and some not, and ask the pupil to PREDICT which line is longest before measuring — and to say why. Many pick a long-looking slanted chord. Then measure: the longest is always the line through the centre — the diameter. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part; the result forces the defining property that a diameter must pass through the centre and is the longest chord.
probeDeeper: If I make the circle twice as big, is the diameter still twice the radius? Why?
This line goes across the circle but not through the centre — is it a diameter? Why not?
A circle's diameter is 10 cm — what is its radius, and how did you work it out?
Which straight line across a circle is the longest, and where must it pass?
assess.correctAnswer: The diameter is 9 cm, because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). The centre-to-edge line is the radius and the edge-to-edge line through the centre is the diameter; a radius goes from the centre to the edge and a diameter passes through the centre, so the third line is neither (it is a chord) because it does not pass through the centre.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or a line to the edge as a radius, ignoring the centre — the defining property
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold a paper circle to find the centre; only a line through the centre is a diameter (and it is the longest line across), and a radius must start at the centre
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the off-centre chord as the diameter, or draws a 'radius' that does not reach the centre

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the circumference with a straight measurement — calls a diameter or a line across 'the circumference'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a finger all the way round the edge — the circumference is the distance around, not a straight line across
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels a straight line as the circumference

responseLevels.gap: Uses the terms interchangeably or halves/doubles in the wrong direction; treats any line across the circle as a diameter.
responseLevels.full: States and applies d = 2r in both directions with a reason, identifies parts by their defining properties (radius from the centre, diameter through the centre, circumference around), rejects an off-centre chord as a diameter, and knows the relationship holds at any size.
responseLevels.partial: Converts one way (e.g. radius to diameter) and labels a standard diagram, but slips on the reverse conversion or on a non-standard/off-centre line — knows the names without the defining property.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A circle has a radius of 4.5 cm. What is its diameter, and how do you know? Then look at this diagram of a circle with its centre marked and three straight lines drawn on it: one from the centre to the edge, one from edge to edge passing through the centre, and one from edge to edge that does NOT pass through the centre. Which line is the radius, which is the diameter, and how can you tell?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reason tier separates a pupil who applies d = 2r with understanding from one who guesses or halves. The diagram forces the defining-property test: a pupil who thinks any line across the circle is a diameter picks the off-centre chord, whereas a pupil who knows the property rejects it because it misses the centre. Together the tiers catch both the half/twice swap and the through-centre confusion.

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils should be taught to illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter and circumference, and know that the diameter is twice the radius; the non-statutory guidance expresses this as d = 2 × r.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 6 Geometry (gov.uk)

sources.claim: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.
sources.source: NCTM, 'Discovering the Area Formula for Circles' (Measures of Circles, Lesson 2), Classroom Resources / ARCs

sources.claim: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
sources.source: Gunčaga, Tkačík & Žilková (2017), 'Understanding of Selected Geometric Concepts by Pupils of Pre-Primary and Primary Level Education', European Journal of Contemporary Education 6(3)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Geometry notation and sketching
topic.description: Use conventional geometric terms and notation to describe, sketch, and draw points, lines, parallel and perpendicular lines, right angles, regular polygons, and reflectively/rotationally symmetric polygons
evidence: Use correct notation for line segments (AB), angles (∠ABC), and parallel lines (AB ∥ CD)
Sketch a regular hexagon and describe its rotational and reflective symmetry
Identify and label perpendicular and parallel lines in a given figure using standard symbols
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to describe a triangle using proper geometry notation — naming its angles and sides with letters — can they do it clearly enough for someone else to draw it?

pedagogy.summary: This is a LANGUAGE objective: at age 11-13 pupils become fluent in the conventional TERMS and NOTATION of geometry — naming points and segments (AB), angles (∠ABC with the vertex in the middle), marking parallel (∥, arrows) and perpendicular (the right-angle square), and describing regular polygons and their reflective/rotational symmetry — and, crucially, USING them accurately to describe, sketch and draw figures. The teaching goal is productive, property-based communication, not reciting definitions. The dominant obstacle is the prototype phenomenon: even pupils who can state a correct definition identify and name shapes by their prototypical picture, so a tilted square is denied its name and 'parallel'/'perpendicular' are muddled or thought to require equal lengths. Effective instruction ties every term to the defining property (not the look), presents figures in varied orientations and as non-examples, and gives pupils reasons to USE the notation — barrier/describe-and-draw tasks where imprecise language visibly breaks the communication.
bestPractices: Teach terms and notation for USE, not definition-reciting: set describe-and-draw / barrier tasks where a partner must reproduce a figure from the pupil's words and marks, so precise language has visible payoff
Confront the prototype phenomenon: present shapes tilted, scaled and as non-examples, so pupils name by property (equal sides and angles → regular) rather than by the prototypical picture
Anchor ∥ and ⊥ to their defining properties (never-meeting / constant distance; square corner) and correct the 'parallel lines must be the same length' error explicitly
Model the angle-notation convention — the middle letter of ∠ABC is the vertex — and require three-letter naming whenever a point carries more than one angle
Connect symmetry language to action: fold or rotate a regular polygon to justify its lines of symmetry and order of rotational symmetry rather than asserting them
keyRepresentations: Conventional notation set: AB, ∠ABC, AB ∥ CD, right-angle square, parallel arrows, equal-length tick marks
Barrier / describe-and-draw game (speaker uses terms, listener reconstructs)
Same shape shown in many orientations and as near-miss non-examples
Fold-lines and rotation overlays to demonstrate reflective and rotational symmetry
Regular vs irregular polygon pairs to force the equal-sides-AND-equal-angles criterion
commonMisconceptions: Prototype-driven naming: a shape is denied its name when tilted or non-standard (a 'slanted' square isn't called a square), even when the pupil knows the definition
Confusing or swapping 'parallel' and 'perpendicular', or believing parallel lines must be equal in length
Calling a polygon 'regular' when it has equal sides OR equal angles but not both (or just because it 'looks neat')
Writing ∠ABC with the vertex not in the middle, or naming an angle by a single letter where it is ambiguous
Using vague everyday words ('slanty line', 'pointy corner') instead of conventional terms and notation

learn.summary: A language objective for ages 11-13: pupils become fluent in conventional geometric terms and notation (AB for segments, ∠ABC with the vertex as the middle letter, ∥ and arrows for parallel, the right-angle square for perpendicular, tick marks for equal lengths, and the vocabulary of regular polygons and their reflective/rotational symmetry) and USE them accurately to describe, sketch and draw figures. The goal is productive, property-based communication, not reciting definitions. The dominant obstacle is the prototype phenomenon: pupils who can state a correct definition still name shapes by their prototypical picture, so a tilted square is denied its name and 'parallel'/'perpendicular' get muddled or wrongly thought to require equal lengths. Effective teaching ties each term to its defining property (not its look), shows figures tilted, scaled and as non-examples, and gives pupils a reason to USE the notation through barrier/describe-and-draw tasks where imprecise language visibly breaks communication.

activities.title: Barrier game: describe a figure so a partner can draw it
feedback: When the reconstruction comes out wrong, trace the mismatch back to the word or mark that caused it: 'Your partner drew this the wrong way round — which word or symbol could you add to make it unambiguous?'

If a pupil calls a perpendicular pair 'parallel' or vice versa, the partner's drawing will show the error; reground each term on its defining property (parallel: never meeting / constant distance; perpendicular: a square corner)
If a pupil refuses to name the tilted hexagon or square, point out that the partner still drew a valid shape — name follows the defining property, not the orientation

If a pupil claims the two rails can't be parallel because they are different lengths, have them show 'parallel' with their hands and check whether length changes whether the lines would ever meet if extended indefinitely, or whether the distance between them stays the same
activities.rationale: Because this is a productive-use objective, a describe-and-draw/barrier task is well-suited to growing it: when a term is misused or a prototype error creeps in, the drawing can visibly fail, giving the pupil meaningful feedback at the point of error. Using deliberately tilted shapes and unequal-length parallels is intended to surface the prototype and equal-length errors. This mechanism is a research-informed design proposal, not an established efficacy result.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use conventional terms and notations: points, lines, vertices, edges, planes, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, right angles, polygons, regular polygons and polygons with reflection and/or rotation symmetries' and 'use the standard conventions for labelling and referring to the sides and angles of triangles'.

Documented vocabulary confusions include swapping/confusing parallel and perpendicular and the belief that parallel lines must be the same length; remedied by prototype and 'nearly' examples presented in varied orientations.
learnerActions: Sit on one side of a barrier (screen, book, or divider) with a figure the partner cannot see: a tilted regular hexagon, a pair of parallel lines of clearly different lengths, and a perpendicular crossing

Describe the figure precisely enough that the unseen partner can reproduce it, naming which lines are parallel (∥ / arrows) and which are perpendicular (right-angle square), naming angles as ∠ABC with the vertex as the middle letter, and calling the hexagon 'regular' because its sides AND angles are equal
Place or speak the notation marks the partner needs — parallel arrows, right-angle squares, ∠ABC labels, equal-length tick marks
Compare the partner's drawing with the original and discuss where it diverged
Swap roles and repeat with a new figure
activities.intendedInsight: Precise words and marks make the drawing come out right while vague ones do not, so geometric language becomes a tool with consequences rather than a list to memorise.

activities.title: Label-and-rebuild: mark the notation and check it reconstructs
feedback: Highlight the specific mismatched mark rather than marking the whole answer wrong, and ask the pupil to say what that symbol means
If the vertex of ∠ABC is not the middle letter, show how the three-letter name points to a different corner and have them rewrite it
Where a point carries more than one angle, require the three-letter name so the angle is unambiguous
activities.rationale: Placing and checking notation builds the productive, property-based use the objective targets. An optional auto-drawer or partner reconstruction is intended to make the consequence of each mark concrete and localise the error for correction; where no auto-drawer exists, a partner is the default reconstructor.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use conventional terms and notations: points, lines, vertices, edges, planes, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, right angles, polygons, regular polygons and polygons with reflection and/or rotation symmetries' and 'use the standard conventions for labelling and referring to the sides and angles of triangles'.
learnerActions: Label a given figure on paper or screen using on-screen/drawn notation: ∥ arrows, right-angle squares, ∠ABC labels, 'regular', and equal-length tick marks
Have a partner (or an auto-drawer, if available) rebuild the figure from only your labels
Where the rebuild mismatches the original, find the misused term or misplaced mark and correct it
Deliberately include tilted shapes and unequal-length parallels so length and orientation errors show up
activities.intendedInsight: Notation is a precise instruction set: a mark in the wrong place or a term misused produces a different figure, so the marks carry real meaning.

activities.title: Defeat the prototype: name shapes by property across orientations
feedback: If a pupil names shapes correctly only when 'upright', re-present the figure tilted and ask which property changed (none)

If a pupil calls a polygon regular from only one condition or because it 'looks neat', show a counterexample with equal sides but unequal angles (a non-square rhombus) AND one with equal angles but unequal sides (a non-square rectangle), and tie 'regular' to both conditions holding together
A reveal-on-tap reference exposes the correct term but does not force the pupil to produce it, so follow it with a task where the pupil must name or label unaided
activities.rationale: The prototype phenomenon means even pupils who know a definition classify by a visual prototype; presenting varied orientations and non-examples and requiring property-based naming confronts this directly. Using both one-condition counterexamples ensures the 'equal sides OR equal angles but not both' error is addressed in full.
sourceClaims: The prototype phenomenon: more than half of even above-average learners recognise and name shapes by prototypical examples even when they can state the correct definition (concept image overrides definition), e.g. a tilted square is denied its name because prototypes are 'not slanted'; classification is often based on comparison to a visual prototype rather than properties.

Documented vocabulary confusions include swapping/confusing parallel and perpendicular and the belief that parallel lines must be the same length; remedied by prototype and 'nearly' examples presented in varied orientations.
learnerActions: Examine the same shape shown in many orientations (upright, tilted, rotated) and as near-miss non-examples
Decide and justify a name for each using the defining property — e.g. 'regular' only when sides AND angles are both equal — not its appearance

Compare a regular hexagon with an irregular polygon that has equal sides but unequal angles (e.g. a non-square rhombus), and separately with one that has equal angles but unequal sides (e.g. a non-square rectangle), and explain why neither of the latter two is regular
For a tilted square or hexagon, state that it keeps its name because the defining property still holds
Optionally tap a segment, angle, or line-pair in an interactive figure to reveal its correct term/notation (e.g. AB, ∠ABC with vertex B, ∥ or ⊥) and confirm a tilted square is still a square
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's name follows its defining properties, so orientation and scale do not change it, and 'regular' requires BOTH equal sides and equal angles — meeting only one condition is not enough.

activities.title: Symmetry by action: fold and rotate a regular polygon
feedback: If a pupil asserts a symmetry count without checking, have them fold or rotate to confirm or revise it
Connect the number of symmetry lines and the order of rotation to the polygon's equal sides and angles
activities.rationale: Connecting symmetry language to the actions of folding and rotating is intended to let pupils justify their claims and use the conventional symmetry vocabulary meaningfully — the vocabulary element being the part the KS3 claim supports (not the fold/rotate justification method, which is an unvalidated design proposal). A paper cut-out has real thickness and is only an approximation of the ideal plane figure; treat the folds and rotations as evidence about the mathematical shape represented, not about the card itself.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use conventional terms and notations: points, lines, vertices, edges, planes, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, right angles, polygons, regular polygons and polygons with reflection and/or rotation symmetries' and 'use the standard conventions for labelling and referring to the sides and angles of triangles'.
learnerActions: Take a cut-out regular hexagon (or other regular polygon) and fold it to find each line of reflective symmetry, counting them
Rotate the polygon over a fixed outline to find its order of rotational symmetry, counting the positions where it maps onto itself
State the result in conventional terms — e.g. a regular hexagon has 6 lines of reflective symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 6 — justified by the folding and rotating, not asserted
Optionally use rotation overlays or fold-line marks to record each symmetry found
activities.intendedInsight: Lines of symmetry and order of rotational symmetry are demonstrable facts about a figure, justified by physically folding and rotating rather than by memorised numbers.

activities.title: Match and categorise: receptive check with prototype distractors
feedback: Use ∥/⊥ and prototype distractors so a wrong match reveals the specific confusion to address
After a matching/categorising round, move to an open labelling or describe-and-draw task, because recognition does not show whether the pupil can produce the terms unaided
activities.rationale: Matching and categorising check receptive knowledge efficiently with targeted distractors. This is a scaffold: a fixed-answer format checks recognition but does not elicit open, productive language use, so it should feed into the barrier and labelling tasks.
sourceClaims: Documented vocabulary confusions include swapping/confusing parallel and perpendicular and the belief that parallel lines must be the same length; remedied by prototype and 'nearly' examples presented in varied orientations.
learnerActions: Match notation (∥, ⊥, ∠ABC) to the figure it describes, with distractors that swap parallel and perpendicular

Categorise polygons as regular or irregular, including a tilted regular hexagon and both an equal-sides-but-unequal-angles irregular polygon (non-square rhombus) and an equal-angles-but-unequal-sides irregular polygon (non-square rectangle)
Mark the right-angle and parallel symbols in a figure by drawing the symbol in the correct place
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can recognise correct terms and notation and distinguish regular from irregular even when the figure is tilted or a near-miss.

constraints: The teaching goal is productive, property-based USE of terms and notation to describe, sketch and draw — not reciting definitions; assess by how pupils use terms in context, not by asking them to define words.

Always include tilted, scaled and non-example figures (e.g. a tilted regular hexagon, unequal-length parallel rails) so naming is forced onto defining properties; prototypical upright figures alone let prototype errors hide.

Reveal-on-tap interactive references and match/categorise tasks are scaffolds that check or expose receptive knowledge; they do not force the pupil to PRODUCE terms, so pair them with open labelling or describe-and-draw work.

Explicitly correct the 'parallel lines must be the same length' error and the swapping of parallel/perpendicular by regrounding each on its defining property (parallel: never meeting / constant distance; perpendicular: a square corner).

Tie 'regular' to BOTH equal sides AND equal angles; include counterexamples that satisfy only one condition (equal sides only, e.g. a non-square rhombus; equal angles only, e.g. a non-square rectangle).
Require three-letter angle naming (∠ABC with the vertex as the middle letter) whenever a point carries more than one angle, so the angle is unambiguous.

Paper/card cut-outs used for symmetry have real thickness and approximate the ideal plane figure; treat folds and rotations as evidence about the mathematical shape represented, and label any ideal zero-thickness screen model as a model.

A 3D environment is not needed for this planar vocabulary goal and adds cost without serving it; this is a scoped observation for this objective, not a universal rule that 3D adds nothing to geometry learning.

An in-role 'illustrator' conversation can elicit productive term use and let a partner probe misuse, but its reconstruction payload is essentially the barrier game; the persona adds little beyond the describe-and-draw task here (not a claim that dialogue cannot teach).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims cited (KS3 statutory wording, the prototype phenomenon, and NCETM vocabulary-confusion remedies) support the general teaching principles but do not establish that these specific activities were tested or are comparatively more effective than alternatives.

The fold/rotate symmetry method is an unvalidated design proposal; the cited KS3 claim supports only the requirement to use conventional symmetry terminology, not the folding/rotating justification technique itself.

The legacy entry claimed a fixed quiz 'cannot fully assess open, productive language use' and that an auto-drawer gives feedback 'exactly when a term is misused'; these are reasonable design observations, not established efficacy claims — retained as scoped scaffolding limits/proposals, not universal laws.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a figure in front of the child — a tilted regular hexagon, a pair of parallel lines of clearly different lengths, and a perpendicular crossing. Listen for how they USE the conventional terms and notation in context; do not ask them to define any word.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tilted, unequal-length figure forces property-based language: a child who owns the terms names the slanted shape correctly and treats unequal-length lines as parallel; a child anchored to prototypes reverts to 'slanty line', denies the tilted square/hexagon its name, or muddles ∥ and ⊥. topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Ruler and compass constructions
topic.description: Use ruler and compasses to perform standard constructions: perpendicular bisector of a line segment, perpendicular to a line from or at a given point, and bisecting an angle
evidence: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment using compasses and a straight edge
Construct an angle bisector and verify by measuring both halves
Construct a perpendicular from a point to a line using compasses only
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has only a ruler and a pair of compasses, can they construct a line that cuts another line segment exactly in half at a right angle — without using a protractor?

pedagogy.summary: At age 12-14 pupils learn the classical ruler-and-compass constructions — perpendicular bisector of a segment, perpendicular to a line from/at a point, and angle bisector — using ONLY compasses and a straight edge, with no measuring of lengths or angles. The essential shift is from DRAWING (find a midpoint with a ruler, judge a right angle by eye or protractor) to CONSTRUCTING (produce the result from geometric properties). The unifying property is the rhombus: equal-radius arcs from two points create four equal lengths, so the figure is a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other and bisect their angles. Taught this way, every construction is a deduction, and the commonest error — changing the compass radius between the two endpoints — is instantly diagnosable: unequal radii give a KITE (diagonals perpendicular but NOT bisecting), so the line is perpendicular but misses the midpoint. Because compasses are usually new at KS3, motor coordination is a real, separable hurdle; developing the concept first with dynamic geometry lets pupils reason about 'perfect' circles before wrestling the physical tool.
bestPractices: Teach the draw-vs-construct distinction explicitly: a construction uses geometric properties (equidistance), not measurement; require pupils to leave their construction arcs as evidence of method
Anchor every construction in the rhombus/isosceles-triangle property (equal radii → rhombus → diagonals perpendicularly bisect and bisect the angle), so steps are deductions, not a memorised routine
Make the equal-radius rule meaningful via the kite counter-case: unequal arcs build a kite whose diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so the midpoint is missed
Ensure the compass opening exceeds half the segment so the arcs intersect above and below; discuss why a smaller radius fails and a huge one is just wasteful

Present non-standard (diagonal, rotated) segments and angles, not only horizontal/vertical prototypes, and give time to build compass dexterity — ideally after establishing the idea with dynamic geometry
keyRepresentations: Two equal-radius circles/arcs from the segment ends and the rhombus they define
The rhombus-around-a-diagonal image (segment as one diagonal; the construction produces the other)
Kite counter-example (unequal radii) showing perpendicular-but-not-bisecting diagonals
Isosceles triangle whose altitude bisects the base at right angles and bisects the apex angle
Dynamic-geometry compass/straightedge for concept-before-dexterity
commonMisconceptions: Changing the compass radius between the two endpoints, constructing a kite instead of a rhombus, so the line is perpendicular but does not pass through the midpoint
Drawing rather than constructing — using a ruler to find the midpoint and a protractor/eye for the right angle — and leaving no construction marks
Opening the compasses to less than half the segment, so the arcs never intersect
Memorising the steps as an isolated routine with no link to the properties of circles and rhombuses
Treating the construction as valid only for horizontal/vertical segments (prototype-orientation bias)

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–14 construct a perpendicular bisector, a perpendicular to a line from a point off it or at a point on it, and an angle bisector using compasses and an unmarked straight edge. Explain the equal-distance and congruent-triangle properties, leaving arcs visible rather than finding positions by measurement. Equal-radius circles centred at segment endpoints yield a perpendicular bisector; unequal radii can still give a perpendicular common chord, but it misses the segment midpoint. Optional dynamic geometry can separate reasoning from tool dexterity; physical compass practice remains part of the proposed tasks. Verification by measurement may check accuracy afterwards, but it does not justify the construction.

activities.title: Construct the perpendicular bisector with compasses and straight edge
feedback: If the line does not cross PQ at its midpoint, check whether the two sets of arcs have equal radii: unequal radii make a KITE (the line is perpendicular to PQ but does not bisect it), equal radii make a rhombus (the line is perpendicular to PQ AND bisects it).

If equal-radius arcs do not cross at two points, check the opening: below half PQ they do not meet; at exactly half they touch only at the midpoint. Use an opening greater than half PQ and allow enough space on the page.

If there are no arcs on the page and the midpoint was found with a ruler or the angle judged by eye, that is drawing, not constructing: redo it so every point of the line is equidistant from P and Q, shown by equal arcs.
Keeping the compass width unchanged between P and Q is the whole point — it is what forces the rhombus.
activities.rationale: Constructing is a doing-and-reasoning skill: pupils must physically execute equal-radius arcs and justify them from the rhombus/equidistance property. A finished static picture cannot be manipulated and does not require the pupil to perform the arcs or articulate the reasoning, so it serves at most as a labelled reference for the rhombus property. Leaving arcs visible makes the method inspectable and distinguishes construction from measurement.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.

A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Take a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal or vertical), a pair of compasses and a straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor.
Open the compasses to MORE than half of PQ; discuss why an opening of half or less means the arcs only touch or never meet, and why an enormous opening just wastes space.
Place the compass point on P and sweep an arc above and below the segment; WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on Q and sweep again so the arcs cross at two points.
Rule the straight line through the two crossing points, leaving all construction arcs visible as evidence of method.
Explain why the line passes through the midpoint at 90°: the four equal radii form a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other.
Repeat on segments at several different orientations, not only horizontal/vertical ones.
activities.intendedInsight: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from P and Q. Equal-radius arcs locate two such points, and the straight line through them is the perpendicular bisector; visible arcs make the method inspectable, though arcs alone do not prove they were placed correctly.

activities.title: Bisect an angle using the same equal-arc idea
feedback: If the line does not appear to split the angle equally, check that the two inner arcs were drawn with the same radius from each arm-crossing point.

Leave your arcs visible — they show you constructed the bisector from equal lengths rather than measuring halves with a protractor. (The congruent halves follow from the equal arcs, so no measuring is needed to justify it.)
activities.rationale: Equal lengths and congruent triangles provide the justification for the angle bisector. After constructing, measuring both angles can be an optional check of drawing accuracy; it is not the construction method or a proof. This is a proposed property-based activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.

A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Take a marked angle (try one at a non-standard orientation), compasses and a straight edge.
Place the compass point at the vertex and sweep an arc that crosses both arms of the angle at two points.
WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on each of those two crossing points in turn and sweep equal arcs that meet inside the angle.
Rule the line from the vertex through that meeting point, leaving the arcs visible.
Explain how this reuses the equal-radius property: equal lengths from the vertex and equal arcs from the arm-crossings force the two halves to be congruent, so the line bisects the angle.
activities.intendedInsight: The same equidistance principle that bisects a segment also bisects an angle — one property, reused, rather than a second memorised routine.

activities.title: See the rhombus break into a kite with a dynamic compass (concept-before-dexterity scaffold)
feedback: When the figure flips to KITE, note exactly where the line crosses PQ relative to the midpoint — that gap is why unequal radii fail.
If you can state why the rhombus's crossing line bisects PQ but the kite's does not, you are reasoning from the property; move on to building the same construction by hand.
activities.rationale: A dynamic-geometry tool can separate the concept (equidistance locus, rhombus-vs-kite) from manual dexterity, and may let pupils reason about ideal 'perfect' circles before coping with the practical difficulties of real compasses, which some pupils may still find hard to control. The live slider and label flip are intended to make the failure mode concrete. This is a proposed scaffold: it does not develop the manual construction skill, which must be practised separately on paper, and its effectiveness over other media is untested.
sourceClaims: A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Use an on-screen compass whose radius locks once set: plant it on P and sweep an arc, then on Q and sweep an equal arc so the two equal circles cross at two points.
Rule the line through the crossings and observe the highlighted locus showing every point on it is equidistant from P and Q.

Now drag a slider that shrinks the second circle's radius (keeping it large enough that the two circles still cross); watch the crossing points drift, the line slide sideways while staying perpendicular to PQ, and the label flip from RHOMBUS to KITE — the line visibly misses the midpoint.
Articulate in your own words why 'keep the compass fixed' is a consequence of the rhombus property, not an arbitrary rule.
Transfer to real compasses and paper once the concept is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: When two circles cross, their common chord is perpendicular to the line through their centres. With equal radii, that chord also bisects PQ; with unequal radii it does not. Keep both circles crossing during the comparison, and explain the equal-radius rule rather than memorising it.

activities.title: Diagnose: construction or drawing? Which radius? Which shape failed?
feedback: For the 8 cm segment, any opening at or below 4 cm leaves arcs that cannot cross on both sides (at exactly 4 cm they only touch at the midpoint); the opening must exceed half the length.
The diagram with no arcs cannot be shown to be a construction — without equal arcs there is no evidence the equidistance property was used.
Unequal arcs give a kite: perpendicular, yes, but the line through the crossings does not bisect PQ (only PQ bisects it), so the line misses the midpoint.
activities.rationale: Questions of this kind assess the reasoning behind the construction and surface the specific misconceptions (radius too small, kite error, drawing vs constructing). They complement but cannot replace the performance task, since recognising a correct diagram is not the same as producing one.
